Regulation Status: Afghanistan under the Islamic Emirate has no AI-specific legislation, decree or draft instrument, and no sectoral AI rules. Pre-2021 general instruments such as the Cyber Crime Law (2017) contain no provisions written for AI systems, and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology has issued no AI governance measure while the state itself deploys AI-enabled CCTV and facial-recognition surveillance in Kabul without a legal framework.
Policy Lever: No policy lever is applied to AI: there is no national AI strategy, no published guidance, no sandbox, no funding line and no body with an AI mandate. Government engagement with AI is limited to procuring and operating AI-enabled surveillance systems.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in the Islamic Emirate's supreme leadership and ministries, with no dedicated AI regulator, no coordination mechanism and no provincial rule-making role. Courts, ombudsman structures and independent oversight bodies capable of reviewing AI-related state action do not operate independently.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making on technology excludes industry, civil society and academia, and domestic academic discussion of AI remains without institutional channel. The unrecognized administration does not participate in international AI governance processes or declarations.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI rule, penalty, enforcement body or monitoring mechanism exists.

Regulation Status: Albania has no AI statute in force; the one binding AI-specific instrument is Council of Ministers Decision No. 479, dated 24 July 2024, approving a methodology and technical standards for AI use in the Republic of Albania, which reaches public institutions only. A full draft Law 'On Artificial Intelligence' of 106 articles in 9 chapters, transposing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, was published by AKSHI for public consultation from 29 May to 26 June 2026 and is not yet enacted. AI systems otherwise fall under Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection and Law No. 25/2024 on Cybersecurity, which contain no AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through sub-legal acts and administrative capacity rather than statute: Decision No. 479/2024 sets AI standards for public bodies, while AKSHI operates an AI laboratory and deploys systems such as Diella in e-Albania and public procurement. Funding is project-based, with no operating regulatory sandbox or AI-specific procurement rules, and no body yet holds a legal AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Oversight is split between AKSHI as de facto lead for government AI and sectoral bodies covering data protection, cybersecurity, finance and competition, coordinated informally. Courts have begun to engage with AI through litigation over the Diella system, and no subnational tier plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through the government's online public consultation portal, where civil society organisations such as SCiDEV commented on the draft AI law and the draft National AI Strategy 2025-2030, with no permanent multi-stakeholder forum for industry or universities. Internationally, Albania signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence in June 2026, moved its ratification through the Council of Ministers to Parliament in 2026, and aligns with the EU AI Act under accession negotiations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through data-protection and cybersecurity law, as no AI-specific penalties, supervisory authority or audit regime is yet in force.
Specific Laws: Council of Ministers Decision No. 479, dated 24 July 2024, on the methodology and technical standards for the use of artificial intelligence in the Republic of Albania (2024), Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection (2024), Law No. 25/2024 on Cybersecurity (2024), Law on Electronic Governance (amended), National Strategy for Digital Agenda 2022-2026, National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025-2030 (2025), Draft Law 'On Artificial Intelligence' in public consultation 29 May - 26 June 2026, Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 15 June 2026, ratification bill before Parliament 2026)

Regulation Status: Algeria governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024), whose six pillars include a future regulatory framework that has not been drafted into legislation. Binding obligations touching AI come only from general instruments — Law No. 25-11 amending Law No. 18-07 on personal data protection and the cybersecurity decrees — none of which is written for AI systems. Activity in 2026 was institutional: the Prime Minister reviewed strategy progress on 25 May 2026, an interministerial follow-up commission was installed on 5 August 2026, and five thematic commissions on data and infrastructure, financing, large language models, AI doctoral training and continuing AI education were installed on 8 September 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy works through the non-binding 2024 strategy, ministry-led coordination structures, and state funding for AI skills, research and startups, including a target of 50,000 AI specialists by 2030 and a national AI and data research centre. No binding AI instrument, published AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and the bodies involved hold advisory rather than compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the executive, with the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research chairing implementation alongside the AI Council, the Scientific Council for Artificial Intelligence and the High Commission for Digitalisation. Coordination was formalized in 2026 through an interministerial follow-up commission and five thematic commissions, while sub-national authorities have no role and no court or independent body shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Academia dominates the domestic process through the Scientific Council for Artificial Intelligence and the higher education ministry, while industry input is informal and civil society is absent from AI policy forums. Internationally, Algeria endorses declarations — the African Union Continental AI Strategy and the 2026 UNESCO Riyadh declaration — without binding treaty or standards-body commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under general data protection and cybersecurity law, with no AI-specific penalty, decision, authority or audit programme in place.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024), Law No. 25-11 amending Law No. 18-07 on Personal Data Protection (2025), Presidential Decree No. 26-07 on Cybersecurity Units in Public Institutions (2026), Presidential Decree No. 25-298 amending Presidential Decree No. 20-05 on Information Systems Security (2025), African Union Continental AI Strategy (2024)

Regulation Status: Andorra has no dedicated AI statute; AI is addressed through adapted general law, principally the Penal Code reform approved on 15 July 2026, which criminalises AI-generated non-consensual sexual imagery, and the Llei 29/2021 de protecció de dades personals as amended by Llei 12/2024. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS 225), signed on 5 September 2024, remains unratified, and the February 2024 Codi d'Ètica de la Intel·ligència Artificial is voluntary.
Policy Lever: Policy rests on the voluntary Code of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence, the Estratègia de Transformació Digital 2030 and business digitalisation grants, with a single AI-written criminal provision as the only binding lever. Institutional capacity sits with the Agència Andorrana de Protecció de Dades under data-protection law and with an advisory data-intelligence unit inside Andorra Digital.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the national executive and the APDA, without sectoral AI regulators, a formal coordination mechanism or any parish-level role. Independent scrutiny comes from the APDA's advisory interventions in the legislature and from ordinary courts applying data-protection and criminal law.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy-making is government-led, with no standing roles for industry, NGOs, unions or the Universitat d'Andorra. External engagement is limited to early signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and alignment with UNESCO and OECD principles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI is incidental to data-protection supervision by the APDA and to ordinary criminal prosecution, with no AI audits, AI-specific decisions or dedicated AI authority.
Specific Laws: Llei 29/2021 de protecció de dades personals (LQPD) (2021), Llei 12/2024 (amendment to LQPD) (2024), Codi d'Ètica de la Intel·ligència Artificial d'Andorra (2024), Reforma del Codi penal criminalising AI-generated non-consensual sexual images (approved 15 July 2026), Estratègia de Transformació Digital 2030 (2024), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS 225 (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: Angola's horizontal AI framework remains a bill: the MINTTICS Proposta de Lei sobre Inteligência Artificial, presented in September 2025 with risk-based classification, strict liability, mandatory watermarking and extraterritorial reach, obtained general approval in the National Assembly but has not been enacted. The only binding rules touching AI in force are in Law No. 6/26 Against False Information on the Internet, promulgated 21 July 2026 and published 4 August 2026, which defines deepfakes and artificial dissemination networks and imposes platform duties for that content type. A revised Personal Data Protection Law containing a chapter on data processing by artificial intelligence systems went through public consultation in 2025 and is still pending.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the ICT Strategic Framework 2023-2027, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise led by MINTTICS, and bills before the National Assembly rather than instruments in force. No dedicated AI funding line, procurement rule, sandbox or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in MINTTICS at central government level, with the Agency for Data Protection confined to data-protection supervision and no standing coordination mechanism. Provinces play no role and independent review of AI questions has not occurred.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through time-limited public consultations on the AI bill and the data protection revision, supplemented by professional forums such as the Fórum Nacional de Inteligência Artificial. Internationally Angola engages via UNESCO and African Union processes; domestically no industry, civil society or academic body holds a standing role.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist for AI-related content offences under Law No. 6/26 and large fines and prison terms sit in the unenacted AI bill, but no AI-based enforcement decision, dedicated authority or audit practice exists.
Specific Laws: Law No. 6/26 Against False Information on the Internet (2026), Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (proposed 2025, general parliamentary approval 2025-2026), Draft Personal Data Protection Law revising Law No. 22/11 with a chapter on processing by artificial intelligence systems (public consultation 2025), ICT Strategic Framework 2023-2027 (Livro Branco das TIC / LBTIC), Personal Data Protection Law No. 22/11 (2011)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific legislation is in force and no AI bill is before Parliament, although the Prime Minister has confirmed that draft AI legislation has been prepared. Governance of AI-related harms rests on the Data Protection Act, 2013 and the Electronic Crimes Act, 2013, which contain no provisions written for AI; the UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report launched on 24 June 2025 identifies modernisation of these frameworks, including impact assessments for high-risk applications, as an outstanding gap.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise completed with the Ministry of Information, Communication Technologies, Utilities and Energy and an AI policy focal point inside that ministry, with no national AI strategy adopted. Deployment projects such as Project Optimus and a planned government data centre with AI capability proceed without a sandbox, AI procurement rules or dedicated funding programmes.
Governance Type: AI matters are concentrated in one ministry with a single designated focal point, supported by episodic workshops rather than a standing coordination body. Telecommunications oversight through the Telecommunications Division and the regional ECTEL framework carries no AI mandate, and no judicial or independent review of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation has been limited to one-off UNESCO-sponsored workshops and conferences involving ministries, industry, civil society and the University of the West Indies, with no standing consultative body. International engagement is the most developed channel, spanning the Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI (2023), UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology, the Commonwealth AI Consortium and the CARICOM-endorsed Caribbean AI Roadmap.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent: no AI obligations exist to enforce, no authority holds an AI remit, and oversight is limited to the single 2025 readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2013 (No. 10 of 2013), Electronic Crimes Act, 2013, UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report for Antigua and Barbuda (2025), Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI (2023)

Regulation Status: Argentina has no enacted binding AI-specific legislation at national level; the Personal Data Protection Law 25.326 (2000) remains the operative instrument, supplemented by Disposición AAIP 2/2023 on Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence and SIGEN Resolución 197/2026 approving an AI control guide for public-sector internal audit. Several AI bills are before Congress, including the framework bill that obtained a majority committee dictamen in the Chamber of Deputies and the Executive's May 2026 bill creating AI-operated corporate forms, while President Milei has publicly committed to keeping AI development free of preventive regulation. Coverage of private-sector or high-risk AI uses rests on general data-protection, consumer and sectoral rules.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by soft instruments and investment incentives rather than binding rules: the 2019 Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, Resolución 90/2021, AAIP Resolución 161/2023 and Disposición 2/2023, and the 2026 SIGEN AI control guide, alongside the RIGI incentive regime attracting AI data-centre investment. No body holds a statutory AI mandate or compliance powers over AI systems.
Governance Type: Governance is fragmented and lead-body-plus-sectoral in form: the Secretaría de Innovación, Ciencia y Tecnología coordinates AI policy, the AAIP covers data protection, SIGEN covers public-sector AI controls, and no formal inter-agency mechanism links them. Provinces act autonomously, as Buenos Aires Province's Decreto 742/2026 shows, and courts intervene only case by case.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society take part through congressional committee hearings and AAIP consultations rather than standing bodies, and the government's 2026 posture has favoured dialogue with technology investors. Internationally Argentina adheres to non-binding instruments and holds observer status in Council of Europe AI standard-setting, without signing the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through the AAIP's general data-protection powers under Law 25.326, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or audit reporting in place.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection Law 25.326 (2000), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ArgenIA (2019), Resolución 90/2021 – Programa de Inteligencia Artificial, AAIP Resolución 161/2023 – Programa de Transparencia y Protección de Datos Personales en el uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, Disposición AAIP 2/2023 – Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence, BCRA Comunicación A 7724 (2023), SIGEN Resolución 197/2026 – Guía de Controles Inteligencia Artificial, Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones under Law 27.742 (2024) extended by Decreto 105/2026, Decreto 742/2026 of the Province of Buenos Aires – Marco Provincial para el Desarrollo, Uso y Gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial (subnational), Bill 3003-D-2024 on responsible AI (pending, majority committee dictamen), Executive bill reforming the Ley General de Sociedades to create AI-operated companies (2026, pending), data-protection reform bills 1751-D-2026 and 3397-D-2026 (pending)

Regulation Status: No domestic AI-specific binding instrument exists; the only binding AI text touching Armenia is the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (STCE n°225), signed on 27 January 2026 and not yet ratified. AI appears in national law only through the August 2026 amendment to the Law on the Structure and Activities of the Government, which renamed the Ministry of High-Tech Industry as the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence and gave it responsibility for AI and cloud computing policy. General instruments such as the Law on Personal Data Protection and the Law on Cybersecurity, in force since 4 January 2026, contain no provision written for AI.
Policy Lever: Armenia governs AI through funding and promotion rather than regulation: state subsidies for high-performance computing, the Firebird and Eleveight AI data centres, Law No. HO-498-N on State Support for the High-Tech Sector, the AI Virtual Institute, and an AI literacy framework. The ministry gained a statutory AI remit in August 2026, but it is a policy-development mandate without inspection, approval or sanctioning powers.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in a single executive body, the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence, renamed in August 2026 to reflect its AI mandate, with no dedicated AI regulator, no formal inter-agency coordination mechanism and no subnational layer. Independent scrutiny is limited to occasional expert and media commentary on AI infrastructure projects.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is dominated by the government and technology industry partners, with universities contributing research capacity and civil society consulted only through occasional forums. International engagement is the strongest channel, anchored by the Council of Europe Framework Convention signature, EU4Digital cooperation and bilateral AI cooperation with the United States.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI obligations does not exist because no AI-specific duties or penalties have been enacted, leaving only general data protection and cybersecurity powers available.
Specific Laws: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (STCE n°225) (signed 2026), Law on the Structure and Activities of the Government as amended to rename the Ministry of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence (2026), Law No. HO-498-N on State Support for the High-Tech Sector (2025), Law of the Republic of Armenia on Cybersecurity (in force 2026), Law No. 49-ZR on the Protection of Personal Data (2015), Digital Transformation Strategy (2021-2025)

Regulation Status: Australia has no AI Act: the National AI Plan of 2 December 2025 confirmed reliance on existing laws and sector regulators instead of the 2024 mandatory guardrails proposal, and the Prime Minister's 15 July 2026 announcement of legislated Australian Standards for AI, endorsed by National Cabinet on 26 August 2026, targets legislation in early 2027 starting with large data centres and model training inputs. Binding AI obligations in force are domain-specific: the eSafety Age-Restricted Material Codes (effective 9 March 2026) impose age-assurance duties on generative AI and AI companion services, and the Digital Transformation Agency's Policy for the responsible use of AI in government binds 94 non-corporate Commonwealth entities. The cross-sector automated decision-making transparency obligation added to Australian Privacy Principle 1 by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 commences 10 December 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law plus funding: voluntary guardrails, Guidance for AI Adoption, a funded AI Safety Institute working with the Australian Signals Directorate and CSIRO, and a coordinating Office of AI established in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet on 15 July 2026. Binding levers remain confined to the online safety codes, the public-sector AI policy and the forthcoming Privacy Act automated decision-making obligation.
Governance Type: Oversight is dispersed across independent regulators with a new central coordinator in PM&C and shared Commonwealth-state commitments through National Cabinet. States implement national settings and manage their own agency AI use; courts and tribunals intervene case by case.
Actor Involvement: Government consults industry, creators, civil society and researchers through published processes such as the data centre and frontier AI consultation paper and the OAIC automated decision-making consultation, with no standing statutory advisory body. International engagement is extensive, spanning the OECD, GPAI, the AI safety institute network and international standards development.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is carried out by existing regulators using penalty-backed powers, with eSafety taking published action against generative AI services and OAIC preparing to enforce the December 2026 automated decision-making obligation.
Specific Laws: Privacy Act 1988 as amended by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (automated decision-making transparency obligation commencing 10 December 2026), Online Safety Act 2021 and the Age-Restricted Material (Phase 2) Industry Codes (2025, in force 9 March 2026), Australian Consumer Law (Competition and Consumer Act 2010), Copyright Act 1968, National AI Plan (2025), Voluntary AI Safety Standard (2024), Guidance for AI Adoption (2025), Policy for the responsible use of AI in government version 2.0 (2025)

Regulation Status: Austria regulates AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act, amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI that entered into force on 24 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to 2 August 2028; prohibitions, AI literacy, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency apply today. Nationally, the Nationalrat adopted an amendment to the Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz and the Verwaltungsstrafgesetz on 23 September 2026 creating the legal basis for chatbots, fully automated decisions and no-stop procedures in administrative proceedings. National execution lags: no implementing act exists, and the notifying and market surveillance authorities required by Article 70 remain undesignated.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act plus two national AI-specific statutes (the KI-Servicestelle provisions in the KommAustria-Gesetz and TKG 2021, and the 2026 AVG/VStG amendment), complemented by RTR and Datenschutzbehörde guidance and by funding and public-sector AI programmes such as aws AI Adoption, AIM AT 2030 funding, Digital Überall Plus and Public AI. Institutional capacity is advisory: the KI-Servicestelle and the eleven-member KI-Beirat advise, and no body holds AI Act compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is federal and centred on the RTR KI-Servicestelle as information hub, with the Datenschutzbehörde and sectoral regulators applying their own remits and the Bundeskanzleramt digitalisation section leading AI Act implementation. Coordination runs through the inter-ministerial AI Policy Forum, the KI-Beirat, the AI Stakeholder Forum and the Public AI Initiative, which also links the Länder and municipalities; courts and the Datenschutzbehörde review individual AI uses.
Actor Involvement: Structured consultation runs through the AI Stakeholder Forum and ministerial Begutachtung procedures, with the KI-Beirat giving academic and legal experts a standing advisory seat; industry and civil society participate as consultees rather than as permanent members. Internationally, Austria acts through the European AI Board, the OECD and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process.
Enforcement Level: AI Act penalties are legally available but unenforceable in practice because Austria has designated no market surveillance authority and passed no penalties regime, leaving data protection law as the only route under which AI decisions have been taken.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), AVG and VStG amendment on digitalisation and AI in administrative procedures (2026), KommAustria-Gesetz amendment establishing KI-Servicestelle / BGBl. I Nr. 6/2024 (2024), TKG 2021 §194a (2024 amendment), Digital Austria Act 2.0 (2025), Public AI Initiative (2026), KI-Maßnahmenpaket (2025), AIM AT 2030 / Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030 (2021), KI-Umsetzungsplan 2024 (2024), Austrian Data Protection Act / DSG (2018, amended), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016)

Regulation Status: Azerbaijan's primary AI governance instrument remains the AI Strategy 2025–2028 (Presidential Decree No. 530, March 2025), which is non-binding but mandates establishing a dedicated AI legal framework by 2027. The April 2026 Criminal Code amendments (Articles 148-2 and 242-1) introduced the first binding AI-specific criminal penalties—targeting deepfakes and non-consensual AI-generated content—but these are narrow, use-case-specific provisions rather than horizontal AI regulation. No comprehensive binding AI law is in force or in active parliamentary process.
Policy Lever: Policy relies on presidential strategies (AI Strategy 2025–2028, Digital Economy Strategy 2026–2029) and targeted criminal code amendments; there is one binding instrument (the April 2026 criminal penalties) limited to specific AI misuse. The strategy mentions preferential loans and a planned AI innovation hub, but no operational sandbox or mature suite of guidance exists, and AI oversight capacity sits within the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport without dedicated AI staffing.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralized: the Presidential Administration drives AI strategy via decree, with the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport as the lead implementing body and no independent AI regulator. Azerbaijan is a unitary state with no subnational AI role; courts may apply the new criminal provisions but no standing independent review mechanism for AI exists.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia have limited structured input, mainly through working groups referenced in strategy documentation, while domestic civil society engagement is minimal given Azerbaijan's constrained NGO environment. Internationally, Azerbaijan participates in Turkic States AI cooperation frameworks, maintains bilateral AI partnerships with Turkey and Israel, and is a Council of Europe member engaged in digital governance discussions, though it has not signed the CoE AI Convention (CETS 225).
Enforcement Level: A narrow sanctions framework exists via the April 2026 criminal code amendments (imprisonment up to three years for AI-generated deepfakes/non-consensual content), but no dedicated AI enforcement authority exists, no AI-specific enforcement actions have been recorded, and no routine monitoring or public AI compliance reporting is in place.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2025–2028 (Presidential Decree No. 530, 2025), Digital Economy Development Strategy 2026–2029 (Presidential Decree, 2025), Criminal Code amendments introducing Articles 148-2 and 242-1 on illegal AI use (2026), Action Plan for Accelerating Digital Development 2026–2028 (2026)

Regulation Status: AI obligations in The Bahamas sit inside sectoral and general instruments: clause 2.8 of URCA's Code of Practice for Content Regulation (Revised 2024) requires licensed broadcasters to maintain internal policies on AI and synthetic media, section 18 of the Electricity Act, 2024 empowers URCA to make AI regulations for the electricity sector on stated principles, and the Data Protection Act, 2025 defines profiling to include artificial intelligence and restricts decisions based solely on automated processing. The Speech from the Throne of May 2026 committed the government to an Artificial Intelligence Governance Act establishing a national AI commission, and the Ministry of Innovation and National Development announced in June 2026 a national AI Committee to draft that legislation, which has not been tabled. Coverage therefore remains narrow and content-specific rather than horizontal.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are thin: a single binding AI provision in URCA's broadcasting content code, an unused regulation-making power for AI in the electricity sector, announced AI literacy and skills funding financed by an IDB loan, and a national AI Committee tasked with drafting the first AI legislation. No national AI strategy, guidance suite, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule has been published.
Governance Type: Governance is sectorally fragmented: URCA regulates AI use by communications and broadcasting licensees and may regulate it in electricity, while the Data Protection Commissioner oversees automated processing and profiling. Coordination is informal pending the promised national AI commission, there is no subnational tier, and judicial or tribunal review of AI matters has not been exercised.
Actor Involvement: Structured domestic input on AI has come through regulator consultations, notably URCA's 2024 content code consultation with broadcast licensees and the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner's 2025 consultation on the draft Data Protection Bill. Internationally the country participates in CARICOM and UNESCO Caribbean AI processes and ILO discussions, without treaty-level AI commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of the few AI provisions rests on URCA's general licensing powers, and no AI-related sanction, decision or audit has been published.
Specific Laws: Electricity Act (2024), URCA Code of Practice for Content Regulation (Revised 2024, ECS 78/2024), Data Protection Act (2025), Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act (2003), Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (announced in the Speech from the Throne, 2026, not yet tabled)

Regulation Status: Bahrain's standalone 38-article Artificial Intelligence Regulation Law, unanimously approved by the Shura Council in April 2024, was returned by the Cabinet with objections and was still not enacted when the Shura Legislative and Legal Affairs Committee described continued drafting on an EU- and Arab-model basis in June 2026. The instrument that applies today is the Information & eGovernment Authority's General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence (Version 1.0, 30 July 2025), an AI-specific directive limited to government entities, alongside the Personal Data Protection Law (2018) and the Information Technology Crimes Law (2014), which contain no provisions written for AI.
Policy Lever: Bahrain relies on an administrative public-sector directive plus guidance — the General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence, the GCC Guiding Manual on the Ethics of AI Use, and World Economic Forum-developed AI procurement guidelines — combined with funded skills and talent programmes run by Tamkeen, the iGA and Bahrain Polytechnic. The regulatory sandbox the government proposed as an alternative to the draft AI law has not been established, and no body holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Information & eGovernment Authority under the Ministerial Committee for Information Technology and Communication, with sectoral authorities such as the Central Bank of Bahrain and the Personal Data Protection Authority touching AI only through existing remits. Governorates play no role, and no court or independent body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Policy development draws on government bodies, state-linked institutions, industry-facing agencies such as Tamkeen and academic input from Bahrain Polytechnic, with no standing advisory body for non-governmental actors. Domestic civil society has no documented role, while international engagement runs through the GCC Ministerial Committee for eGovernment and UNESCO's ethics and readiness work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to general data protection and cybercrime powers, as the penalty regime of the draft AI Regulation Law is not in force and no AI oversight unit has been established.
Specific Laws: Draft Artificial Intelligence Regulation Law (38 articles, Shura Council approved April 2024, pending in the Council of Representatives), General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence Version 1.0 (2025), GCC Guiding Manual on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Use (adopted 2025), Personal Data Protection Law No. 30 of 2018, Information Technology Crimes Law No. 60 of 2014

Regulation Status: Bangladesh has no AI-specific statute; the Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026, passed on 30 June 2026, inserts obligations on removal of harmful and defamatory AI-generated content and platform response timeframes, giving the country one narrow binding AI rule. The National AI Policy 2026-2030 (Draft v2, 9 February 2026) completed public consultation on 8 February 2026 and remains unadopted, while the Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Ministry said on 2 September 2026 that a draft AI law will go to parliament after expert review. Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 and National Data Governance Ordinance 2025, gazetted on 9 November 2025, touch AI only incidentally.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a drafting ministry rather than statutory levers: the ICT Division steers the draft National AI Policy 2026-2030, and the single binding AI measure sits inside cyber security law enforced by the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission and the National Cyber Security Agency. Proposed sandboxes, an AI cloud and research funding remain on paper.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the ICT Division of the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, supported by a cross-ministry National AI Policy Steering Committee and, for AI-generated content, the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission and National Cyber Security Agency. No subnational tier and no independent review body shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society entered the process through a time-limited public consultation on the draft National AI Policy and through the UNESCO-supported readiness assessment, in consultative rather than standing roles. International engagement runs through UNESCO and UN digital governance forums.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only through cyber security content powers exercised by the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission and National Cyber Security Agency, with no published decisions or audits under the new AI-content provisions.
Specific Laws: Cyber Security (Amendment) Act (2026), Cyber Security Ordinance (2025), Personal Data Protection Ordinance (2025), National Data Governance Ordinance (2025), National AI Policy 2026-2030 (Draft v2, 2026), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020)

Regulation Status: Barbados governs AI through general law only: the Data Protection Act, 2019-29 covers automated processing and profiling and requires data protection impact assessments for decisions based on automated processing, but contains nothing written for AI systems. No AI bill has been laid before Parliament, and the Cybercrime Bill, 2024 debate concerned online speech rather than AI. Government activity in 2026 consisted of ministerial statements, skills programmes and international advocacy rather than legislation.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to capacity-building and rhetoric: the National Digital Skills Empowerment Campaign launched in July 2026 and a deep tech fellowship programme address digital and AI skills, while an announced assessment of AI's impact on the Barbadian workforce was made in October 2026. No AI-specific binding instrument, national guidance document, sandbox or dedicated body exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in a single ministry, with the Data Protection Commissioner the only regulator whose remit reaches automated processing. Independent review exists on paper through the Data Protection Tribunal and the courts, and no subnational tier plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is led by government and directed outward: Barbados advocates inclusive global AI rules at the United Nations, hosts the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and takes part in CARICOM and Caribbean Telecommunications Union AI work including the Caribbean AI Task Force. Domestic involvement of industry, unions and academia is occasional and event-based rather than structured.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI is limited to the general powers of the Data Protection Commissioner under the Data Protection Act, 2019-29, and no AI-related action or audit has been taken.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2019-29 (2019)

Regulation Status: Belarus has no enacted AI-specific legislation. A national law on AI technologies, drafted by the United Institute of Informatics Problems of the National Academy of Sciences on the basis of the CIS Model Law on Artificial Intelligence Technologies and worked on by a 42-member cross-ministerial group, remains at the preparatory stage; on 6 September 2026 the Council of the Republic's expert advisory council confirmed that legislative work continues without a bill before parliament. The only AI-specific binding text in preparation is a July 2026 draft amendment to Law No. 99-Z on Personal Data Protection requiring notification and consent where AI is used for legally significant decisions.
Policy Lever: Belarus governs AI through programs, standards and tax incentives rather than binding rules: the State Program "Digital Belarus" 2026–2030 and the State Program "Belarus Intellectual" 2026–2030 fund AI deployment, Gosstandart builds a national AI standards base, and the High-Tech Park regime under Decree No. 8 provides sector-wide tax benefits. No body holds a legal AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized and executive-led: the National Academy of Sciences drafts AI legislation and is slated to become the sectoral AI regulator, while the Ministry of Communications and Informatization runs the Digital Belarus program and Gosstandart issues AI standards. Coordination occurs through temporary working groups and presidential advisory councils, with no subnational tier and no independent judicial or ombudsman oversight.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is driven by state institutions, with the National Academy of Sciences as the lead expert body and industry engaged through the High-Tech Park and UNDP-supported forums in Minsk. Domestic civil society is excluded, and international engagement is confined to CIS, EAEU and Union State channels plus UNDP technical cooperation.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligations, penalties or enforcement body exist, leaving only general personal data and administrative law available against AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: State Program "Digital Belarus" for 2026–2030 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 793 of 30 December 2025), State Program "Belarus Intellectual" for 2026–2030 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 796 of 30 December 2025), Law of the Republic of Belarus No. 99-Z on Personal Data Protection (2021) and its draft 2026 amendments on decisions taken with artificial intelligence, Decree No. 8 on the Development of the Digital Economy (2017), CIS Model Law on Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2025, drafted by the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus and adopted by the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly)

Regulation Status: Belgium is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689): prohibited practices and AI-literacy duties since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI model and penalty provisions since 2 August 2025, and Article 50 transparency duties since 2 August 2026, while Annex III high-risk obligations now fall on 2 December 2027 under Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. No national AI statute has been enacted; BIPT's role rests on the Government Declaration of 31 January 2025 and the 2025-2029 Federal Government Agreement rather than legislation. A Royal Decree of 20 July 2026 approving the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents code of ethics, in force 1 October 2026, adds a binding AI chapter for one profession.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act plus a narrow Royal Decree AI chapter for real-estate agents, supplemented by soft law from BIPT, FPS Economy and the APD/GBA and by a new federal AI strategy presented by Minister Vanessa Matz in September 2026. Funding runs through TRAIL, regional programmes and EuroHPC, but no regulatory sandbox operates and no authority yet holds statutory AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is dispersed across a politically designated lead regulator (BIPT), sectoral supervisors, the APD/GBA and 21 fundamental-rights bodies under Article 77, coordinated by FPS Economy and an AI Steering Committee created by Royal Decree. Regions hold their own AI strategies and budgets, while independent review of AI reaches courts and the data protection authority only occasionally.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold seats in the AI Steering Committee and the Data and AI Ethics Advisory Committee, and AI4Belgium channels broader stakeholder input, while civil society participates through consultation rather than standing roles. Internationally Belgium acts through the EU AI Board, EuroHPC JU and OECD work on the EU coordinated plan.
Enforcement Level: The AI Act penalty ceilings apply in principle, but Belgium has no enabling statute, no resourced AI supervisor and no published AI-specific enforcement decision.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Royal Decree of 20 July 2026 approving the code of ethics of the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents, including its artificial intelligence chapter (2026), Royal Decree establishing the AI Steering Committee (2024), Royal Decree establishing the Data and AI Ethics Advisory Committee (2023/2024), Federal Government Agreement 2025-2029 (2025), Government Declaration of 31 January 2025 designating BIPT (2025), National Convergence Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence (2019), Federal AI strategy presented September 2026 (2026), Flanders AI Policy Plan 2024-2028 (2024), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016)

Regulation Status: Belize has no AI statute and no national AI strategy; the Data Protection Act 2021, Digital Government Act 2022 and Telecommunications Act (Cap. 229) contain no AI-specific provisions. The single binding AI-specific instrument is Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025, Ethical Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings, in force in the Senior Courts since 12 August 2025, which sets disclosure and verification duties for judges, attorneys and court staff. Economy-wide AI activity remains confined to policy documents such as the Global Digital Services Investment Policy and Strategy (2025) and the National Digital Infrastructure Plan (2025), which impose no obligations.
Policy Lever: Belize relies on one narrow binding instrument for the courts plus judiciary-level guidance and training workshops, with no national AI principles document, funding scheme, sandbox or AI procurement rules. Institutional capacity sits with the Ministry of E-Governance and the Data Protection Commissioner, neither of which holds an AI-specific legal mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is fragmented across central-government bodies with no designated AI regulator and no formal coordination structure, while the independent judiciary is the only institution to have issued binding AI rules. Local government plays no role.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement on AI is limited to sectoral workshops with industry and informal academic contributions from the University of Belize, with civil society absent from any AI policy process. Belize's most substantive involvement is regional, through the Caribbean Telecommunications Union AI work and its 2026 presidency of the SICA regional digital strategy group.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to judges applying Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025 within court proceedings, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions or routine monitoring elsewhere.
Specific Laws: Practice Direction No. 18 of 2025 (Ethical Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings), Senior Courts Act (2022), Digital Government Act (2022), Data Protection Act (2021), Telecommunications Act (Cap. 229), National Digital Agenda 2022-2025, Global Digital Services Investment Policy and Strategy (2025), National Digital Infrastructure Plan (2025)

Regulation Status: Benin regulates AI through a strategy rather than law: the SNIAM 2023-2027, approved by the Council of Ministers on 18 January 2023, sets objectives and four programmes but imposes no obligations. Binding rules touching AI come only from general instruments, the Code du Numérique (Loi No. 2017-20 of 2018, amended by Loi No. 2020-35 of 2021) and Loi No. 2009-09 on personal data, neither of which contains provisions written for AI systems. Creation in May 2026 of a Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation explicitly charged with the national AI strategy did not add any binding instrument.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy, skills and ecosystem funding rather than regulation, with the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation steering SNIAM implementation and the Agence des Systèmes d'Information et du Numérique executing state digital projects. The only binding levers reaching AI are the general digital code and data protection law enforced by the APDP.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Innovation, which since May 2026 carries explicit responsibility for the national AI strategy, supported operationally by the Agence des Systèmes d'Information et du Numérique. Independent oversight is limited to the general data protection authority, and local governments and courts play no AI-specific role.
Actor Involvement: Domestic involvement is consultative and project-based: industry, startups and universities contributed to the SNIAM and to training and innovation programmes, while civil society participation has not been institutionalised. Internationally Benin aligns with African Union and Smart Africa frameworks and pursues bilateral digital cooperation, without treaty-level AI commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through general data protection and digital code powers held by the APDP, with no AI-specific sanctions, authority or published decisions.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle et des Mégadonnées (SNIAM) 2023-2027, Code du Numérique (Loi No. 2017-20 of 2018, amended by Loi No. 2020-35 of 2021), Loi No. 2009-09 of 2009 on Protection of Personally Identifiable Information

Regulation Status: Bhutan governs AI through soft instruments: the National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2025, the Guideline for Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Civil Service 2024 issued by the Royal Civil Service Commission with GovTech, and the Bhutan AI Readiness Assessment (AIRA) 2024. The National Assembly's June 2025 motion called for a regulatory framework, but no AI bill has reached the legislature and Bhutan also lacks a general data protection statute. Coverage of AI obligations extends only to civil servants, on a non-binding basis.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft guidance and capacity-building: NAIS 2025, the 2024 civil-service generative AI guideline, and GovTech's AI Startup Program and AI Lab Program. No binding AI rule, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement requirement is in place, and GovTech holds no statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralized in GovTech, with the Prime Minister-chaired GovTech Commission providing general digital oversight and the GNH Commission supplying values framing. Local governments have no AI function and no independent or judicial body reviews AI decisions.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: industry, universities and development partners contributed to AIRA 2024 and the NAIS 2025 drafting, but no standing formal role exists for industry, civil society or academia. International engagement runs through UNDP, UNESCO and the 50-in-5 campaign rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Bhutan has no AI enforcement machinery, penalties or audit regime, and oversight consists of one-off readiness studies.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2025, Guideline for Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Civil Service (2024), Bhutan AI Readiness Assessment (AIRA) Report (2024), Digital Strategy: Intelligent Bhutan (2024), National Digital Identity Act of Bhutan (2023)

Regulation Status: Bolivia has no enacted AI law. The only AI-specific legislative instrument, Proyecto de Ley 178/2024-2025 on the promotion, management and use of artificial intelligence, was passed by the Senate on 22 October 2025 with 31 articles creating an AI regulatory authority, prohibited practices and fines, and awaits treatment in the Chamber of Deputies. Regional commitments under the Santiago Declaration (2023) and Cartagena Declaration (2024) remain non-binding.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of state projects and international cooperation rather than rules: the sovereign BolivIA platform presented by the Ministry of Planning, Development and Environment in August 2026, and the AGETIC-UNESCO agreement of 27 August 2026 to run the Readiness Assessment Methodology. No AI guidance, sandbox, funding line or legally mandated AI body exists.
Governance Type: AI-related activity is concentrated in central executive bodies, chiefly AGETIC under the Ministry of the Presidency and the Ministry of Planning, Development and Environment, with the general ICT council CTIC-EPB as the only standing coordination forum. Departments and municipalities play no role, and courts and independent bodies have not intervened in AI matters.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is overwhelmingly external: regional declarations, the UNESCO readiness assessment agreed with AGETIC in August 2026, and the Vice-President's attendance at a regional AI meeting in Asunción in September 2026. Domestic industry and civil society have no structured channel into AI policy, and academic involvement is limited to commentary and expert participation.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligations, penalties or enforcement authority are in force, and the only oversight activity is the one-off UNESCO readiness assessment begun in August 2026.
Specific Laws: Proyecto de Ley 178/2024-2025, Promoción, Gestión y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (approved by the Senate 22 October 2025, pending in the Chamber of Deputies), Santiago Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2023), Cartagena Declaration on Artificial Intelligence (2024)

Regulation Status: There is no dedicated AI law, no state-level AI strategy and no binding AI-specific rule in force or before the Parliamentary Assembly. The only national commitment to binding AI obligations is the signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law on 9 December 2025, which has not been ratified; AI reaches domestic law only through the automated decision-making provisions of the Law on Personal Data Protection (Official Gazette of BiH 12/25).
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to non-binding internal guidance: recommendations from the General Secretariat of the Council of Ministers for institutional use of AI tools and the Parliamentary Assembly's Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence (2026) governing AI use in its own operations. Funding, procurement rules, sandboxes and a mandated AI institution are all absent, and AI-related capacity building is carried by UNDP, OHCHR and OSCE support.
Governance Type: Authority over AI is dispersed by the constitutional structure: the state level has no lead AI body, while the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska and Brčko District retain the legislative powers that would carry AI rules and have produced only development strategies mentioning AI. Inter-institutional contact occurs through one-off conferences rather than a formal coordination mechanism, and no judicial or independent-review body has engaged with AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement is limited to donor-organised events, notably the 26-27 November 2025 conference convened by the Ministry of Human Rights and Refugees and the Ministry of Communications and Transport with UNDP, OHCHR and OSCE, which brought in academia, civil society and industry without creating any standing role. International exposure is the most developed strand: signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and EU candidate status driving alignment expectations with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: sanctions and supervision reach AI only through data protection and criminal law, no AI case has been decided, and oversight consists of one-off donor-supported surveys.
Specific Laws: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 9 December 2025, not ratified), Law on Personal Data Protection of Bosnia and Herzegovina (2025, Official Gazette of BiH 12/25), Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina (2026), Development Strategy of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina 2021-2027 (entity-level, mentions artificial intelligence)

Regulation Status: Botswana has no AI-specific legislation in force or before Parliament; the first National Artificial Intelligence Policy, informed by the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology completed in 2024-2025, is still at drafting stage. AI is reached only incidentally by general digital law: the Data Protection Act, 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024, effective 14 January 2025) regulates solely automated decision-making and profiling and requires impact assessments for automated processing, while the Digital Services Act, 2025 and Cybersecurity Act, 2025 carry no AI provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of preparatory work only: a draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise, and collaboration with Estonia on an AI strategy. Funding flows to general digital transformation under SmartBots and the Digital Delta Data Centre rather than to AI-specific programs, and no sandbox, procurement rule or AI body exists.
Governance Type: AI-adjacent governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communications and Innovation and BOCRA, which also hosts the Information and Data Protection Commission, with the Digital Services Authority and National Cyber Security Authority created in 2025 for adjacent fields. There is no dedicated AI body, no formal coordination mechanism, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent review of AI matters.
Actor Involvement: AI policy-making is government-led, with occasional industry exposure at summits and academic research feeding analysis rather than formal advisory structures, and no documented domestic civil society participation. International engagement is the strongest channel: the UNESCO readiness assessment, the Estonia partnership, Smart Africa Alliance membership and African Union digital economy frameworks.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction or enforcement authority exists, and oversight is limited to general data protection and cybersecurity powers that have produced no recorded AI-related action.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2024 (Act No. 18 of 2024), Digital Services Act, 2025, Cybersecurity Act, 2025, draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2025, not adopted)

Regulation Status: Brazil regulates AI through a patchwork of sector-specific binding instruments — TSE Resolution 23.755 of 2 March 2026 on synthetic content in electoral propaganda, CFM Resolution 2.454/2026 on AI in medicine, Portaria MGI 3.485 of 24 April 2026 on AI governance in the federal administration, and Lei 15.123/2025 criminalising AI-assisted violence against women — alongside general law (LGPD Law 13.709/2018, Marco Civil Law 12.965/2014, ECA Digital Law 15.211/2025 in force since 17 March 2026). The horizontal AI Legal Framework, PL 2338/2023, was approved by the Senate on 10 December 2024 but remains before the Chamber of Deputies special committee, with the rapporteur confirming on 24 August 2026 that the vote would follow the October 2026 elections. Obligations therefore apply only in defined domains, not economy-wide.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through indirect binding law (LGPD, ECA Digital), narrow AI-specific norms in elections, medicine and public administration, and a substantial soft-law and funding layer: PBIA 2024–2028, the ANPD AI regulatory sandbox now in its testing phase, and Lei 15.504/2026 incentives for data centres. The ANPD, upgraded to a regulatory agency by Lei 15.352/2026, publishes AI guidance and priority-themes plans while lacking a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is plural and uncoordinated: the ANPD is the presumptive lead under the pending bill while the TSE, CFM, Banco Central, ANVISA, CADE and SENACON regulate AI inside their own sectors without a formal cross-agency AI body. Courts, particularly the electoral courts and the Supreme Federal Court, actively shape the applicable rules, and states such as Goiás and the Federal District have adopted their own AI policies.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia participate through public hearings, consultations and the ANPD sandbox rather than standing co-governance bodies. Internationally Brazil is a leading actor, shaping G20, UNESCO, BRICS and Latin American regional AI governance instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs mainly through LGPD sanctions (up to 2% of Brazilian turnover) and ECA Digital fines of up to R$50 million administered by the ANPD, with the electoral courts issuing the only decisions applying AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados - LGPD (Law No. 13,709/2018), Marco Civil da Internet (Law No. 12,965/2014), Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente Digital - ECA Digital (Law No. 15,211/2025, in force 17 March 2026), Lei No. 15,123/2025 (AI-enabled violence against women - Criminal Code amendment), Lei No. 15,352/2026 (ANPD converted into a regulatory agency), Lei No. 15,504/2026 (data centre tax incentives for AI investment), Resolução TSE No. 23,755/2026 amending Resolução TSE No. 23,610/2019 (AI and synthetic content in electoral propaganda), Resolução CFM No. 2,454/2026 (AI in medicine), Portaria MGI No. 3,485/2026 (AI governance policy for the federal public administration), Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial - PBIA 2024-2028, Estratégia Brasileira de Inteligência Artificial - EBIA (2021), PL 2338/2023 (AI Legal Framework - pending in the Chamber of Deputies), Goiás State Complementary Laws No. 205/2025 and No. 215/2026, Distrito Federal Decreto No. 48,901/2026, Ceará State Law No. 17,611/2021

Regulation Status: Brunei regulates AI through voluntary means: the Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam, issued by AITI in April 2025 and reissued as a second edition in 2026, carries no legal force. The binding law reaching AI is general: the Personal Data Protection Order 2025, whose substantive provisions commenced on 1 January 2026 and which AITI administers. No AI-specific binding instrument exists or is before the legislature.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law and strategy: AITI's two editions of the Guide on AI Governance and Ethics, the Digital Brunei 2030 transformation plan launched 2 June 2026, and the regional ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. The only binding lever touching AI is the general Personal Data Protection Order 2025.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in AITI under the Ministry of Transport and Infocommunications, with cross-ministry coordination through the Digital Brunei Council that issued Digital Brunei 2030. There is no subnational tier and no independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI governance.
Actor Involvement: Government, industry and academia sit together on AITI's AI Governance and Ethics Working Group, and two public consultation papers (July 2024 and November 2025) drew comment from technology communities and the public. Civil society has no standing role, and international engagement runs through ASEAN instruments rather than treaties or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Compliance with Brunei's AI guide is voluntary and unenforced, with the only applicable penalties coming from the general Personal Data Protection Order 2025.
Specific Laws: Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam, Second Edition (2026), Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics for Brunei Darussalam (2025), Personal Data Protection Order (2025), Digital Brunei 2030: The Digital Brunei Transformation Plan (2026), Digital Economy Masterplan 2025, ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2024)

Regulation Status: Bulgaria's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), whose prohibitions, AI-literacy, general-purpose AI and transparency duties apply, while high-risk obligations were pushed to 2 December 2027 by the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendment. No national supplementary law is in force: a government bill was announced as nearing public consultation in September 2026 and an opposition Act on the Use and Development of Artificial Intelligence (bill 52-654-01-151) was tabled in the National Assembly on 24 September 2026 after an earlier version was rejected in committee.
Policy Lever: Policy rests almost entirely on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus the 2020 national AI Concept, with institutional work limited to the designation of seven Article 77 fundamental-rights bodies and preparatory drafting by the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation, which absorbed the Ministry of Electronic Governance in May 2026. Economic levers are research and infrastructure funding rather than regulatory tools; the planned AI regulatory sandbox was deprioritised and the EU deadline for one operating sandbox now runs to 2 August 2027.
Governance Type: Governance is ministry-led and only partially plural: the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation coordinates, seven bodies designated in June 2025 cover fundamental rights, and sectoral regulators would take enforcement roles under the pending bills. Coordination remains informal, there is no subnational layer, and independent review of AI decisions has not yet been exercised.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is strongest at EU level through the European AI Board and AI Act coordination formats, while domestic participation is consultative: industry associations and academic institutions feed into draft legislation and parliamentary hearings without formal standing roles, and civil society is consulted only occasionally.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is effectively dormant: no national sanctions regime, no designated AI market surveillance authority, and no AI-specific decisions, leaving only directly applicable EU-level obligations and general-law action.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (2026), Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030 (2020), Council of Ministers Decision No. 398 (2025), draft Act on the Use and Development of Artificial Intelligence (bill 52-654-01-151, 2026)

Regulation Status: Burkina Faso has no dedicated AI law and none before the Assemblée législative du peuple; the only binding provision written for AI is Article 19 of Loi n°001-2021/AN portant protection des données à caractère personnel, which obliges controllers to disclose the criteria and data underlying AI-based processing. The Feuille de route nationale sur l'intelligence artificielle 2026-2030, validated on 17 June 2026 under the Plan RELANCE 2026-2030 and the 'IA pour tous' programme, is a strategy without binding force, and deputies were given an AI briefing on 15 July 2026 to prepare future digital legislation.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy and capacity-building rather than regulation: a national AI roadmap for 2026-2030, the 'IA pour tous' programme, awareness campaigns for ministry chiefs of staff in April 2026 and Primature training sessions in May and July 2026. The only binding levers touching AI remain the general data protection and information-systems security laws, and SPIVTEN acts as a ministry unit without compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Digital Transition and its SPIVTEN secretariat under a centralized military transitional authority, with the data protection commission as the only other body whose remit touches AI. Coordination occurs through one-off interministerial and parliamentary sessions, there is no subnational competence, and a pending reform would merge the Commission de l'Informatique et des Libertés with the Conseil supérieur de la communication.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through ministry-convened workshops that brought in the private sector, universities, youth and civil society during the preparation and 17 June 2026 validation of the national AI roadmap, without any permanent consultative structure. Internationally, the Minister of Digital Transition championed the UNESCO-supported regional AI guidelines adopted by six francophone West African states in July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: oversight rests with the general data protection commission, and no AI audit, investigation or sanction has been recorded.
Specific Laws: Feuille de route nationale sur l'intelligence artificielle 2026-2030 (2026), Loi n°001-2021/AN portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2021), Loi portant sécurité des systèmes d'information (2024), Stratégie nationale de développement de l'économie numérique SN@DEN 2018-2027 (2018), Lignes directrices communes ouest-africaines sur la gouvernance de l'intelligence artificielle (2026)

Regulation Status: Burundi has no binding AI legislation; its only AI-specific instrument is the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030, validated in Bujumbura on 21-22 April 2026 by the Ministry of Finance, Budget and Digital Economy with UNDP support, which is a six-pillar non-binding roadmap promising later regulatory and ethical frameworks. General law reaches AI indirectly through Loi n°1/03 of 10 March 2026 on personal data protection and Loi n°1/10 of 16 March 2022 on cybercrime, neither of which regulates AI systems as such.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of non-binding planning documents, the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030 and the Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données validated 7 November 2025, supported by UNDP. Funding, a sandbox and AI procurement rules are absent, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one ministry, the Ministère des Finances, du Budget et de l'Économie numérique, working with UNDP, with coordination limited to ad hoc workshops. No subnational tier, court or independent oversight body plays any role in AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Involvement is limited to the UNDP-supported strategy validation workshop of 21-22 April 2026, which drew ministries, the private sector and academics on a one-off basis. International engagement consists of African Union and UNESCO membership and the September 2026 KOAFEC ministerial in Seoul, with no treaty or standards participation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI rules is impossible because no AI-specific obligation, supervisory authority or monitoring programme exists, leaving only general data protection and cybercrime penalties.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle 2026-2030 (validated April 2026), Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (2025), Loi n°1/03 du 10 mars 2026 portant protection des données à caractère personnel, Loi n°1/10 du 16 mars 2022 portant prévention et répression de la cybercriminalité au Burundi

Regulation Status: Cambodia governs AI through general instruments only: Sub-Decree 110 (2017) on the ICT Licensing Regime covers the supply side of AI, and the Law on Anti-Technology Fraud passed on 3 April 2026 criminalises technology-enabled fraud without AI-specific provisions. The Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, the Draft MPTC AI Promotion Strategy and the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection are all still in consultation, and the strategy itself commits to a light-touch, step-by-step approach rather than a comprehensive AI law.
Policy Lever: Policy runs entirely through soft instruments: a published UNESCO-supported AI Readiness Assessment, a draft National AI Strategy prepared with UN-ESCAP support, a draft MPTC AI Promotion Strategy, and AI governance and ethics guidelines still being drafted. Government AI deployments such as verify.gov.kh, TranslateKH and the ai.gov.kh platform are service projects rather than funded AI programmes, and no sandbox, AI procurement rule or mandated AI body exists.
Governance Type: The Ministry of Post and Telecommunications is the lead AI policy body, with MISTI and the National Council of Science, Technology and Innovation contributing on the industrial and research side, and implementation of the draft strategy assigned on paper to the Digital Government Committee supported by an Inter-Ministerial Working Group on AI. Coordination is ad hoc and centralised in Phnom Penh, with no provincial role and no independent or judicial oversight of AI.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: workshops and a public consultation on the draft strategies drew industry, academic and civil society participants, including roughly 80 attendees at the April 2026 MPTC workshop, but no actor holds a standing formal role. International engagement is the most developed strand, running through ASEAN, UNESCO, UN-ESCAP and multilateral AI governance meetings.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI-specific obligation to enforce, no designated AI authority and no AI oversight practice beyond one-off readiness studies, leaving general ICT licensing and anti-fraud powers as the only levers that touch AI.
Specific Laws: Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030 (2025, not yet adopted), Draft MPTC AI Promotion Strategy (2026, not yet adopted), Draft Law on Personal Data Protection (2025, not yet enacted), Sub-Decree 110 on the ICT Licensing Regime (2017), Law on Anti-Technology Fraud (2026), Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021-2035 (2021)

Regulation Status: Cameroon has no binding AI-specific legislation and no AI bill before the legislature. The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA), unveiled in July 2025 by the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications, is a non-binding roadmap whose first pillar proposes a Cameroonian AI Authority, a Presidential Council on AI and a future framework law. Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 on personal data protection became fully applicable on 24 June 2026 after its eighteen-month compliance period, but it is a general-purpose instrument.
Policy Lever: Policy action rests on the non-binding SNIA roadmap plus the general data protection law, with no AI-specific binding instrument, regulatory sandbox or funded AI programme in operation. Institutional capacity is limited to ministerial stewardship; the AI Authority and Presidential Council on AI envisaged by the strategy do not exist.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, with ANTIC and ART active on cybersecurity and telecoms but holding no AI competence. Coordination is occasional and consultative rather than institutionalised, and neither subnational authorities nor independent review bodies play any part.
Actor Involvement: Stakeholder input has come mainly through the single CONIA national consultation of June 2024, which gathered public bodies, the private sector, civil society and researchers ahead of SNIA, with no permanent advisory structures since. International engagement is limited to continental and multilateral alignment, notably with the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity for AI is absent: no AI obligations, no competent authority and no monitoring, while even the general data protection regime that became fully applicable on 24 June 2026 lacks an operating supervisory authority.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy - SNIA (2025), Law No. 2024/017 of 23 December 2024 on Personal Data Protection

Regulation Status: Canada has no binding federal AI statute: AIDA died with Bill C-27 in January 2025 and the June 2026 national strategy AI for All chose targeted legislation over a standalone AI act. Binding federal AI rules exist only inside government through the Treasury Board Directive on Automated Decision-Making, whose 2025 version and Algorithmic Impact Assessment apply to federal automated decision systems including generative AI. Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, which would impose duties on AI chatbot services, and Bill C-36, which adds automated-decision transparency rights, were tabled in June 2026 and remain before the House of Commons.
Policy Lever: Federal levers are predominantly soft: the mandatory Directive on Automated Decision-Making for government systems, a layered set of guidance and voluntary codes, and large funding envelopes under AI for All covering compute, the three national AI institutes and the Canadian AI Safety Institute. No federal body holds statutory AI compliance powers; the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation leads policy and sponsors Bills C-34 and C-36.
Governance Type: Authority is dispersed: a lead ministry without regulatory powers, independent federal regulators applying general law to AI, and provinces legislating their own AI-adjacent rules. Coordination is practice-based, shown by the joint OPC, Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta investigation of OpenAI, rather than embedded in a statutory mechanism.
Actor Involvement: Policy development is industry-led through the appointed AI Strategy Task Force with strong academic participation via CIFAR and the national AI institutes, while domestic civil society publicly protested its exclusion and boycotted the 2025 consultation. Internationally Canada is a treaty signatory and standards participant across Council of Europe, OECD, GPAI and the AI safety institute network.
Enforcement Level: AI-specific enforcement is confined to administrative compliance inside the federal public service, while regulators reach private-sector AI only through general privacy and consumer law, as in the OpenAI findings of May 2026.
Specific Laws: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (2019, fourth version in force 24 June 2025), AI for All: Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), Bill C-34 Safe Social Media Act enacting the Digital Safety Act and Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act (introduced 10 June 2026), Bill C-36 Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act (introduced 15 June 2026), AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025-2027, Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems (2023), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 11 February 2025), Quebec Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information / Law 25 (2021), Ontario Strengthening Cyber Security and Building Trust in the Public Sector Act / Bill 194 (2024)

Regulation Status: Cabo Verde has no AI-specific legislation and none in the legislative process; AI is addressed only through strategy documents, notably the Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035 approved by Resolução n.º 72/2026 and the National Data Strategy developed with World Bank support. General instruments — the personal data protection law as amended by Lei n.º 121/IX/2021, the cybercrime law and the electronic commerce law — reach AI uses without containing any AI-written provision, and the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados has publicly framed AI as a data-governance question rather than applying dedicated rules.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to strategy and capacity-building: the Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035, the National Data Strategy, and announced plans for a Centro de Excelência Digital e de Inteligência Artificial, alongside training delivered under the Cabo Verde–Nigeria Digital Africa Corridor. No binding AI instrument, published AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive, with the Secretaria de Estado da Economia Digital and NOSi leading digital policy and no body holding an AI mandate. The independent data protection commission is the only non-governmental-style check active in the AI debate, and sub-national authorities have no role.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation in AI policy is informal: business engagement occurs through technology forums and academics contributed to digital governance strategy work, while no civil society organisation holds a consultative role. International engagement is the most developed channel, through the Smart Africa Alliance, African Union frameworks, the Lusophone data protection network and the Cabo Verde–Nigeria Digital Africa Corridor.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced; only general data protection and cybercrime penalties could reach AI uses, and no decision, audit or monitoring programme has been recorded.
Specific Laws: Agenda Digital de Cabo Verde 2035 (Resolução n.º 72/2026), Estratégia Nacional de Dados (2025), Lei n.º 121/IX/2021 amending the Personal Data Protection Law (Lei n.º 41/VIII/2013), Estratégia Nacional para a Governação Digital de Cabo Verde
