Regulation Status: The Central African Republic has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no national AI strategy. The only binding text reaching algorithmic activity is Loi n° 24-001 (2024) on personal data protection, which regulates processing of personal data generally and for which no supervisory authority has been publicly identified. Ongoing conflict and limited state capacity keep AI rulemaking absent from the legislative agenda.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of announcements rather than instruments: a planned AI centre of excellence with an Indian partner, a Huawei-supported administration digitalisation programme, and presidential meetings on data and AI investment held during the 81st UN General Assembly. No AI guidance, funding programme, sandbox or procurement rule is in operation.
Governance Type: Governance of AI is not organised: no lead authority, sectoral regulator with an AI remit, coordination body or independent review mechanism exists, and the Ministry in charge of the digital economy handles technology matters without an AI mandate. Prefectures have no regulatory role.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI runs through presidential-level bilateral contacts with foreign technology firms and development partners rather than domestic consultation. Industry, civil society and academia have no structured role, and international involvement is confined to passive African Union and United Nations membership.
Enforcement Level: Nothing specific to AI is enforced or monitored, and documented misuse of AI tools inside the country has drawn political criticism but no regulatory or judicial response.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 24-001 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2024)

Regulation Status: Chad has no AI-specific legislation or regulatory framework. AI activity falls only under general digital law — Loi n°007/PR/2015 on personal data protection and Loi n°009/PR/2015 on cybersecurity and cybercrime, both administered by the Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique (ANSICE) — and the draft Code du numérique in preparation since December 2025 adds no AI-specific obligations. The only AI-specific state act is Décret n°2690/PR/PM/MTENDA/2025 of 21 October 2025, which reorganised the Ministry of Telecommunications, Digital Economy and Digitalisation of the Administration and created a Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle without conferring regulatory powers.
Policy Lever: Chad's only AI policy lever is institutional: a Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle inside the digital economy ministry, created in October 2025 with a promotional rather than regulatory remit. Activity otherwise consists of donor-supported capacity building — the UNDP-backed AI forum project, the ADETIC training initiative for 2,000 young people, and the UNECA-led AI readiness exercise of May 2026 — with no published AI strategy, guidance, sandbox or procurement rule.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the executive, specifically the Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle within the Ministry of Telecommunications, Digital Economy and Digitalisation of the Administration, with ANSICE and ARCEP operating general digital remits. Inter-institutional contact occurs only through one-off internationally supported workshops, and neither provinces nor courts play any part.
Actor Involvement: International organisations drive what AI engagement exists: UNESCO through the completed Readiness Assessment Methodology, UNECA through the May 2026 data governance and AI readiness work in N'Djamena, and UNDP through a planned national AI forum. Domestic industry, civil society and academia take part in forums such as the Chad Internet Governance Forum and the TchadIA research days, but none has a formal role in policy-making.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction or enforcement action exists in Chad, and oversight of AI is confined to general data protection and cybersecurity powers held by ANSICE plus two one-off readiness assessments.
Specific Laws: Décret n°2690/PR/PM/MTENDA/2025 portant réorganisation du Ministère des Télécommunications, de l'Économie numérique et de la Digitalisation de l'Administration, créant la Direction générale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (2025), Loi n°007/PR/2015 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2015), Loi n°006/PR/2015 portant création de l'Agence Nationale de Sécurité Informatique et de Certification Électronique (2015), Loi n°009/PR/2015 sur la cybersécurité et la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2015), Stratégie nationale de développement du numérique 2020-2030

Regulation Status: No AI-specific statute binds in Chile: the government AI bill (Boletín 16821-19) is in its second constitutional stage before the Senate Future Challenges Committee, and the Executive announced in May 2026 and reiterated in October 2026 a total substitutive indication that would drop the EU-style risk tiers for an innovation-oriented framework. A separate bill sanctioning AI-generated deepfakes passed the Chamber of Deputies in general on 23 July 2026 and returned to committee. Binding rules reaching AI are general: Law 21.663 on cybersecurity (in force since 2025) and Law 21.719 on personal data protection, which takes effect 1 December 2026 and whose postponement to 2027 is sought by Boletín 18.623-07.
Policy Lever: Chile governs AI mainly through soft law and funding: the updated National AI Policy and action plan, the MinCiencia–Segpres instructive on AI in public services, SERNAC consumer guidance, and state-backed research through CENIA and Latam-GPT. The only enforceable instruments are general cybersecurity and, from December 2026, data protection law, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: A lead ministry (MinCiencia) sets AI policy and coordinates sectoral regulators through the National AI Policy action plan, with the proposed AI authority still contained in a pending bill. Courts have intervened occasionally, notably the Supreme Court's Worldcoin decision, while no subnational tier plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia feed into AI policy through published consultations, Senate committee hearings and expert reports rather than standing formal seats. Internationally Chile is prominent, leading the regional AI ethics agenda from the Santiago Declaration and participating in OECD, UNESCO and United Nations AI governance processes.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligations are enforceable, so action is confined to general-law instruments such as ANCI's cybersecurity supervision of 1,154 designated Operators of Vital Importance and occasional court rulings.
Specific Laws: AI Systems Regulation Bill (Boletín 16821-19, 2024, second constitutional stage in the Senate; Executive substitutive indication announced 2026), Bill regulating AI-generated content and deepfakes (approved in general by the Chamber of Deputies, 2026), Law 21.719 on Protection of Personal Data (2024, effective 1 December 2026; postponement sought by Boletín 18.623-07, 2026), Law 21.806 amending Law 21.719 (2026), Law 21.663 on Cybersecurity Framework (2024, in force 2025), National AI Policy and Action Plan update (Decreto N° 12 of 2025), MinCiencia–Segpres Oficio N° 711/2023 on AI use in the State, Santiago Declaration on Ethical AI in Latin America and the Caribbean (2023)

Regulation Status: China regulates AI through a stack of dedicated binding administrative measures rather than a single statute: algorithmic recommendation, deep synthesis, generative AI services, AI-generated content labeling, and, since 15 July 2026, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, reinforced by the amended Cybersecurity Law in force 1 January 2026. Obligations such as algorithm filing, security assessment and content labeling apply today across online services, finance, education and healthcare platforms, but the generative AI rules exempt non-public-facing systems and the State Council's 2026 Legislative Work Plan still lists comprehensive AI legislation as pending.
Policy Lever: Policy combines licensing, filing, pre-launch security assessment, mandatory labeling and data rules with a maintained suite of national standards and TC260 guidance, plus industrial levers such as the AI Plus Action Plan and state AI funds. CAC, MIIT, NDRC and SAMR exercise approval and compliance powers routinely.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized under the CAC, which coordinates national AI policy and shares implementation with sectoral ministries through repeated joint rulemaking; local governments implement national rules and add promotion-oriented local legislation. Courts resolve private AI disputes, but no independent body reviews or shapes AI regulatory decisions.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is channelled through state-run consultations, TC260 technical committees and state-affiliated academic institutes, with independent civil society excluded. Internationally China is a leading actor, hosting the new World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization and pushing the Global AI Governance Initiative and Action Plan alongside ISO, ITU and UN work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is active and visible through registration gatekeeping, periodic nationwide rectification campaigns and published sanctions against non-compliant AI services, though individual decisions are mostly reported in aggregate.
Specific Laws: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions (2022), Internet Information Service Deep Synthesis Management Provisions (2022), Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (2023), Measures for Labeling Artificial Intelligence-Generated Synthetic Content and GB 45438-2025 (2025), Cybersecurity Law Amendment with artificial intelligence provisions (effective 1 January 2026), Interim Measures for the Administration of Artificial Intelligence Anthropomorphic Interaction Services (2026), Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of Intelligent Agents (2026), Opinions of the State Council on Deepening Implementation of the Artificial Intelligence Plus Initiative (2025), AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (2025), New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan (2017)

Regulation Status: Colombia still has no horizontal AI statute: the government bill PL 043-25/324-25-C was archived on transit of legislature in mid-2026 and replaced by Proyecto de Ley 025 de 2026, which replicates most of the earlier risk-based text and is before Congress. The binding rules that exist are AI provisions inserted into general law—Ley 2502 de 2025 on AI-assisted identity impersonation and SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024 on personal data in AI systems—while CONPES 4144 de 2025 remains a non-binding policy roadmap.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law and spending: CONPES 4144 de 2025 with its COP 479 billion action plan, MinTIC's ethical guide and MSPI AI security lineamientos, and the CRC's regulatory sandbox hosting AI experiments. The only binding levers are SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024 and the AI aggravation in Ley 2502 de 2025, and no body holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in MinCiencias and MinTIC, with the SIC and CRC applying AI to their sectoral remits and the DNP tracking CONPES 4144 implementation. Subnational authorities implement national programmes without regulating, and judicial review has intervened once, in Constitutional Court judgment T-323 de 2024.
Actor Involvement: AI policy has been drafted through consultation with industry, academia and civil society rather than through standing bodies, and the CRC sandbox gives firms a structured channel. Internationally Colombia works through the OECD, UNESCO and the Latin American Santiago and Cartagena Declarations without signing a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI flows through general data-protection, consumer and criminal powers, with the single AI-specific penalty being the Ley 2502 de 2025 aggravation and no AI audit or monitoring regime.
Specific Laws: CONPES 4144 – Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Ley 2502 de 2025 – Penal Code reform on identity impersonation using artificial intelligence (2025), Ley 1581 de 2012 – Data Protection Law (2012), SIC External Circular No. 2 of 2024 – AI Personal Data Processing Guidelines (2024), Guía Ética para la Implementación, Desarrollo y Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial en Entidades Públicas de Colombia (2025), Lineamientos de Seguridad y Privacidad de la Información para Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial – MSPI update (2026), Proyecto de Ley 025 de 2026 – AI regulation bill (pending)

Regulation Status: Comoros has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or binding rule, and no AI provision within general law. Digital policy rests on the non-binding Stratégie Comores Numérique 2028 (2019), which targets connectivity, e-government and cybersecurity without addressing AI systems. The country signed the African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection on 29 January 2018 but has not ratified it, and no data protection authority has been appointed.
Policy Lever: Comoros deploys no AI policy instrument of any kind, binding or voluntary, and operates no AI funding, sandbox or procurement programme. Institutional capacity is limited to the telecommunications regulator ANRTIC and the digital development agency ANADEN, neither of which holds an AI remit.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent: digital matters sit with the Ministry responsible for telecommunications, ANRTIC and ANADEN, none of which has an AI mandate, and there is no coordinating body. The autonomous islands play no role, and no court or independent oversight body has addressed AI.
Actor Involvement: No domestic industry, civil society or academic actors have been mobilised around AI governance, and no consultation has been held. International involvement is passive membership of the African Union and the United Nations, under which the non-binding Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy and the Global Digital Compact apply without national follow-up.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is non-existent, with no AI obligations, no designated authority, no sanctions and no monitoring of AI systems.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale Comores Numérique 2028 (2019), Décret 065/2009 établissant l'ANRTIC (2009)

Regulation Status: The National Assembly adopted on 8 April 2026 a draft law on the orientation and development of scientific research that introduces an ethical framework for artificial intelligence and institutes a national committee to oversee responsible AI use. Apart from that text, AI is reached only by general law, principally Loi n° 29-2019 du 10 octobre 2019 portant protection des données à caractère personnel. A national AI strategy is under preparation by a technical committee launched on 6 May 2026 with UNDP support, and the Agence de régulation des postes et des communications électroniques held a five-day seminar on digital regulation and AI governance from 12 January 2026.
Policy Lever: Congo relies on promotional instruments: a UNECA-backed AI research centre in Brazzaville, UNDP-supported AI training and strategy drafting, and the research law's planned AI ethics committee. No AI-specific binding instrument, published national AI guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is executive-led, centred on the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and the Digital Economy, the ARPCE and the Ministry of Scientific Research and Technological Innovation, coordinated through a temporary technical committee rather than standing institutions. Departments play no part and no judicial or independent oversight of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Participation is concentrated in government, academia and international partners (UNECA, UNDP, UNESCO), with industry drawn into ARPCE-convened consultations. Domestic civil society has no documented standing role in AI policy-making.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligation is enforceable today, no authority owns AI supervision, and no AI-related sanction or audit has been recorded.
Specific Laws: Loi portant orientation et développement de la recherche scientifique (adopted by the National Assembly, 2026), Loi n° 29-2019 du 10 octobre 2019 portant protection des données à caractère personnel, Loi n° 11-2009 du 25 novembre 2009 creating the Agence de régulation des postes et des communications électroniques, Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle (under preparation since 2026), Vision Congo Digital 2025

Regulation Status: Costa Rica governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (ENIA) 2024-2027, its August 2025 Action Plan and the voluntary INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 technical standard formalized in March 2026. Three AI bills (Expedientes 23771, 23919, 24484) remain pending in the Legislative Assembly, with 23771 carrying an affirmative majority committee report and sitting on the plenary agenda, and a privately drafted AI-and-digital-assets mega-bill was circulated by the Cámara Blockchain e IA in September 2026. The only binding law applied to AI is the general data-protection Law No. 8968.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft-law levers: the ENIA strategy and Action Plan, the voluntary INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 standard, and capacity-building programs run with UNESCO, UNDP, Cisco and a 2026 cooperation agreement with Google. MICITT leads without a legal AI mandate, and the sandbox foreseen in the ENIA has not been established.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in MICITT, with PRODHAB enforcing the general data-protection regime and no sectoral AI regulators or sub-national competence. Interaction between bodies is organized through the ENIA Action Plan rather than a formal coordination mechanism, and independent review has been limited to university opinions on pending bills.
Actor Involvement: The ENIA was drafted through structured consultation with the private sector, civil society and academia, with European Union support, and Costa Rica convened a UN-backed National Dialogue on AI Ethics and Governance. Internationally it works through the OECD, UNESCO and UNDP and leads Central American AI governance dialogue, without having signed a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is limited to general data-protection powers held by PRODHAB, with no AI-specific sanctions, supervisory authority or routine auditing.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy ENIA 2024-2027 (2024), ENIA Action Plan (2025), INTE/ISO/IEC 42001:2026 (2026), Law No. 8968 – Protection in the Handling of Personal Data (2011), Bill 23771 – Ley de Regulación de la Inteligencia Artificial en Costa Rica (pending), Bill 23919 – Ley para la Promoción Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial en Costa Rica (pending), Bill 24484 – Ley para la Implementación de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (pending)

Regulation Status: Croatia's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), whose prohibitions, general-purpose AI duties and Article 50 transparency obligations apply, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force since 27 July 2026, moved high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. The national Act on Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 remains a draft scheduled for public consultation by the Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation, and no market surveillance or notifying authority has been designated. Croatia has designated seven fundamental-rights authorities under Article 77, including the Personal Data Protection Agency, the Ombudswoman and the Agency for Electronic Media.
Policy Lever: Croatia relies on the EU AI Act as its single binding lever, supplemented by Personal Data Protection Agency guidance on AI and data protection and on AI system development, and by compute and digital-transition funding under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, the Digital Croatia Strategy 2032 and EuroHPC projects. Institutional capacity rests on an inter-ministerial working group chaired by the Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation and on bodies that lack an AI-specific enforcement mandate, and the required national AI regulatory sandbox is not operating.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-ministry-plus-sectoral-bodies model: the Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation drafts policy and the implementing law, seven designated authorities cover fundamental-rights oversight, and coordination occurs in an inter-ministerial working group rather than a statutory mechanism. No subnational tier regulates AI, while the ombudsperson offices and courts provide periodic independent scrutiny.
Actor Involvement: Ministries, the Personal Data Protection Agency, ombudsperson offices, academia, industry and civil society are represented in the working groups preparing the national implementing law and the National Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence, but these roles are project-based rather than standing. Internationally Croatia acts through the European AI Board, the European Data Protection Board where its agency holds the deputy chair, and EU digital policy coordination.
Enforcement Level: The AI Act's penalty ceilings apply in Croatia, yet no market surveillance authority is designated, no AI-specific decision has been taken, and oversight is limited to data-protection questionnaires on AI systems.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Draft Act on Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), Digital Croatia Strategy 2032, National Roadmap for Digital Decade Policy, Act on Implementation of the Digital Services Act (2025), National Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence to 2032 with Action Plan 2026-2028 (draft)

Regulation Status: Cuba governs AI through the Estrategia para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, approved in May 2024 as part of the Política para la Transformación Digital y Agenda Digital, a policy document without binding force. Obligations touching AI arise only from general law, notably the automated-processing provisions of Ley 149 de Protección de Datos Personales and Decreto-Ley 35 on telecommunications. No AI bill is before the Asamblea Nacional del Poder Popular.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the 2024 AI Strategy and its six axes (ethics, human capital, applications, public administration, innovation, communication), coordinated by MINCOM, with the Consorcio de Inteligencia Artificial de Cuba as the main delivery vehicle since November 2025. The Ley General de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación, approved on 18 December 2025, frames science and innovation generally rather than creating AI obligations or funding lines.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in MINCOM under a Council of Ministers policy, with inter-ministerial responsibilities named in the digital transformation policy and the AI Consortium coordinated by the Parque Científico Tecnológico de La Habana and the Academia de Ciencias de Cuba. No subnational tier and no independent judicial or oversight body shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Participation is structured but state-channelled: universities, state enterprises, ministries and the Unión de Informáticos de Cuba sit in the AI Consortium, while independent civil society is absent. Internationally Cuba acts at declaratory level through UNESCO, CELAC and the Santiago Declaration rather than through binding treaties or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific enforcement framework, sanction or monitoring programme exists, and oversight is limited to general data-protection and telecommunications powers plus one-off strategy monitoring.
Specific Laws: Política para la Transformación Digital, Agenda Digital Cubana y Estrategia para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (2024), Ley 149 de Protección de Datos Personales (2022, in force 2023), Resolución 58 de 2022 del Ministerio de Comunicaciones, Decreto Ley 35 de Telecomunicaciones (2021), Ley General de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (2025)

Regulation Status: Cyprus is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations bind today, while high-risk system obligations were pushed back to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI. Nationally, Council of Ministers decisions of January 2025 designated competent authorities, and the Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 — which would set the supervision framework, authority powers, penalties and an AI regulatory sandbox — completed public consultation on 16 September 2026 without yet being passed.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the directly applicable AI Act plus EU-funded capacity building: the Pharos-CY AI Factory Antenna, an 'AI for Government' scheme, and access to EuroHPC resources. National soft law is confined to the ai.cy information portal and the National AI Strategy 2032 consulted in July–August 2026, while the regulatory sandbox foreseen in the draft Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 is not yet operating.
Governance Type: Cyprus uses a compact, centralised structure: the Commissioner of Communications is notifying authority, lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, the Commissioner for Personal Data Protection supervises within her competence, and the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy coordinates nationally and in the European AI Board. The National AI Strategy 2032 proposes a National AI Authority and an Interministerial AI Council, neither of which exists yet, and there is no sub-national tier.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is consultative rather than institutionalised: the National AI Taskforce supplies advisory input from academia, industry and law, and open e-consultations on both the Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 and the National AI Strategy 2032 drew comments from employer federations and disability groups. International involvement runs through the European AI Board and EU-funded programmes rather than independent treaty or standards activity.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is latent: EU-level penalty ceilings apply and authorities are named, but national penalty rules, inspection procedures and monitoring remain in the draft Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 and no action has been taken.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Artificial Intelligence Law of 2026 (draft, public consultation closed 16 September 2026), Council of Ministers decisions designating AI Act competent authorities (January 2025), National AI Strategy of Cyprus 2032 (2026), Cyprus National AI Strategy (2020), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016), Processing of Personal Data (Protection of the Individual) Law 125(I)/2018

Regulation Status: Czechia regulates AI chiefly through the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose AI and Article 50 transparency duties apply, while Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The national adaptation Act on Artificial Intelligence prepared by the Ministry of Industry and Trade, which would designate market surveillance authorities, create a sandbox and set administrative offences, has not been enacted. Sector statutes written for specific AI applications are in force: the amendment to Act No. 273/2008 Coll. on the Police allowing biometric identification and the amendment to Act No. 361/2000 Coll. permitting SAE Level 3 automated driving.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act plus narrow national statutes on police biometric identification and automated driving, supported by the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2030, the AI Implementation Plan approved by Government Resolution No. 394 of 28 May 2025 and CZK 207 million of implementation funding for 2026–2028. The Czech Standardisation Agency is to run the regulatory sandbox foreseen in the draft Act, which is not yet operating, and the Czech Telecommunication Office's new AI unit awaits its legal powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centred on the Ministry of Industry and Trade as coordinator with the Czech Telecommunication Office as prospective lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, flanked by sectoral bodies for data protection, finance, standardisation and conformity assessment. Coordination runs through the inter-ministerial Committee for Artificial Intelligence; there is no sub-national regulatory tier, and independent scrutiny rests with the courts and, once the draft Act passes, the Public Defender of Rights.
Actor Involvement: Policy development runs through the Committee for Artificial Intelligence, which seats ministries, regulators, industry bodies such as the Czech AI Association and the Confederation of Industry, and academic institutions, with non-profits and social partners drawn into the National AI Strategy 2030 update and the inter-ministerial comment procedure on the draft Act. Externally Czechia acts through the EU AI Board and European standardisation bodies and participates in OECD AI governance.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is still preparatory: the EU penalty ceilings apply but national procedural and sanctioning rules are unadopted, the designated supervisor has a small new unit without statutory powers, and no AI-specific decision has been issued.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI – Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Czech Republic 2030 (2024), AI Implementation Plan of the EU AI Act in the Czech Republic – Government Resolution No. 394 (2025), Czech Cybersecurity Act No. 265/2025 Coll. (2025), Amendment to Act on Police of the Czech Republic No. 273/2008 Coll. – biometric identification (2025), Amendment to Road Traffic Act No. 361/2000 Coll. – SAE Level 3 automated driving (in force January 2026), Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence and amending Act No. 87/2023 Coll. on market surveillance (draft, 2025)

Regulation Status: Côte d'Ivoire has no binding AI-specific legislation. Governance rests on the Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA 2030), launched 13 March 2025, the Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (SNGD 2030, April 2025) and the digital roadmap to 2035 presented on 1 June 2026, all non-binding strategic documents, while general instruments such as Loi 2013-450 on personal data protection touch AI only incidentally. Parliament opened its October 2026 session with AI on the agenda for member training rather than a bill.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are entirely soft: the SNIA 2030 and SNGD 2030 strategies, a proposed 'Safe AI Côte d'Ivoire' label, a public-private AI pact signed with CGECI and CCI-CI on 11 September 2026, and large announced but undisbursed investment envelopes. Institutional capacity rests on a ministry unit and the telecom/data regulator ARTCI, neither holding a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministère de la Transition numérique et de l'Innovation technologique, which drafted and owns SNIA 2030, with ARTCI and the Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d'Information acting within pre-existing digital remits. The planned national AI committee and national AI agency remain unestablished, and neither subnational authorities nor courts play any role in AI rule-making.
Actor Involvement: The SNIA 2030 was prepared through a participatory process involving public administration, private sector, academia and civil society, and industry engagement was formalised in the September 2026 AI pact with CGECI and CCI-CI, though none of these actors holds a standing statutory role. Internationally, the country works with UNESCO on AI ethics readiness and aligns with the African Union Continental AI Strategy and Smart Africa, without participation in AI standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforceable, so supervision is confined to general data protection and cybersecurity powers held by ARTCI and ANSSI, with no AI case, audit or sanction on record.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale de l'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA 2030, 2025), Stratégie Nationale de Gouvernance des Données (SNGD 2030, 2025), Stratégie numérique à l'horizon 2035 (2026), Loi 2013-450 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2013), Loi 2017-803 sur l'orientation de la société de l'information (2017)

Regulation Status: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has no AI-specific legislation or bill; AI reaches the statute book only through the Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 du 13 mars 2023 portant Code du numérique, which covers personal data, cybersecurity and digital services and mentions artificial intelligence among the ethics matters a national digital body must watch over. Policy direction now rests on the Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle (SNIA) and the Politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique (PSEN), both presented and validated by the government in Kinshasa on 4 August 2026, which carry no binding force. UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology report for the country records the absence of a dedicated AI legal framework, coordination organ or national ethics commission.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to strategy and announced spending: the SNIA and PSEN of August 2026, the Plan national du numérique 2026-2030 with its roughly USD 1.5 billion envelope, and a planned national AI academy. Institutional responsibility is shared between the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Digital Economy, the Ministry of Scientific Research and Technological Innovation and the Agence de développement du numérique, none of which holds a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Digital Economy drives AI strategy, with the research ministry and the Agence de développement du numérique holding adjacent responsibilities and the telecoms regulator ARPTC provisionally exercising the Code du numérique's digital-regulation and data-protection functions. Coordination happens through one-off drafting and validation committees, provinces play no part, and no judicial or independent review of AI has taken place.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is project-based and donor-driven: UNESCO supported the RAM assessment and the drafting of the SNIA, and public bodies, technical and financial partners and sector experts attended the validation ceremony of 4 August 2026. Domestic industry, civil society and universities contribute through these one-off processes rather than standing bodies, and international involvement runs through UNESCO and African Union membership rather than treaty or standards work.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligations exist to enforce, no authority is designated for AI oversight, and scrutiny has consisted of a single UNESCO readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 du 13 mars 2023 portant Code du numérique, Stratégie nationale de l'intelligence artificielle (2026), Politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique (2026), Plan national du numérique 2026-2030 (2026), Loi n° 20/017 du 25 novembre 2020 relative aux télécommunications et aux technologies de l'information et de la communication

Regulation Status: Denmark applies the EU AI Act directly, supplemented by Law No. 467 of 14 May 2025 (Act on Supplementary Provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence), in force from 2 August 2025, which designates Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen as national competent authorities and sets national fine powers. Prohibited-practice rules have applied since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI rules since 2 August 2025 and most remaining provisions since 2 August 2026, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) pushed Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028. A bill amending the Copyright Act to protect against realistic digitally generated imitations of personal characteristics follows the June 2025 cross-party agreement and has not entered into force.
Policy Lever: Denmark pairs the directly applicable EU AI Act with national enforcement powers under Law No. 467 of 14 May 2025, a maintained body of regulator guidance on prohibited practices and GDPR-AI interaction, and an operating AI regulatory sandbox run jointly by Datatilsynet and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen. Funding flows through the national digitalisation strategy allocation, the AI-Boost European Digital Innovation Hub and the public-sector AI taskforce.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in Digitaliseringsstyrelsen as notifying authority, lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, sharing Article 5 supervision with Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen under a statutory split. Local government implements rather than regulates, and independent review runs through the courts and the Ombudsman since administrative appeal is excluded.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society organisations and researchers contribute through public hearings, the Data Ethics Council and the regulatory sandbox, without standing seats in AI rule-making. Denmark is highly active internationally, holding the EU Council Presidency during the Digital Omnibus negotiations and sitting on the EU AI Board.
Enforcement Level: Denmark has a complete national penalty framework and has begun published sectoral inspections of prohibited AI practices, but no infringement decision or sanction under AI-specific law has been issued.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Act on Supplementary Provisions to the Regulation on Artificial Intelligence / Lov nr. 467 af 14. maj 2025 (2025), Danish Data Protection Act (2018), Joint Government Digital Strategy 2026-2029 / Den fællesoffentlige digitaliseringsstrategi 2026-2029 (2025), Bill amending the Copyright Act on protection against digitally generated imitations of personal characteristics (2025, pending)

Regulation Status: Djibouti governs AI through general digital law rather than AI-specific rules: the Code du numérique, in force since 2023 and extended in June 2025 with a 156-article personal data regime, plus Loi n°195/AN/25/9ème L creating the Autorité Nationale de Cybersécurité. The first Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA) 2026-2030 was presented at the national AI forum on 3 September 2026 as a non-binding roadmap, and the UNESCO readiness assessment accompanying it places the country at an "emerging" stage with regulation as the weakest area.
Policy Lever: Policy action rests on the SNIA 2026-2030 strategy, UNESCO- and ESCWA-supported diagnostics, skills programmes such as E-SKILLS, and a national AI prototyping competition, none of which carries legal obligations. Instruments that bind AI developers are general-purpose, and no body has a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one ministry working with the General Secretariat of the Government, with inter-ministerial focal points convened case by case for the strategy and forum. Regions have no role, and no independent body or court has reviewed AI matters, the data protection commission created by the Code du numérique still awaiting establishment.
Actor Involvement: Strategy development drew industry, academia, youth innovators and some civil society representatives into UNESCO- and ESCWA-facilitated consultations in January 2026 and the national forum in September 2026, without any permanent consultative body. Internationally, the country engages through UNESCO, ESCWA, the ITU, Smart Africa and the African Union continental framework.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: sanctions exist only in general digital and data law, no authority supervises AI, and oversight amounts to a single readiness study.
Specific Laws: Stratégie Nationale d'Intelligence Artificielle (SNIA) 2026-2030, Code du numérique (Loi n°19/AN/23/9ème L, 2023, personal data protection provisions 2025), Loi n°195/AN/25/9ème L portant création de l'Autorité Nationale de Cybersécurité (2025), Stratégie Nationale de Cybersécurité 2024-2030, Loi n°18/AN/23/9ème L portant ratification de la Convention de l'Union Africaine sur la Cybersécurité et la Protection des données à caractère personnel (2024)

Regulation Status: Dominica has no dedicated AI legislation, no binding AI rules and no national AI strategy; the September 2026 Cullen International review of the Caribbean lists only Cuba and the Dominican Republic as having adopted national AI strategies. The only adjacent national instrument is the National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, which sets digital-government and connectivity goals rather than AI obligations, and the country has not enacted comprehensive data protection legislation that regulators could apply to AI.
Policy Lever: Dominica uses no AI-specific policy levers: there are no binding instruments, no published guidance, no sandbox or AI procurement rules, and no body with an AI mandate. Digital policy runs through the National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, delivered with UNDP support, which contains no AI-specific measures.
Governance Type: AI governance in Dominica is undefined: no ministry, regulator or oversight body has been assigned responsibility for AI, and no coordination, subnational or independent-review mechanism touches it. Engagement happens through regional structures, notably the Caribbean Telecommunications Union and CARICOM, rather than any domestic institution.
Actor Involvement: Dominica runs no domestic stakeholder process on AI, so industry, civil society and academia have no structured input. Its involvement is collective and regional, as a CARICOM and Caribbean Telecommunications Union member associated with the UNESCO Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Policy Roadmap and the Caribbean Artificial Intelligence Task Force process concluded at the first Caribbean AI Forum in July 2026.
Enforcement Level: Dominica has no AI-specific obligations, penalties, supervisory authority or monitoring programme, so nothing is enforced.
Specific Laws: Dominica National Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026 (not AI-specific)

Regulation Status: The only binding AI rules are the articles of the new Penal Code (Ley 74-25), effective 3 August 2026, that criminalise the use of artificial intelligence to fabricate and disseminate false or intimate content. Governance otherwise rests on Decreto 498-23, which approved the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (ENIA) and its action plan to 31 December 2030 and obliges executive entities to coordinate AI projects with the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital. Two Senate AI bills were merged into a single text in committee on 15 September 2026 and no AI statute has been enacted.
Policy Lever: Levers are executive and promotional: Decreto 498-23 and Decreto 338-23 assign AI coordination to OGTIC and the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital, the ENIA sets priorities to 2030, and investment runs through the NVIDIA-supported Centro de Excelencia en Inteligencia Artificial (CEIA-RD) and public-sector AI training. The draft National AI Ethics Code and the merged Senate AI bill are the pending additions.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in OGTIC under the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital, with the Ministerio de Administración Pública and DIGEIG contributing public-sector ethics and interoperability work and the Chamber of Deputies running a Permanent AI Commission. Sub-national bodies hold no regulatory role, and judicial or independent review of AI has not occurred.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: industry, academia and civil society were drawn into the ENIA, the draft National AI Ethics Code and committee hearings on the AI bills, without standing statutory roles. Internationally the country is highly active through UNESCO ethics processes, the Santiago and Cartagena declarations, PARLATINO model-law work and the Red GEALC presidency.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity is limited to criminal prosecution of AI-generated harmful content under Ley 74-25, with no AI regulator, administrative sanctions or published cases.
Specific Laws: Ley 74-25 Código Penal (2025, in force 3 August 2026, AI-generated content offences), Decreto 498-23 approving the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ENIA and its action plan (2023), Decreto 338-23 creating the Gabinete de Innovación y Desarrollo Digital (2023), Draft National Artificial Intelligence Ethics Code for the public administration (DIGEIG, 2026), Merged Senate bill on the ethical and safe use of artificial intelligence (in committee, merged September 2026), National Innovation Policy 2030 (2022), Ley 172-13 on Personal Data Protection (2013)

Regulation Status: Timor-Leste has no AI-specific legislation, and the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report completed in 2025 with the Ministry of Transport and Communications confirms the absence of AI provisions in existing ICT and data-privacy law. Governance activity is confined to the Timor Digital 2032 national digital strategy, which is being revised to incorporate AI, and to foundational connectivity and cybersecurity work. Constitutional data-protection rights and general telecommunications and electronic-commerce rules apply without any provision written for AI.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of soft commitments: endorsement of the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, the 2025 UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment delivered with the Ministry of Transport and Communications, TIC Timor and Catalpa International, and the planned revision of Timor Digital 2032. No binding instrument, funded AI programme, sandbox or dedicated institution backs these commitments.
Governance Type: AI matters sit with central government, principally the Ministry of Transport and Communications and TIC Timor, with the Presidency of the Council of Ministers convening a Government Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence in August 2026. Coordination occurs through one-off projects and events rather than a standing mechanism, and neither municipalities nor independent review bodies play any part.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholder involvement has been limited to the UNESCO-led readiness workshops of April and May 2025, which convened ministries, academia, civil society and development partners on a one-off basis. International engagement is the more active channel, through the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, observer participation at the ASEAN AI Summit 2025 and accession to ASEAN and its non-binding AI governance instruments.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, penalty or competent authority exists, and the sole oversight output is the one-off 2025 UNESCO readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: Timor Digital 2032 National Digital Strategy (2023-2032), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology country report for Timor-Leste (2025)

Regulation Status: Ecuador regulates AI through subordinate rules of the data protection authority: the Norma General para la Garantía del Derecho de Protección de Datos Personales en el Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0009-R), reformed in September 2026, which imposes risk management, impact assessment, transparency and security duties on anyone using AI to process personal data, alongside the biometric-data norm that bans mass facial recognition. No statutory AI law exists: the Asamblea Nacional archived the Proyecto de Ley Orgánica de Regulación y Promoción de la Inteligencia Artificial in September 2026, and the Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el Desarrollo, Uso Ético y Gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial is before the Comisión de Educación.
Policy Lever: Ecuador combines one binding AI instrument issued by the data protection authority with a ministerial AI strategy and an advisory Comité de Inteligencia Artificial created by Acuerdo MINTEL-MINTEL-2023-0019. Funding is decentralised, and no sandbox or AI-specific procurement rules exist.
Governance Type: Governance splits between the Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales, which issues and supervises the binding AI rules, and the digital-transformation ministry that owns the national AI strategy, linked by the advisory Comité de Inteligencia Artificial. Courts and the judiciary address AI only through general constitutional standards and an unfinished internal protocol.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed into AI policy through the Comité de Inteligencia Artificial and public consultations on the Superintendencia's resolutions, with no standing formal decision role. International engagement runs through UNESCO and UNDP assistance and bilateral AI cooperation with the United Arab Emirates.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests with the Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales using the sanction powers of the Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales, and no decision under the AI norm has been published.
Specific Laws: Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0009-R, Norma General para la Garantía del Derecho de Protección de Datos Personales en el Uso de Sistemas de Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0037-R reforming that norm (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0039-R, Norma General para el Tratamiento de Datos Biométricos (2026), Resolución SPDP-SPD-2026-0007-R, Política para el Desarrollo y Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial en Procesos Administrativos de la SPDP (2026), Acuerdo Ministerial MINTEL-MINTEL-2025-0030, Estrategia para el Fomento del Desarrollo y Uso Ético y Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial en el Ecuador 2025-2029 (2026), Acuerdo Ministerial MINTEL-MINTEL-2023-0019 creating the Comité de Inteligencia Artificial (2023), Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (2021), Ley Orgánica para la Transformación Digital y Audiovisual (2023), Ley Orgánica para el Fortalecimiento de la Ciberseguridad (2026), Política Pública de Transformación Digital 2025-2030 (2025)

Regulation Status: Egypt governs AI through dedicated non-binding instruments: the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023), the National AI Strategy Second Edition (2025-2030), and the March 2026 suite comprising the Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework (edition 2.0), the National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI (edition 2.0) and the National Generative AI Guidelines, which set a four-tier risk classification and compliance pathways without legal force. The only binding instruments reaching AI are general: Personal Data Protection Law No. 151/2020 with Executive Regulations No. 816/2025 (in force 2 November 2025, compliance deadline 1 November 2026), the Fintech Law No. 5 of 2022, and the cybercrime amendments passed in February 2026, which parliament deliberately kept technology-neutral. The Draft Artificial Intelligence Law has not reached enactment.
Policy Lever: Egypt's toolkit is soft law plus capacity building: a March 2026 package of governance framework, responsible-AI guidelines and generative-AI guidelines, backed by training programmes, the Applied Innovation Center and the Egyptian AI Institute. Institutions are designated rather than empowered, and the planned AI sandbox under the July 2026 UNDP agreement has not begun operating.
Governance Type: Authority is centralised in MCIT, with the National Council for Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Computing and Emerging Technologies, renamed by Cabinet in January 2026, as apex coordinator and ECRAI operationalising the framework alongside ITIDA for technical evaluation, verification and validation. Sectoral regulators have assigned but largely dormant roles, governorates have none, and independent review of AI is limited to general court jurisdiction.
Actor Involvement: Policy development runs through MCIT with standing industry representation on the NCAI and heavy academic involvement in ECRAI's drafting committees, while domestic civil society contributes only through external commentary. International engagement is extensive, spanning the OECD, UNESCO, ITU and UNDP, without accession to a binding AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection and cybercrime law, since ECRAI's certification and audit functions under the March 2026 framework lack statutory backing and have produced no decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy First Edition (2021), Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023), National AI Strategy Second Edition (2025-2030), Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework (2026), Egypt National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI (2026), Egypt's National Generative AI Guidelines (2026), Personal Data Protection Law No. 151/2020, Personal Data Protection Law Executive Regulations issued by Minister of Communications and Information Technology Decree No. 816 of 2025, Fintech Law No. 5 of 2022, Cloud First Policy (2024), Draft Artificial Intelligence Law (2024, pending)

Regulation Status: El Salvador governs AI through a dedicated statute, the Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías (Decreto Legislativo 234 of 26 February 2025), reformed by Decreto 363 (2025), and operative secondary rules in ANIA Resolución 0001/2025, applicable since 2 September 2025, which define 'consequential decisions' and require registration in six domains spanning health, credit and insurance, biometrics, public powers, employment and education. Duties also include disclosure that a decision was AI-driven and a route to contest it before a human reviewer. Obligations apply across sectors today, but there is no penalty regime and compliance rests on self-certification and evidence requests.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through binding instruments concentrated in ANIA: Decreto 234 and its Decreto 363 reform, Resolución 0001/2025 setting registration and verification rules, and the September 2026 special provisions declaring national AI and robotics projects of public utility with direct contracting and fast-tracked permits and visas. Soft-law output is limited to ANIA's National AI Strategy Report 2026 and the UNESCO–ANIA readiness assessment; the statutory sandbox is a compliance pathway rather than a documented operating programme.
Governance Type: Authority is centralized in ANIA, a presidential agency given technical and administrative autonomy by Decreto 363, with the Agencia de Ciberseguridad del Estado handling adjacent data protection and cybersecurity duties. There is no formal multi-regulator coordination mechanism, no subnational role, and independent review is confined to internal contestation rights and Corte de Cuentas audits of AI procurement.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is executive-led, with industry involved through ANIA advisers, summits and vendor partnerships rather than published consultation, and domestic civil society and universities holding no formal role. International engagement is prominent: co-chairing the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, the UNESCO readiness assessment, and accession to the US-led Pax Silica initiative.
Enforcement Level: Supervision is designed to be supportive rather than punitive: ANIA verifies that registered entities hold controls, no AI-specific penalties are defined, and no enforcement decision has been published.
Specific Laws: Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías, Decreto Legislativo No. 234 (2025), Reformas a la Ley de Fomento a Inteligencia Artificial y Tecnologías, Decreto Legislativo No. 363 (2025), Resolución No. 0001/2025 de la Agencia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Disposiciones Especiales para la Ejecución de los Proyectos Nacionales de Inteligencia Artificial, Robótica y Otras Tecnologías Similares (2026), Ley para la Protección de Datos Personales (2024), Ley de Ciberseguridad (2024)

Regulation Status: Equatorial Guinea has no AI-specific law in force and no published national AI strategy. The Ministry of Transport, Telecommunications and Artificial Intelligence Systems has run drafting sessions in Malabo on terms of reference for a future AI law, including a proposed national AI and data authority, but no text has been published, tabled or enacted. The nearest binding instrument, Ley 1/2016 de Protección de Datos de Carácter Personal, says nothing about AI and its supervisory body remains unappointed.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of preparatory drafting work by the Ministry of Transport, Telecommunications and Artificial Intelligence Systems through its Directorate General for Artificial Intelligence Systems, listed among the government's 2025 digital regulation actions. There is no AI guidance, funding programme, sandbox or procurement rule.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one central ministry with no coordinating mechanism, no provincial involvement and no independent review. The data protection supervisory body foreseen by Ley 1/2016 remains unappointed, so no institution outside the executive touches AI.
Actor Involvement: Participation is ministry-led and episodic: sector technicians joined closed drafting sessions, and universities joined a national AI forum sponsored by Deep Learning Indaba. Domestic civil society is absent, and international engagement is limited to African Union membership and bilateral training cooperation with China and Russia.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforceable, no authority is responsible, and the one adjacent regime, Ley 1/2016, has never been enforced because its supervisory body was never appointed.
Specific Laws: Ley 1/2016 de Protección de Datos de Carácter Personal (2016), Agenda Digital para Guinea Ecuatorial (ADIGE) 2019-2025, Anteproyecto de Ley reguladora de la Inteligencia Artificial (draft, 2025)

Regulation Status: Eritrea has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no AI provision inside general law. The only relevant legal anchors are the Communications Proclamation No. 102/1998, administered by the Ministry of Transport and Communications, and the privacy guarantee of the 1997 Constitution, which has never entered into force; neither mentions artificial intelligence. There is also no data protection law or authority to which AI governance could attach.
Policy Lever: Eritrea deploys no policy levers for AI: neither binding rules nor guidance, funding, sandboxes or procurement requirements, and no body carries an AI mandate. Government activity in the digital domain is limited to state control of telecommunications through EriTel and the Ministry of Transport and Communications.
Governance Type: Governance is fully centralized in the one-party state: a single ministry oversees communications, regional administrations have no regulatory competence, and no independent court or oversight institution reviews executive decisions. Nothing in that structure is directed at AI.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is closed to industry, civil society and academia, all of which are either state-controlled or absent. International exposure is nominal: Eritrea falls within the African Union's Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024) by virtue of membership, without national follow-up, declarations or standards work.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI enforcement in Eritrea: no obligations, no penalties, no designated authority and no monitoring.

Regulation Status: Estonia enacted no standalone national AI statute and relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy duty, GPAI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations apply while Annex III high-risk duties were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. National implementation consists of authority designations published on kratid.ee and TTJA guidance, with the amendment to the General Part of the Economic Activities Code Act and the State Fees Act creating the AI regulatory sandbox and the penalty regime still in the legislative pipeline. Domestic soft-law instruments, the AI and Data Action Plan (Kratt) 2024–2026 and the Data and AI White Paper 2024–2030, carry no binding force.
Policy Lever: Estonia leans on the EU AI Act as its single binding lever and layers domestic guidance, the AI and Data Action Plan (Kratt) 2024–2026 and the Data and AI White Paper 2024–2030 on top. Funding runs through Eesti.ai and the AI Leap programme, while the regulatory sandbox and penalty provisions awaited adoption of the amendment to the General Part of the Economic Activities Code Act.
Governance Type: AI governance is split between a lead market surveillance body, TTJA, and sectoral bodies including the Data Protection Inspectorate, the Gender Equality and Equal Treatment Commissioner and RIA, coordinated by the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications. There is no sub-national layer, and independent review of AI decisions has not yet materialised in case law, although the Riigikogu State Budget Control Select Committee examined public-sector AI use in April 2026.
Actor Involvement: Industry sits at the centre of Estonian AI policy through the Eesti.ai advisory board and corporate partnerships in the AI Leap programme, while domestic civil society has no structured role. Academic input is advisory and project-based, and international engagement runs through the EU AI Board and OECD channels.
Enforcement Level: The EU penalty framework applies directly and TTJA is designated to supervise, but no enforcement action has been taken and monitoring is limited to occasional studies and parliamentary scrutiny.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), AI and Data Action Plan (Kratt) 2024–2026 (2024), Data and AI White Paper 2024–2030 (2024), Draft Act amending the General Part of the Economic Activities Code Act and the State Fees Act establishing the AI regulatory sandbox (2025), GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (2016), Personal Data Protection Act (2018), AI Action Plan (Kratt) 2022–2023 (2022), National AI Strategy (Kratt 1.0) (2019)

Regulation Status: Ethiopia governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Policy adopted by the Council of Ministers in June 2024, supported by Artificial Intelligence Institute Establishment Council of Ministers Regulation No. 510/2022, which creates the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute and gives it evaluation and certification functions over imported AI systems. Binding obligations on AI developers and deployers come only from general law, chiefly the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, and the draft National Data Governance Proclamation referred to the House of Peoples' Representatives on 28 September 2026 regulates data use for AI rather than AI systems. No cross-sector AI statute has been tabled.
Policy Lever: Ethiopia relies on institutional and promotional levers: EAII under Regulation No. 510/2022, the 2024 National Artificial Intelligence Policy, an AI Startup Center with incubation cohorts, and the general regulatory sandbox created by Startup Proclamation No. 1396/2025. No AI-specific standards, codes or procurement rules have been issued, and no compliance powers over AI systems have been exercised.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized on the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute, an autonomous federal body reporting to the Prime Minister's Office, with the Ethiopian Communications Authority enforcing data protection, the Ministry of Innovation and Technology providing policy oversight and INSA covering cybersecurity. Coordination remains informal, regional states play no role, and independent or judicial scrutiny of AI governance is absent.
Actor Involvement: The National Artificial Intelligence Policy emerged from a multi-year consultative process with industry, academia and civil society, but participation is episodic rather than institutionalized in standing bodies. Internationally Ethiopia is highly active, hosting continental AI governance dialogues in Addis Ababa, completing the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology, endorsing the Paris AI Action Summit statement and working within the African Union Continental AI Strategy and Smart Africa Alliance.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalties, enforcement decisions or audits exist, and even the general data-protection regime under Proclamation No. 1321/2024 has yet to produce published enforcement action.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2024), Artificial Intelligence Institute Establishment Council of Ministers Regulation No. 510/2022, Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, Startup Proclamation No. 1396/2025, Cybersecurity Policy (2024), Digital Ethiopia 2025 Strategy, draft National Data Governance Proclamation (2026)

Regulation Status: Fiji has no binding AI-specific legislation; AI governance commitments sit in the Cabinet-approved National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, a non-binding planning document, alongside a 2024 ministerial announcement of a framework to protect users from AI threats. Oversight of AI-related harms falls back on the Online Safety Act 2018 and the Cybercrime Act 2021, which contain no AI-written provisions, and the Ministry of Education's AI policy for schools was still at consultation stage in September 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are non-binding: the National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, a draft Ministry of Education AI policy, and the Cabinet-endorsed national privacy and personal data protection policy of October 2025. Practical activity is concentrated in donor-supported capacity programmes such as the AI Hub launched in 2024, rather than in regulatory instruments or a mandated institution.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Communications, with the Ministries of Education and Trade pursuing sector initiatives and no regulator holding an explicit AI mandate. Coordination is informal, there is no subnational tier of AI rule-making, and courts have not addressed AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic actors feed into AI policy through digital strategy consultations and the AI Hub, while domestic civil-society involvement on AI is occasional rather than structured. Internationally Fiji works through the Pacific Islands Forum, endorsing the region's first collective AI position in September 2026 and bilateral digital cooperation with Australia and India.
Enforcement Level: With no AI-specific obligations in force and no designated authority, enforcement is limited to whatever general online safety and cybercrime provisions happen to capture AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, Online Safety Act (2018), Cybercrime Act (2021), National Privacy and Personal Data Protection Policy (2025), Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026)

Regulation Status: Finland is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, supplemented by the national Act on the Supervision of Certain Artificial Intelligence Systems (1377/2025) and amendments to market surveillance, Financial Supervisory Authority and Energy Authority legislation in force since 1 January 2026. Prohibited-practice, general-purpose AI and Article 50 transparency obligations bind actors today, with Traficom supervising transparency since 2 August 2026, while high-risk system duties were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI. The second national implementing act, covering the regulatory sandbox and the register of high-risk AI used in critical infrastructure, remains in preparation.
Policy Lever: Finland combines binding EU and national AI instruments with regulator guidance from Traficom and the Data Protection Ombudsman, public AI literacy work including the Ministry of Education and Culture citizens' AI competence framework (2026), and innovation funding through Business Finland. Supervisory bodies are repurposed sectoral authorities with legal AI mandates; the statutory regulatory sandbox is not yet operating.
Governance Type: Governance is highly decentralised: fifteen sectoral authorities supervise the AI Act under Traficom's statutory coordination and single-point-of-contact role, with ministries steering legislative preparation. There is no subnational regulatory layer, and judicial and ombudsman review operates on general grounds rather than through established AI case law.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia engage through published consultations, the ministry implementation working group and stakeholder events rather than standing institutional roles. Internationally Finland is an active participant in EU AI Act governance, EU digital consortia and OECD AI cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Finland has full penalty powers and designated supervisors in place since 1 January 2026, but enforcement so far consists of guidance, complaint handling and transparency monitoring with no published AI Act decisions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Regulation (2024/1689), Digital Omnibus on AI amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), Act on the Supervision of Certain Artificial Intelligence Systems (1377/2025), Amendments to Market Surveillance of Products Act (2025), Finland's Digital Compass (2022), Artificial Intelligence 4.0 Programme (2020-2022), Finland AI Strategy (2017)

Regulation Status: France applies the EU AI Act directly: prohibitions and AI literacy since 2 February 2025, GPAI obligations since 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency since 2 August 2026, with high-risk obligations postponed to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Domestic AI-specific rules exist for deepfakes (loi SREN of 21 May 2024), algorithmic video surveillance (loi of 19 May 2023, experiment extended to 1 March 2027) and patient information on medical AI (Article L.4001-3 of the Code de la santé publique). The national designation of competent authorities and penalty rules remains in the DDADUE bill before the Assemblée nationale, leaving implementation incomplete.
Policy Lever: France relies on directly applicable EU rules plus domestic AI-specific statutes, a maintained body of CNIL, ANSSI and HAS guidance, and France 2030 funding channelled through Bpifrance and the national AI strategy. Institutional capacity rests on CNIL's AI department, PEReN's technical expertise and INESIA's evaluation work, none of which yet exercise statutory AI Act powers.
Governance Type: AI oversight is distributed across about fifteen sectoral regulators under a Ministry of the Economy-led scheme, with DGCCRF as single point of contact and CNIL slated to become the reference and coordinating authority once the DDADUE bill passes. Sub-national bodies have no regulatory role, while courts, the Défenseur des droits and the independent CNIL act as external checks.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is real but discretionary: industry and civil society respond to CNIL and ministry consultations, academia is embedded in INESIA and CNIL's audit methodology work, and no stakeholder group holds a standing statutory role. Internationally France is among the most active states, hosting the AI Action Summit and participating in Council of Europe, OECD and European standardisation processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement against AI in France is carried out under the GDPR by CNIL, with AI Act sanctioning powers not yet conferred on any authority by national statute.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, 2024), Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act (2026), General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation 2016/679), Loi n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant à sécuriser et réguler l'espace numérique (SREN), Loi n° 2023-380 du 19 mai 2023 relative aux Jeux Olympiques et Paralympiques de 2024 (algorithmic video surveillance, extended to 1 March 2027), Loi n° 78-17 Informatique et Libertés (1978, amended), Code de la santé publique Article L.4001-3 (2021), National AI Strategy under France 2030 (2021, updated 2025), National Strategy on Data and AI in Healthcare 2025-2028, INESIA Roadmap 2026-2027 (2026), Projet de loi DDADUE n° 118 (2025-2026) designating AI Act competent authorities (pending), Proposition de loi relative à l'instauration d'une présomption d'utilisation des contenus culturels par les fournisseurs d'intelligence artificielle (adopted by the Senate 8 April 2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Gabon's binding AI rules sit inside Ordonnance n°0011/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 on the use of social networks via digital platforms, which defines AI systems and AI-generated content, prohibits non-consensual deepfakes and false-attribution deepfakes, imposes labelling of synthetic content and a 24-hour takedown right, and gives the Haute Autorité de la Communication audit powers over detection systems. Loi n°025/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 amending the personal data protection law adds AI definitions and rules on automated decision-making and profiling. Coverage is confined to online content and personal data, and operators have a twelve-month period to come into conformity.;
Policy Lever: Policy runs through one binding ordinance on AI-generated content, an institutional build-out (Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes, Comité Technique National sur l'IA), and preparatory work: the UNESCO readiness assessment of 2024 and the national AI strategy drafting launched with UNDP on 28 September 2026. Economic levers remain generic innovation measures, with no AI sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Digital Economy and its Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes set policy, the Haute Autorité de la Communication regulates AI-generated content under powers enlarged by Ordonnance n°0013/PR/2026, and the Comité Technique National sur l'IA coordinates. The rules were made by presidential ordinance, and judicial or independent review of AI measures has so far been limited to a pending constitutional challenge over platform suspension.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society were convened by the Ministry of Digital Economy and UNDP for the national AI strategy diagnostic in Libreville from 28 September to 2 October 2026, and sit on the Comité Technique National sur l'IA, but these are episodic consultations rather than standing roles; the February 2026 ordinances were issued without such consultation. Internationally Gabon works through UNESCO, UNDP, UNECA, ITU and African Union frameworks.
Enforcement Level: AI-related penalties exist on paper, including imprisonment and fines up to 50,000,000 FCFA and AI use as an aggravating circumstance, but the Haute Autorité de la Communication has issued no published decision under the AI provisions and operators remain within a twelve-month compliance window.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance n°0011/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 portant réglementation de l'usage des réseaux sociaux via les plateformes numériques en République Gabonaise (2026), Ordonnance n°0012/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 modifiant le Code de la communication (2026), Ordonnance n°0013/PR/2026 du 26 février 2026 modifiant la loi n°014/2023 relative à la Haute Autorité de la Communication (2026), Loi n°025/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 portant modification de la loi n°001/2011 du 25 septembre 2011 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2023), Loi n°027/2023 du 12 juillet 2023 portant réglementation de la cybersécurité et de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2023), Décret portant création, attributions et organisation de la Direction Générale des Technologies Émergentes (2026), Stratégie nationale d'intelligence artificielle (in preparation, 2026)

Regulation Status: Gambia has no dedicated AI legislation, strategy, or binding regulatory instrument as of mid-2026. Existing ICT and data protection frameworks do not directly address artificial intelligence, and no AI-specific bills have been introduced into the National Assembly.
Policy Lever: No AI-specific policy mechanisms exist; Gambia relies on general ICT governance overseen by GICIA with no AI-targeted provisions, funding programs, sandboxes, or dedicated institutional capacity for AI.
Governance Type: Technology governance is handled centrally by the Ministry of Communication and Digital Economy and GICIA with no AI-specific remit, no inter-agency coordination mechanisms for AI, no subnational role, and no independent or judicial review of AI matters.
Actor Involvement: No structured domestic consultations with industry, civil society, or academia on AI policy have been recorded; Gambia holds AU membership and is nominally covered by the African Union AI Continental Strategy but has not actively participated in international AI governance forums or signed AI-specific declarations.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, dedicated authority, or monitoring practice exists; there are no defined sanctions or recorded enforcement actions related to AI.
Specific Laws: Information and Communications Act (2009), Gambia Information and Communications Infrastructure Authority Act

Regulation Status: Georgia has no cross-sector AI law and no adopted national AI strategy; the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report delivered in February 2026 and the June 2026 UNESCO roadmap article describe the country as at a foundational stage and propose a phased path to regulation. The one binding AI-specific instrument is the National Bank of Georgia Regulation on Managing Risks for Data-based Statistical, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models, which applies to financial institutions. The Law on Personal Data Protection No. 3144/2023, in force since March 2024, covers profiling and automated decision-making, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225), signed in September 2024, is not ratified.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by funding and donor-supported assessment rather than regulation: the 2026 State Budget earmarks AI research money, GITA supports startups, and the EU/UNESCO/PMCG readiness assessment produced the analytical base for a first national AI strategy that has not been adopted. The single binding lever is the National Bank of Georgia model risk regulation; institutional responsibility remains fragmented and thinly resourced.
Governance Type: AI-relevant authority is dispersed informally across GITA, the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development, the Digital Governance Agency, the Personal Data Protection Service and the National Bank of Georgia, without a lead body or formal coordination mechanism. Oversight from outside government is limited to analytical output such as the Public Defender's 2025 special report on AI.
