Actor Involvement: Participation is project-based: industry, civil society and academia were consulted through the EU-funded UNESCO/PMCG readiness assessment and its April 2026 Tbilisi forum, but no standing advisory structure exists. Internationally Georgia is a Council of Europe AI Convention signatory, a UNESCO Recommendation adherent and a participant in EU4Digital and Eastern Partnership digital cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement rests on general data protection powers and banking supervision, with no AI-specific penalties, no published AI enforcement decisions and no routine AI auditing.
Specific Laws: Law on Personal Data Protection No. 3144/2023 (in force March 2024), National Bank of Georgia Regulation on Managing Risks for Data-based Statistical, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models (2022), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence CETS No. 225 (signed September 2024, not ratified), Digital Governance Strategy of Georgia 2024-2029

Regulation Status: Germany applies the directly binding EU AI Act and executes it nationally through the Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-MIG), in force since 29 July 2026, which designates competent authorities, sets the national penalty framework and creates an AI regulatory sandbox. Prohibitions, general-purpose AI duties and transparency obligations apply, and penalties became applicable on 2 August 2026, but Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, leaving the regime horizontal in design yet incomplete in application.
Policy Lever: Germany combines directly applicable EU binding law with a national execution statute, a dense standards and guidance layer (DIN Normungsroadmap KI, BSI, Datenschutzkonferenz, federal administration guidelines) and economic levers including Hightech Agenda Deutschland KI funding, AI compute investment and a statutory AI regulatory sandbox at the Bundesnetzagentur. The supervisory machinery is designated and resourced but has not yet exercised compliance powers.
Governance Type: Germany runs a hybrid model: one designated central authority, the Bundesnetzagentur, with a statutory coordination function and complaints office, sitting on top of retained sectoral regulators and Länder data protection authorities, plus an instruction-free market surveillance chamber for biometric applications. Courts actively shape AI-related duties, particularly on copyright and automated data analysis, and the agency reports annually to the Bundestag.
Actor Involvement: Industry associations and research institutes have repeated, institutionalised roles in German AI policy-making and in the Hightech Agenda roadmaps, while civil society is consulted through ordinary legislative and consultation channels without a permanent seat. Germany is a frontline actor in EU law-making, Council of Europe treaty work and international AI standardisation.
Enforcement Level: A comprehensive statutory penalty and supervision framework with a designated authority and complaints channel is in force, but active enforcement began only on 2 August 2026 and no decisions, sanctions or audit results have been published.
Specific Laws: Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-MIG, 2026), EU AI Act - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI - Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Hightech Agenda Deutschland and KI-Roadmap (2025/2026), Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (2018), Federal guidelines for AI use in public administration (2025), Normungsroadmap Künstliche Intelligenz (2023), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (2024)

Regulation Status: Ghana has no binding AI legislation; the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035, launched by President Mahama on 24 April 2026, is a policy roadmap, while the Emerging Technologies Bill, 2025 (proposing an Emerging Technologies Agency) sits in public consultation and the Data Protection Bill, 2025, which would regulate AI systems, automated decision-making and deepfakes, has not been enacted. Operative rules reaching AI are the general Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), applied by the Data Protection Commission and Cyber Security Authority without AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Ghana relies on non-binding levers: the National AI Strategy 2025-2035, a UNESCO-supported readiness assessment, and funding commitments including USD 250 million for an AI Computing Centre and USD 20 million for strategy implementation. No AI-specific binding instrument, AI procurement rule or AI regulatory sandbox is in operation, and institutional capacity rests in a ministry directorate and a university lab.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, with the Data Protection Commission, Cyber Security Authority and National Communications Authority applying sectoral mandates and KNUST's Responsible AI Lab providing technical leadership. Inter-agency coordination is ad hoc through consultations and validation workshops, subnational bodies have no role, and courts have not reviewed AI matters.
Actor Involvement: Strategy development and the UNESCO readiness assessment were run by the Ministry with KNUST's Responsible AI Lab, supported by UNESCO, Smart Africa, GIZ FAIR Forward and The Future Society, and validated in separate academic, private-sector and civil-society sessions. Industry and civil society are consulted episodically rather than holding standing roles in AI policy-making.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is confined to the Data Protection Commission's general compliance drive, which moved from education to spot checks and sanctions on 5 October 2026, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or audits.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035 (launched 2026), Emerging Technologies Bill, 2025 (proposed), Data Protection Bill, 2025 (proposed)

Regulation Status: Greece is covered by the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and has enacted Law 5321/2026 on measures implementing it, published in Government Gazette A' 114 of 20 July 2026, which designates competent authorities, creates complaint and sanction procedures, a public-sector AI registry, an AI Observatory and deepfake transparency duties, and repeals the AI chapter of Law 4961/2022. Prohibited practices, general-purpose AI duties and Article 50 transparency obligations apply today, while the Annex III high-risk regime was deferred to 2 December 2027 and the Annex I regime to 2 August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). Implementation is advanced on institutions but incomplete on deadlines, standards and the regulatory sandbox.
Policy Lever: Greece combines the binding EU AI Act with national Law 5321/2026, a Special Secretariat for AI and Data Governance in the Ministry of Digital Governance and AI, literacy guidance such as the 'Artificial Intelligence for All' guide, and funded compute programmes (Pharos AI Factory, DAEDALUS supercomputer). The statutory AI regulatory sandbox and real-world testing regime exist in law but are not yet in operation.
Governance Type: Governance is decentralised across the Ministry of Digital Governance and AI with its Special Secretariat for AI and Data Governance, the HDPA as lead market surveillance authority and single point of contact, EETT as notifying authority, and sectoral regulators, with statutory coordination introduced by Law 5321/2026. Independent bodies with fundamental-rights powers and judicial remedies provide external checks; no subnational tier regulates AI.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making draws on an academic-led High-Level Advisory Committee, public consultations and two AI Act Consultation Forums attended by industry and the digital-rights NGO Homo Digitalis, with academic partnerships such as the Athena Research Center MoU. Internationally, Greece acts through the EU AI Board, EuroHPC, OECD and UNESCO-linked initiatives rather than through ratified AI treaties.
Enforcement Level: A complete national sanctions and complaints framework has existed only since Law 5321/2026 took effect in July 2026, and no AI-specific enforcement decision has been published.
Specific Laws: Law 5321/2026 on Measures Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (2026), EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI amending the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Law 4961/2022 on Emerging Information and Communication Technologies and Digital Governance (2022, AI provisions repealed by Law 5321/2026), A Blueprint for Greece's AI Transformation (2024), Law 5188/2025 implementing the Data Governance Act (2025)

Regulation Status: Grenada has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or regulatory proposal, and the September 2026 Caribbean regulatory review confirms no Caribbean state covered, including Grenada, has adopted an AI-specific framework. The closest adjacent instrument, the Data Protection Act, No. 1 of 2023, was assented to on 9 May 2023 but has not been brought into force and contains no provision written for AI. Government AI activity is confined to adoption of tools in Parliament and the public service rather than regulation.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of public-sector AI adoption — AI tools for parliamentarians and AI-enabled government services under the Division of ICT — rather than governance instruments. No national AI strategy, guidance document, sandbox or dedicated institution has been established, and the regional UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap endorsed through CARICOM is the only AI policy text Grenada has signed on to.
Governance Type: AI-related work is concentrated in a single ministry with no statutory mandate, no coordination body and no independent review. External engagement runs through CARICOM, the OECS, the Caribbean Telecommunications Union and UNESCO rather than domestic institutions.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholder engagement on AI is absent, with industry contact limited to regional technology events hosted in Grenada such as the Caribbean Internet Governance Forum. International involvement is the strongest strand: Grenada endorses UNESCO's regional AI roadmap through CARICOM and raises AI responsibly-use themes in United Nations fora.
Enforcement Level: There is nothing to enforce: no AI obligations, penalties, competent authority or monitoring programme exist in Grenada.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, No. 1 of 2023 (assented 9 May 2023, not yet in force)

Regulation Status: Guatemala has no AI-specific law in force and relies on general frameworks such as the Law on Access to Public Information, Decree 57-2008. Two tracks are open in Congress: Iniciativa 6657 (2025), which would criminalise malicious AI-generated content, and competing personal data protection bills (Iniciativas 6105, 6572 and 6626), none of which has been reported out of committee. A government AI strategy led by the Secretaría Nacional de Ciencia y Tecnología is due to be finalised at the end of 2026, with a multisectoral national strategy scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of diagnostics and strategy drafting: the UNDP-supported AI Landscape Assessment, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report delivered to the Superintendencia de Telecomunicaciones in July 2026, and the HumanIA forum convened by the Vice-Presidency and Senacyt. No binding instrument, national AI guidance, sandbox or funded national programme is in place.
Governance Type: AI governance is embryonic and executive-centred: Senacyt drafts the government strategy, the Comisión Presidencial de Gobierno Abierto y Electrónico remains the registered convenor of the Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, and the Superintendencia de Telecomunicaciones received the UNESCO ethics diagnostic. Which institution will lead AI governance is explicitly unresolved and postponed to the multisectoral process beginning in 2027.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is driven by the executive with international partners, principally UNDP and UNESCO, through assessments and the HumanIA dialogue forum. Domestic industry, civil society and academic participation is consultative and occasional rather than institutionalised; the broad multisectoral process is planned for 2027.
Enforcement Level: Guatemala enforces nothing on AI: no sanctions, authority or supervisory practice exists, and oversight to date consists of two external diagnostic studies.
Specific Laws: Law on Access to Public Information, Decree 57-2008 (incidentally touches personal data); Iniciativa 6657, bill penalising malicious use of artificial intelligence and deepfakes (2025, pending); Iniciativa 6626, Personal Data Protection Bill (2025, pending); Iniciativa 6572, Personal Data Protection Bill (2025, pending); Data Protection Bill No. 6,105 (2022, pending); UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report on AI ethics (2026); Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (in preparation)

Regulation Status: Guinea regulates AI through strategy rather than law: the Ministry in charge of Posts, Telecommunications and the Digital Economy validated a National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap for 2026-2035 on 20 December 2025, built on the UNDP Artificial Intelligence Landscape Assessment completed in October 2025. The roadmap sets out development, governance and deployment orientations but creates no obligations, and the general framework law Loi L/2016/037/AN on cybersecurity and personal data protection says nothing about AI systems.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of a validated ten-year AI roadmap, donor-supported capacity projects with the United Nations Development Programme, and the private-sector AI Xcelerate training programme launched on 8 April 2026 by the Confédération Générale des Entreprises de Guinée. Institutional ownership rests with the ICT ministry and a presidential adviser on new technologies and AI, neither vested with regulatory powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive, combining the ICT ministry with a presidential adviser charged with new technologies and artificial intelligence, and coordination with other ministries happens through one-off strategy workshops. No subnational tier and no independent review body plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Stakeholder participation has been consultative and event-based: government, business, universities and civil society were convened for the AILA assessment and the roadmap validation, while the academic DounIA initiative supplies independent analysis. Externally, Guinea works mainly with the United Nations Development Programme and attends international AI fora as an African Union member.
Enforcement Level: Nothing about AI is enforceable in Guinea, and oversight extends only to the one-off national AI landscape diagnostic.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2026-2035 (validated December 2025), Loi L/2016/037/AN relative à la cybersécurité et à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2016), Loi Plan 2026-2040 and Loi-Programme 2026-2030 for the Simandou 2040 programme (2026)

Regulation Status: Guinea-Bissau has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or binding instrument. The main digital-policy act is Decreto n.º 10/2025, which approved the Estratégia Nacional para a Transformação Digital (ENTD.GW), launched on 29 January 2025 and focused on connectivity, public-sector digitalisation and cybersecurity rather than AI obligations. Governance capacity has been further disrupted by the military takeover of 26 November 2025 and the transitional administration that followed.
Policy Lever: Guinea-Bissau deploys no AI policy levers of any kind, binding or non-binding. Digital policy effort is concentrated in the ENTD.GW strategy and donor-funded connectivity and e-government work supported by UNDP and UNU-EGOV.
Governance Type: There is no institutional architecture for AI governance: no lead body, no sectoral AI mandates, no coordination mechanism and no independent review. Digital policy ownership sits with the government ministry responsible for the digital transformation agenda and with ARN for telecommunications.
Actor Involvement: No domestic stakeholder group participates in AI policy, because no such policy process exists. International engagement is limited to development partners—UNDP and UNU-EGOV—supporting the ENTD.GW digital transformation strategy, with no AI-specific international commitment.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, sanction, competent authority or monitoring activity exists in Guinea-Bissau.
Specific Laws: Estratégia Nacional para a Transformação Digital (ENTD.GW), approved by Decreto n.º 10/2025; Lei n.º 5/2010, Lei de Base das Tecnologias de Informação e Comunicação (2010)

Regulation Status: Guyana has no dedicated AI legislation, no adopted national AI strategy and no AI bill before the National Assembly; AI-relevant rules rest entirely on general instruments, namely the Data Protection Act 2023, the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2023 and the Open Data Act 2024, none of which mention AI systems. Government activity is concentrated on AI deployment (health diagnostics with Mount Sinai, AI-backed digitisation of the National Insurance Scheme, the Cerebras sovereign AI data centre at Wales) rather than on regulation, and Minister Kwame McCoy told the 152nd Inter-Parliamentary Union Assembly in April 2026 that legislative frameworks still need to be built.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are limited to general legislation plus deployment and infrastructure deals, with no AI guidance, code of practice, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule issued. The nascent Data Protection Office is the only institution whose work touches AI-adjacent automated data processing, and its statutory remit does not mention AI.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive, with the President and the Minister within the Office of the Prime Minister driving adoption and international engagement. There is no dedicated regulator, no formal coordination structure, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent-review involvement in AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy is made within government, with industry present only as a technology supplier and civil society and academia confined to awareness events. International engagement is the most developed channel, through the Santiago Declaration, the UNESCO Caribbean AI Policy Roadmap, CARICOM and Caribbean Telecommunications Union processes, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: the only applicable penalties come from the Data Protection Act 2023, whose Data Protection Office is still being set up and has taken no AI-related action.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 2023 (No. 18 of 2023), Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2023 (No. 12 of 2023), Open Data Act 2024

Regulation Status: Haiti has no AI-specific law, decree or regulation, and no AI bill in any legislative process; the Parliament is non-functional and the transitional executive has issued no AI decree. The only texts reaching AI indirectly are the Arrêté of 15 May 2018 on personal data protection and the cyber-offence provisions of the 2020 Penal Code. A national roadmap for responsible AI adoption is being drafted outside government by Banj, the Internet Society Haiti Chapter, the École Supérieure d'Infotronique d'Haïti and the Association for Responsible AI under the Inter-American Development Bank-financed ProAI programme.
Policy Lever: Policy activity consists of funded capacity-building rather than rule-making: the IDB-financed ProAI programme run by the incubator Banj, the ProAI network launched 22 August 2026, and a Banque de la République d'Haïti research fund cohort listing AI as a priority theme. No guidance, standard, sandbox, procurement rule or AI-mandated public body exists.
Governance Type: There is no state AI governance architecture: no lead body, no interministerial coordination, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent oversight of AI. What coordination exists is private and donor-driven, through the four-party ProAI protocol and the ProAI network.
Actor Involvement: AI policy discussion in Haiti is carried by a private incubator, a civil-society internet body, a university and an AI association under an IDB-financed programme, not by a government consultation process. Internationally, Haiti participates through ITU and WSIS events and IDB cooperation, and has not joined the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because nothing binding exists; oversight is limited to a single central bank study of AI risks published in July 2026.
Specific Laws: No AI-specific law, decree or national strategy has been adopted; Arrêté fixant les règles relatives à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2018) and the Code Pénal (2020) cyber-offence provisions are the only general texts touching automated systems, and a national AI roadmap is in preparation under the Programme de création d'opportunités numériques en Haïti par l'intelligence artificielle (ProAI, 2026)

Regulation Status: Honduras has no AI-specific legislation in force and no comprehensive AI bill before the Congreso Nacional; the Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026 names AI challenges without creating obligations. The only legislative activity touching AI is a June 2026 proposal to reform the Ley Contra el Acoso Escolar so that AI-generated intimate montages and digital impersonation are punishable, which remains a narrow, unadopted use-case measure.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to soft instruments and projects: the Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026, participation in the SICA regional digital strategy, a CONATEL-ITU cybersecurity project announced in April 2026 citing AI risks, and an IDB-backed digitalisation exercise using AI tooling. No funding programme, sandbox, procurement rule or institution with an AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance of AI is effectively vacant: digital policy sits with DIGER and telecoms with CONATEL, neither with an AI mandate, and no coordinating body, subnational competence or independent review channel addresses AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic stakeholders have no structured channel into AI policy; academic contributions come through UNAH legal research rather than any advisory body. International engagement is declaratory, through the Santiago Declaration and the SICA Estrategia Regional Digital work on AI.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, penalty, supervisory authority or monitoring practice exists in Honduras.
Specific Laws: Plan Nacional de Gobierno Digital 2023-2026, Política Nacional de la República Digital 2022-2025, proposed reform to the Ley Contra el Acoso Escolar (Decreto 96-2014) penalising AI-generated content and digital impersonation (bill, 2026)

Regulation Status: AI regulation rests on the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), implemented nationally by Act LXXV of 2025 and Government Decree 344/2025 (X.31.), in force since 1 December 2025, which designate the AI notifying and market surveillance authorities, fix fine levels in forint and create the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council. Coverage is horizontal and the prohibitions, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency duties apply, but Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026) pushed Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I systems to 2 August 2028. The regulatory sandbox provisions of Act LXXV entered into force on 2 August 2026 without a published operating sandbox.
Policy Lever: Hungary relies on binding EU-derived instruments plus national designation and procedural rules, with the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 as the soft-law layer and the Artificial Intelligence Coalition as a consultation platform. Economic support runs through EuroHPC compute projects (Komondor, LEVENTE), while the statutory AI regulatory sandbox under Section 10 of Act LXXV of 2025 has no published operation and the market surveillance function sits inside a ministry rather than a standalone resourced agency.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the executive: the AI market surveillance authority, transferred to the Minister of Science and Technology by Government Decree 139/2026 (VIII.31.), acts as general authority and single point of contact, with the National Accreditation Authority notifying, the Magyar Nemzeti Bank covering AI in financial services and sectoral market surveillance authorities retaining their remits. Coordination is statutory through the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council and the Government Commissioner for AI, with judicial review available but no AI case law and no subnational role.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic actors have standing advisory seats on the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council and contributed through the Artificial Intelligence Coalition to the 2025–2030 strategy, while domestic civil society has no institutionalised role. International engagement runs mainly through EU channels, including the EU AI Board and EuroHPC projects.
Enforcement Level: Penalties up to HUF 13.3 billion are defined and the authority holds inspection and fining powers, but no AI-specific enforcement decision or monitoring report has been published since the framework took effect on 1 December 2025.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Act LXXV of 2025 on the Implementation in Hungary of the European Union Regulation on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Government Decree 344/2025 (X.31.) on the Implementation of Act LXXV of 2025 (2025), Government Decree 139/2026 (VIII.31.) amending Government Decree 90/2026 (V.13.) on the Duties and Powers of the Members of the Government (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 (2025)

Regulation Status: Iceland has no AI-specific binding law: the EU AI Act remains under scrutiny for EEA incorporation with a draft Joint Committee Decision pending, so AI is governed by the Act on Data Protection and Processing of Personal Data No. 90/2018 plus the non-binding AI Action Plan 2025-2027. The legislative programme for the 158th session of Althingi (2026-2027) lists a Bill on Deepfakes, banning certain uses of AI in line with European rules, scheduled for November 2026, and the Minister of Culture, Innovation and Higher Education announced consultation on AI legislation in autumn 2026. A draft justice-ministry bill on police use of AI facial recognition was in public discussion in September 2026.
Policy Lever: Iceland governs AI through soft law and funding: the AI Policy 2021 and successive AI Action Plans, Persónuvernd guidance, and AI infrastructure and skills measures in the Industrial Policy action plan 2026-2027. Binding levers are limited to general data protection law, and no regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rules operate.
Governance Type: AI oversight is concentrated in Persónuvernd and the Ministry of Culture, Innovation and Higher Education, coordinated case by case through implementation of the AI Action Plan 2025-2027. Municipalities have no regulatory role, and independent review of AI decisions has not yet occurred.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed in through open Samráðsgátt consultations on the AI Action Plans and regulator-industry meetings, not through standing bodies. Internationally Iceland acts through the EEA EFTA incorporation process, observer status on the EU AI Board, and Nordic and OECD cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on data protection powers exercised by Persónuvernd, with no AI-specific sanctions, designated AI authority or AI audit programme.
Specific Laws: Act on Data Protection and Processing of Personal Data No. 90/2018, AI Policy 2021, AI Action Plan 2024-2026 (2025), AI Action Plan 2025-2027 (2025), Bill on Deepfakes announced in the legislative programme of the 158th session of Althingi (2026), Industrial Policy of Iceland action plan 2026-2027 (2026)

Regulation Status: India's first binding AI-specific obligations took effect on 20 February 2026 through the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, which define synthetically generated information and impose labelling, provenance metadata, user declaration and two-to-three-hour takedown duties on intermediaries. Everything beyond synthetic media remains governed by the non-binding India AI Governance Guidelines (November 2025) with their seven Sutras and by general law including the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. MeitY began consultations in July 2026 on a possible dedicated AI law, and the AI (Ethics and Accountability) Bill, 2025 is an unenacted private member's bill.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law and money: the seven-Sutra Guidelines, the RBI FREE-AI framework and sectoral guidance from SEBI and IRDAI sit alongside the IndiaAI Mission's compute, dataset and startup funding. Binding leverage rests on a single AI-specific instrument, the 2026 IT Amendment Rules, administered by MeitY, while the IndiaAI Safety Institute and the AI Governance and Economic Group remain coordination bodies without enforcement mandates.
Governance Type: MeitY is the lead body, now supported by the inter-ministerial AI Governance and Economic Group created in April 2026 and by the IndiaAI Safety Institute's hub-and-spoke network, with sectoral regulators acting inside their remits. Courts have shaped the agenda through deepfake and personality-rights rulings, while state governments confine themselves to AI promotion rather than regulation.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is real but episodic: industry, academic and civil-society comments shaped the 2025 Guidelines and the synthetic-media rules, with academics holding the most durable roles through the drafting committee and the IndiaAI Safety Institute's research network. Internationally India is at the frontier, hosting the February 2026 AI Impact Summit and the resulting New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact alongside GPAI, G20 and AI safety institute network participation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement so far consists of ministry notices and compliance demands to platforms under general intermediary law, with the February 2026 synthetic-media duties backed by loss of safe harbour rather than by published AI-specific sanctions decisions.
Specific Laws: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules (2026), Information Technology Act (2000), Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023), Digital Personal Data Protection Rules (2025), India AI Governance Guidelines – Seven Sutras (2025), IndiaAI Mission (2024), New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact (2026), AI Governance and Economic Group (2026)

Regulation Status: Indonesia has no enacted binding AI-specific instrument: the two Presidential Regulations on AI Ethics and on the 2026-2029 National AI Roadmap, listed among 46 priority Perpres for 2026, were finalised in draft and sent to the State Secretariat but remained unsigned through September 2026. Governance rests on the non-binding Stranas KA 2020-2045, Komdigi's AI ethics circular and 2025 guidance, OJK's 2025 banking AI governance guidance, and general law on electronic systems and personal data. Derivative rules such as mandatory labelling of AI-generated content are drafted but conditional on the Perpres being issued.
Policy Lever: Indonesia governs AI through soft instruments — the national strategy, Komdigi ethics guidance and OJK banking AI governance guidance — combined with capability-building programs such as the AI Center of Excellence and university AI centers. No AI-specific binding instrument, AI procurement rule or statutorily mandated AI body is in force.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in Komdigi as orchestrator, with OJK covering banking AI through guidance and BRIN providing technical advice; inter-ministerial coordination occurs case by case during Perpres drafting. Sub-national governments have no regulatory role and independent review bodies have not engaged with AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through consultations, working groups and research partnerships, while civil society input is occasional and unstructured. Internationally Indonesia works through ASEAN AI governance instruments, the International AI Safety Report panel and bilateral AI partnerships.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs entirely through general electronic information and data protection law, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions, authority or audit regime.
Specific Laws: Indonesian Artificial Intelligence National Strategy 2020–2045 (Stranas KA, 2020), Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Informatics No. 9/2023 on Artificial Intelligence Ethics, Komdigi Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (2025), Indonesian Banking Artificial Intelligence Governance guidance (OJK, 2025), Government Regulation No. 71/2019 on Electronic Systems and Transactions, Law No. 27/2022 on Personal Data Protection, Law No. 1/2024 on the Second Amendment to the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, Draft Presidential Regulation on Artificial Intelligence Ethics (pending 2026), Draft Presidential Regulation on the National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2026–2029 (pending 2026)

Regulation Status: The National AI Development Law, approved by the Majlis on 19 August 2026, confirmed by the Guardian Council on 26 August 2026 and promulgated by Speaker Ghalibaf on 13 September 2026, is Iran's first binding AI-specific statute; it establishes the National AI Organization under the President, a four-tier risk classification of AI systems, and an AI Security Evaluation and Certification Centre. Operative obligations depend on secondary rules that do not yet exist: the organization's statute is still to be submitted to the Council of Ministers, risk-level criteria and cybersecurity directives are unissued, and Article 12 carves out security and defence bodies. Earlier instruments, the National Artificial Intelligence Document (2024) and the National AI Roadmap (2025), remain policy documents.
Policy Lever: Iran's dominant levers are state financing and institution-building: a statutory National AI Development Fund of 10,000 billion tomans, sovereign compute and data-centre programmes, and the creation of the National AI Organization as secretariat of the National AI Steering Council. Regulatory sandboxes and national AI standards are mandated by Article 7 of the National AI Development Law but are not yet operating, and no AI procurement rules or published technical guidance have been issued.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in the presidency through the National AI Organization and the National AI Steering Council, with the Supreme Council of Cyberspace and security institutions shaping digital policy and the Ministry of ICT and Vice Presidency for Science executing parts of the roadmap. There is no provincial role and no independent judicial, ombudsman or civil oversight of AI; the Administrative Justice Court has intervened in internet-access disputes but not in AI matters.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is formulated by the state, with input channelled through government research institutes and the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution rather than structured consultation of industry or civil society. International engagement runs through bilateral technology cooperation with China and Russia and BRICS membership, with no participation in binding multilateral AI governance instruments.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalty or enforcement decision exists; state action against AI services runs through the general filtering and computer-crimes regime while the statutory evaluation and certification machinery is not yet operating.
Specific Laws: National AI Development Law (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Document of the Islamic Republic of Iran (2024), National AI Roadmap (2025), Computer Crimes Law (2009)

Regulation Status: Iraq has no enacted AI legislation and no AI-specific binding instrument in force. The Communications and Media Commission opened a 30-day public consultation on 23 September 2026 on a draft Regulatory Framework for Artificial Intelligence Services in the Republic of Iraq, issued under Legislative Order No. 65 of 2004, which proposes risk-tiered licensing, data localisation, user-protection duties and fines up to IQD 200 million. The Iraqi National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (INSAIN) 2024-2030, reviewed by the Prime Minister-chaired Higher Committee for Artificial Intelligence on 21 August 2024, remains a policy instrument without legal force.
Policy Lever: Iraq relies on executive coordination and a national strategy rather than binding instruments, with the Communications and Media Commission exercising its general telecommunications and IT powers over AI services. Economic levers are limited to AI education and workforce programmes; no regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: AI policy is set top-down by the Prime Minister's Office through the Higher Committee for Artificial Intelligence, with the Communications and Media Commission acting as the sector regulator drafting AI service rules. Subnational and independent-review roles are negligible, with only a Kurdistan Region draft AI law in preparation.
Actor Involvement: The first structured AI consultation is the CMC's open 30-day comment period on the draft AI services regulation, which admits industry, specialists and other stakeholders without creating standing roles. Internationally Iraq works with UNESCO on AI ethics capacity-building and the Minister of Communications has proposed an international framework for AI and social media at the United Nations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through the CMC's general licensing and digital content powers, and the penalties and supervision proposed in the draft AI services regulation have no legal effect.
Specific Laws: Draft Regulatory Framework for Artificial Intelligence Services in the Republic of Iraq (2026, in public consultation), Iraqi National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (INSAIN) 2024-2030, Regulation for Organizing Digital Content in Iraq (2023), Legislative Order No. 65 of 2004 establishing the Communications and Media Commission, Electronic Signature and Electronic Transactions Law No. 78 of 2012

Regulation Status: Ireland's framework combines the directly applicable EU AI Act with the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, signed on 21 July 2026 and commenced on 31 July 2026, which builds the national supervision, investigation and fining machinery. Prohibitions, AI literacy, general-purpose AI duties and, from 2 August 2026, transparency and penalty provisions apply, while Annex III high-risk obligations were pushed to 2 December 2027 and Annex I products to 2 August 2028 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Coverage is horizontal and purpose-built for AI, but the regime is still inside a transition period.
Policy Lever: Ireland relies on binding EU and national AI instruments backed by designated sectoral authorities, supplemented by regulator guidance and funded AI adoption programmes. The statutory regulatory sandbox and the national AI register are provided for in the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 but are not yet operating.
Governance Type: Ireland uses a distributed, sector-based model: existing regulators act as market surveillance authorities in their own domains while Oifig IS na hÉireann coordinates, maintains the national AI register and acts as single point of contact with the European Commission. Courts enter the system mainly through High Court confirmation of fines and judicial review.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic actors hold standing advisory roles through the AI Advisory Council and the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment's AI Act implementation structures, while civil society input came mainly through consultation and Oireachtas committee submissions. Ireland is embedded in EU and Council of Europe AI governance and, as EU base for major platforms, in cross-border enforcement cooperation.
Enforcement Level: A full penalty and investigation regime is law and applicable from August 2026, but enforcement so far consists of a data-protection inquiry into an AI chatbot rather than any decision under AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: EU Artificial Intelligence Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending the AI Act (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Artificial Intelligence Act (Governance and Enforcement) Regulations 2025 / S.I. No. 366/2025 (2025), Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 (No. 31 of 2026), Digital Ireland - Connecting our People, Securing our Future: National Digital and AI Strategy (2026), AI - Here for Good: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Refresh (2024)

Regulation Status: Israel has no horizontal AI statute; regulation runs through the December 2023 Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics, sector guidance, and the Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 as amended by Amendment 13 (in force 14 August 2025). The one AI-specific binding instrument is the election-propaganda AI disclosure regime effective 26 July 2026, requiring prominent labels on AI-created or AI-altered campaign material. Government Resolution 4255 (16 June 2026) and the National AI Strategic Plan (13 August 2026) concentrate on compute, talent and adoption rather than binding obligations.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by funding and soft law: the National AI Directorate's compute, talent and acceleration programmes under Government Resolution 4255, Israel Innovation Authority grants and an operating healthcare AI regulatory sandbox run with the Ministry of Health, alongside non-binding guidance from the Privacy Protection Authority, the National Digital Directorate and financial regulators. The only AI-specific binding lever is the election-advertising labelling requirement.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-body-plus-sectoral model: the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office and the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology set strategy while the Privacy Protection Authority, Bank of Israel, Ministry of Health and Central Elections Committee apply rules in their fields. Courts and the judge-chaired elections committee have actively shaped AI practice, and no subnational tier plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia engage through published consultations, Innovation Authority programmes and advisory work on the national AI strategy, while domestic civil society is limited to occasional public comment. Internationally Israel signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence in 2024, works in OECD AI fora and pursues bilateral compute and AI partnerships.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is concentrated in two places: privacy sanctions under the Protection of Privacy Law, including monetary fines imposed on EY and PwC Israel in March 2025, and election-period removal orders against unlabelled or misleading AI campaign content since July 2026.
Specific Laws: Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 (Amendment 13, in force 2025), Election (Modes of Propaganda) AI disclosure rules for the 2026 Knesset election (2026), Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics (2023), Government Resolution 4255 'Accelerating Artificial Intelligence in Israel and Establishing Global Leadership' (2026), National AI Strategic Plan (2026), National AI Directorate establishment decision (2025), Guide for Responsible AI Use in the Public Sector (2025), Ministry of Justice Regulatory Sandbox Legislative Guidelines (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: Italy applies Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 directly and has completed its own national layer: Law No. 132/2025, the first dedicated national AI statute in the EU, and the legislative decrees adopted on 4 August 2026 under Article 24, of which Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 entered into force on 30 September 2026 covering police use of AI, biometric recognition, civil liability and new criminal provisions including Article 437-bis of the Criminal Code. The framework is horizontal and sector-specific at once, reaching healthcare, employment, education, justice, public administration, copyright and deepfakes. Major AI Act obligations for Annex III high-risk systems were postponed to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, and existing police systems have a one-year adaptation period.
Policy Lever: Italy combines binding instruments (EU AI Act, Law No. 132/2025, Legislative Decree No. 160/2026) with ministerial guidance, an AgID-ACN regulatory sandbox, AI procurement and literacy duties for public bodies, and a €1 billion state-backed venture fund. AgID and ACN carry explicit legal AI mandates; their AI-specific compliance powers entered into force only on 30 September 2026 and have not yet been exercised.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised at national level but distributed among several authorities: AgID as notifying authority, ACN as market surveillance authority and EU contact point, sectoral financial regulators, the Garante and AGCOM, coordinated through a committee at the Presidency of the Council of Ministers. Regions act only through the Unified Conference and service delivery, while courts and the independent data protection authority have both altered outcomes, through the Court of Rome's 2026 annulment of the OpenAI fine and the Garante's binding-condition opinions on the decrees.
Actor Involvement: Industry, unions and academia feed in through AgID consultations, parliamentary hearings on the implementing decrees, ministerial working groups and the expert committee behind the national AI strategy, none of which confers a standing governance role. Internationally Italy is active through its 2024 G7 presidency, EU AI Act negotiation and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI.
Enforcement Level: Penalties for AI-specific obligations are comprehensive and criminal provisions took effect on 30 September 2026, but the enforcement record so far consists of data protection decisions against AI providers rather than decisions under AI-specific law.
Specific Laws: Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapting national law to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026), EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (2026), Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 (2024), Ministry of Labour AI Guidelines No. 180/2025 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI CETS No. 225 (2024)

Regulation Status: Jamaica has no AI-specific binding instrument; the Data Protection Act (2020), the Cybercrimes Act and the Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2026) are the general laws that reach AI uses, and the Opposition's push to add express AI and deepfake provisions to the 2026 amendment was not adopted. The National Artificial Intelligence Task Force delivered policy recommendations in 2024 and the UNESCO Readiness Assessment was launched in April 2026, with drafting of a first National AI Policy and public consultation beginning in September 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through advisory and preparatory instruments: the National AI Task Force, its 2024 policy recommendations, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology report, and a public consultation platform opened in September 2026 ahead of a Cabinet-bound national AI policy. Binding levers remain limited to general data protection and cybercrime law, and the recommended National AI Policy Oversight and Implementation Committee has not been created.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Office of the Prime Minister through the Minister without Portfolio for Science, Technology and Special Projects, supported by the National AI Task Force, with sectoral regulators such as the Office of the Information Commissioner and the Broadcasting Commission of Jamaica engaging within their existing mandates. There is no sub-national regulatory layer and no judicial or independent review practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Participation is channelled through the multi-sectoral National AI Task Force drawing on private sector, academia, public institutions and civil society, reinforced by the UNESCO readiness consultation and a national public consultation platform launched in September 2026. Internationally Jamaica works through UNESCO's ethics framework, the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean AI Task Force and CARICOM regional processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement relating to AI rests entirely on general data protection and cybercrime powers, and no AI-specific sanction, decision or audit regime exists.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (2020), Cybercrimes Act (2015), Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Policy Recommendations (2024), UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report for Jamaica (2026)

Regulation Status: Japan's framework rests on the Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies, a horizontal AI statute in force since 1 September 2025 that creates institutions, effort duties and a cooperation duty rather than enforceable obligations. Implementation is advanced on the policy side, with the AI Basic Plan revised as Phase II on 14 July 2026 and the AI Utilization Guidelines of December 2025 in use, while the July 2026 APPI amendment (Act No. 56 of 2026) adds AI-relevant biometric and children's data rules within general data protection law. Proposals by the Liberal Democratic Party in April 2026 to add penalties for deepfake pornography and AI copyright infringement have not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Japan leans on soft law and money: a maintained guidance suite (AI Business Operator Guidelines v1.1, AI Utilization Guidelines, J-AISI evaluation and data-quality guides), large R&D and compute subsidies, an operating regulatory sandbox, and binding-on-government AI procurement rules requiring Chief AI Officers in each ministry. Institutional capacity is real but non-coercive, since the AI Promotion Act grants the Cabinet Office only information-gathering and advisory powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centrally coordinated through the Prime Minister-chaired AI Strategy Headquarters, with the Cabinet Office secretariat, Digital Agency, METI, MIC and the Personal Information Protection Commission acting in their own remits and J-AISI handling safety evaluation. Prefectural activity is limited to local ordinances and usage rules, and independent oversight is confined to ordinary courts.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold recurring formal advisory roles around the AI Strategy Headquarters and ministry study groups, while civil society input comes mainly through public consultations such as the June 2026 Basic Plan Phase II comment round. Internationally Japan is a convenor, running the Hiroshima AI Process and the AI safety institute network alongside OECD and standards work.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is advisory: the AI Promotion Act offers only information gathering, administrative guidance and publicity, as in the January 2026 approach to X Corp over Grok deepfakes, with monetary sanctions available only under general laws such as the amended APPI.
Specific Laws: Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (AI Promotion Act, Act No. 53 of 2025), AI Basic Plan Phase I (2025) and Phase II (2026), AI Utilization Guidelines (2025), AI Business Operator Guidelines v1.1 (2025), Act Partially Amending the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (Act No. 56 of 2026), Act on the Protection of Personal Information (2003), Copyright Act Article 30-4 (2018), Guideline for Japanese Government's Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI v2.0 (2026), Hiroshima AI Process International Guiding Principles (2023)

Regulation Status: Jordan has no cross-sector AI law; its binding AI layer is sectoral, consisting of the Central Bank of Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Framework for the Banking Sector issued in August 2025 and a Prime Ministry circular of 11 July 2026 barring AI generation or alteration of national emblems, flags and official seals across all government institutions. The economy-wide instruments—the Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Policy (2020), the National Charter of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence (2022) and the Jordanian AI Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027—remain voluntary, and Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023 contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law—the AI Policy 2020, the AI Ethics Charter 2022, the AI Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027 and the Jordanian Digital Transformation Strategy 2026-2028—plus training programs for public-sector leaders. The single binding lever applying to private actors is the Central Bank's banking AI framework, supervised by an existing regulator rather than a purpose-built AI authority.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in MoDEE's AI division, with the Central Bank of Jordan acting as the one sectoral regulator that has issued AI rules. Oversight structures are executive; no independent body or court has shaped AI rules, and no subnational tier regulates AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia were consulted in drafting the AI Policy, Ethics Charter and AI Strategy and appear in strategy governance structures, but hold no standing formal decision roles. Internationally, Jordan works with the EU, UN ESCWA, UNIDO and ITU and joins declarations rather than binding AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nascent: AI obligations carry no dedicated penalties, oversight rests on existing supervisory and administrative powers, and no AI-specific enforcement decision has been published.
Specific Laws: Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Policy (2020), National Charter of Ethics for Artificial Intelligence (2022), Jordanian Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023-2027, Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023, Central Bank of Jordan Artificial Intelligence Framework for the Banking Sector (2025), Prime Ministry Circular on the Use of Artificial Intelligence with National Emblems, Flags and Official Seals (2026), Jordanian Digital Transformation Strategy and Implementation Plan 2026-2028

Regulation Status: Law No. 230-VIII 'On Artificial Intelligence', in force since 18 January 2026, sets a risk-based, cross-sector framework with prohibited practices, labelling of AI-generated content, high-risk system duties and liability insurance, and was amended by Law No. 326-VIII of 24 June 2026. The Digital Code No. 255-VIII took effect on 11 July 2026, adding rights to explanation and human review of fully automated decisions. Implementing ministerial orders on AI-system classification criteria and trusted high-risk system lists were issued in April 2026, with further secondary acts still in preparation.
Policy Lever: Kazakhstan combines binding instruments—the AI Law, the Digital Code and administrative-offence provisions—with large state-funded programmes including the National AI Platform, Alem.ai, Astana Hub and the Qazaqstan Venture Group. Soft law lags: a unified Digital Qazaqstan concept is still being drafted, and compliance powers held by the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development have not been publicly exercised.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development as the authorised body, coordinated through a government implementation plan and the Presidential Council on AI Development. Regions have no regulatory role, and independent review of AI decisions rests on newly created statutory rights rather than an established body of case law.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic experts fed into the AI Law through parliamentary working groups and state-linked institutions such as Alem.ai, Astana Hub and Astana IT University, while structured civil society participation is limited to general public-consultation procedures. Internationally, Kazakhstan positions itself as the Central Asian leader, hosting AI & Digital Bridge-2026 and running a presidential international AI advisory council.
Enforcement Level: Penalties for AI-specific breaches are defined and the authorised ministry monitors AI content and high-risk system registration, but no enforcement decisions under the AI Law have been published.
Specific Laws: Law No. 230-VIII 'On Artificial Intelligence' (2025, in force 18 January 2026), Law No. 231-VIII amending legislation on artificial intelligence and digitalisation (2025), Law No. 232-VIII amending the Code of Administrative Offences (2025), Digital Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 255-VIII (2026, in force 11 July 2026), Law No. 326-VIII amending the Law on Artificial Intelligence (2026), Order No. 171/NҚ on criteria for classifying informatisation objects as artificial intelligence systems (2026), Presidential Decree declaring 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence (2026), Digital Qazaqstan Strategy

Regulation Status: Kenya has no binding AI-specific instrument in force. The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bills No. 4 of 2026), sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu, was published on 19 February 2026, read a First Time on 2 April 2026, referred to the Senate Standing Committee on Information, Communication and Technology, and sits at Second Reading stage; because it touches county functions it must also clear the National Assembly before assent. Regulation of AI today runs through the Data Protection Act, 2019 and the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner's Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026), which explains existing duties rather than creating AI-specific law.
Policy Lever: Kenya governs AI through soft instruments and spending rather than binding rules: the National AI Strategy 2025-2030, the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy 2026 (consultation closed 4 August 2026), the ODPC Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026), and the Kenya Bureau of Standards draft AI Code of Practice. Regulatory sandboxes run by the Communications Authority and the Capital Markets Authority accept AI-based applications, while the statutory AI Commissioner and AI authority remain proposals.
Governance Type: Policy leadership sits with the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, coordinated since 30 June 2026 through a Standing Cabinet Committee on Artificial Intelligence, with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner and sectoral regulators acting inside existing mandates. County governments have no AI role beyond what the draft policy proposes, and judicial engagement is limited to a single constitutional petition on high-risk AI systems.
Actor Involvement: Consultation on the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, the draft AI and Other Emerging Technologies Policy and the ODPC draft guidance notes drew submissions from industry, KICTANet, CIPESA, Amnesty International Kenya and university researchers, through published public-participation processes rather than standing seats. Internationally, Kenya acts through its Special Envoy for Technology, the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, Smart Africa and the African Union, without binding AI treaty commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs entirely through Data Protection Act, 2019 determinations by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or audit programme in operation.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bills No. 4 of 2026), Data Protection Act (2019), Data Protection (General) Regulations (2021), Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act (2018), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030, Draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy (2026), ODPC Guidance Note on Artificial Intelligence (July 2026)

Regulation Status: Kiribati regulates the digital sphere through general instruments - the Data Protection Act 2025, Digital Government Act 2023, Electronic Transactions Act 2021 and Cybercrime Act 2021 - none of which creates obligations for AI systems. The closest provision is the Data Protection Act 2025 right against decisions based solely on automated processing, which binds data controllers generally rather than AI developers or deployers. Parliament has no AI bill before it and the government has published no AI strategy.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is concentrated on connectivity, cybersecurity and digital government, delivered through the National ICT Policy 2019, National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020, Digital Government Master Plan and MICT Strategic Plan 2025-2028. The only AI-specific commitment is the regionally endorsed Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles, with no national guidance, funding line or dedicated AI body.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in one ministry, MICT, with its Digital Transformation Office coordinating digital reform and the Communications Commission of Kiribati handling telecoms licensing. Nothing in the structure is directed at AI, and no independent body or court has engaged with AI questions.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI happens almost entirely at regional level through the Pacific Islands Forum, where leaders endorsed the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026 as the basis for a Pacific AI Governance Framework in 2027. Domestic industry, civil society and academic participation in AI policy is absent.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity is directed at data protection and cybercrime, and no AI-related investigation, sanction or monitoring activity has occurred.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 2025, Digital Government Act 2023, Electronic Transactions Act 2021, Cybercrime Act 2021, Communications Act 2013, National ICT Policy 2019, Kiribati National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020, Digital Government Master Plan, MICT Ministry Strategic Plan 2025-2028, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026)

Regulation Status: Kosovo has no AI-specific legislation, and the only law touching AI is Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection (2019), which the Information and Privacy Commissioner confirms contains no AI-specific provisions. AI appears only in strategy documents, the e-Government Strategy Kosovo 2023-2027 and the Digital Agenda of Kosovo 2030, as a technology to be piloted in public services. Alignment work with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 began with a draft impact assessment presented by the Information and Privacy Agency on 27 February 2025 and a readiness assessment started in 2026, but no draft AI law has reached the Assembly.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to preparatory analysis: the Information and Privacy Agency's EU AI Act impact assessment (2025) and a 2026 readiness assessment for harmonisation with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. No AI-specific binding instrument, guidance, funding line, sandbox or dedicated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance is undeveloped rather than plural: the Information and Privacy Agency acts as the de facto focal point through its data protection mandate, with the Ministry of Digitalization and Public Administration handling digital strategy. Municipalities have no regulatory role, and no judicial or independent review of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Engagement happens through donor- and university-hosted events, notably the Artificial Intelligence Policy Validation Workshop at RIT Kosovo in July 2026 with government, security institutions, industry and academia, rather than through institutionalised consultation. International involvement is limited to EU accession and regional digital governance dialogues, with no AI treaty or standards commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only indirectly through Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection, with no AI-specific sanctions, decisions or auditing practice.
Specific Laws: Law No. 06/L-082 on Personal Data Protection (2019), Law No. 06/L-081 on Access to Public Documents (2019), e-Government Strategy Kosovo 2023-2027 (2023), Digital Agenda of Kosovo 2030

Regulation Status: Kuwait has no AI-specific legislation in force; AI is reached only through general ICT, data-protection and cybercrime instruments. The draft Kuwait National AI Strategy 2025-2028 and CITRA's Guide for Adopting Artificial Intelligence in the State of Kuwait v1.0 set direction without binding anyone, and the parliamentary bill to establish a Public Authority for Artificial Intelligence has not been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments and promotion: the draft National AI Strategy 2025-2028, CITRA's AI adoption guide, the Central Bank of Kuwait Wolooj sandbox AI cohort, and government-Microsoft skilling and data-centre programmes. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry created a commercial activity category for AI services in August 2026, a licensing step rather than an AI compliance regime.
Governance Type: AI responsibilities are spread across CAIT, CITRA, the National Cybersecurity Center, the Central Bank of Kuwait and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, linked only by ad hoc project cooperation. Governance is centralised in the executive, with no sub-national tier and no judicial or independent oversight of AI.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led with business input through CITRA consultation and vendor partnerships, plus an ILO-Kuwait Chamber of Commerce and Industry study of private-sector AI adoption. Domestic civil society is absent while international engagement is prominent through the Digital Cooperation Organization and GCC channels.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced; supervision of AI users rests on general data-protection, cybercrime and banking powers that have produced no recorded AI case.
Specific Laws: Kuwait National AI Strategy 2025-2028 (draft), Guide for Adopting Artificial Intelligence in the State of Kuwait v1.0 (CITRA, 2026), CITRA Data Privacy Protection Regulation (Decision No. 26 of 2024), Cybercrime Law No. 63 of 2015, National Cybersecurity Center (Decision No. 37 of 2022), Kuwait Vision 2035 (2017), draft bill establishing the Public Authority for Artificial Intelligence

Regulation Status: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (Law No. 178 of 31 July 2025), brought into force on 6 February 2026 by Law No. 179, defines AI systems and AI systems of heightened danger, sets principles for their design, development and application, imposes restrictions and liability, and grants a right to human review of algorithmic and automated decisions. These binding provisions apply across sectors but depend on secondary acts that are still at draft stage, and no standalone AI statute has been tabled in the Jogorku Kenesh.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through the AI chapter of the Digital Code plus executive instruments: the Concept of Digital Transformation for 2024-2028, the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development created by Cabinet Resolution No. 29 of 22 January 2025, and a draft Regulation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence under public consultation. Funding, sandbox and procurement levers remain at announcement stage.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies drafts rules and the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development coordinates across ministries. Sub-national bodies have no role, and review of AI decisions exists on paper through the Digital Code's right to human reconsideration rather than through active judicial or independent oversight.
Actor Involvement: Participation is executive-led, with stakeholders reaching AI policy mainly through the public-consultation procedure for Cabinet acts such as the draft AI ethics regulation. Internationally the country works through Eurasian Economic Union, CIS and Central Asian digital cooperation and UNESCO ethics commitments rather than binding AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: AI obligations in the Digital Code are in force but unenforced: penalties remain in a bill at first reading, no supervisory body with an AI remit has been resourced, and the planned ethics and safety assessments for state AI systems are still a draft.
Specific Laws: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (Law No. 178 of 31 July 2025, in force 6 February 2026), Law on Enactment of the Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (No. 179 of 31 July 2025), Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 29 of 22 January 2025 on the National Council on Artificial Intelligence Development (as amended by Resolution No. 844 of 29 December 2025), Concept of Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028, draft Regulation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2026)

Regulation Status: Laos has no binding AI rule in force, before the National Assembly, or formally proposed. The only AI-specific document is the draft National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence 2026-2035, which the government approved in principle at its September 2026 monthly meeting and sent back to the Ministry of Technology and Communications for revision on infrastructure, databases, personnel and priority applications. General ICT instruments, namely the Law on Telecommunications (2011), Law on Electronic Transactions (2012, amended 2022), Law on Cyber Crime (2015) and Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017), address AI nowhere in their text.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy drafting, the UNESCO-supported AI Ethics Readiness Assessment report, and investment promotion for AI and data centres under the 2026-2030 investment plan. No AI-specific binding instrument, national AI guidance, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Authority over AI sits entirely with the Ministry of Technology and Communications, which drafts the national strategy under Prime Ministerial direction. Coordination with other ministries occurs only through cabinet-level review of draft documents, and no subnational, judicial or independent body exercises AI oversight.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academia were consulted once through the UNESCO-led readiness assessment completed in January 2026 but hold no standing role in AI policy formation. International engagement runs through UNESCO, the UN Country Team, ESCAP's APCICT and ASEAN digital instruments rather than binding treaty or standards work.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: sanctions reach AI only through general cybercrime and electronic data law, no authority owns AI enforcement, and the sole assessment is the one-off UNESCO readiness report.
Specific Laws: Draft National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence 2026-2035 (approved in principle September 2026), AI Ethics Readiness Assessment Methodology Country Report (2026), National Digital Economy Strategy (2024), Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017), Law on Cyber Crime (2015), Law on Electronic Transactions (2012, amended 2022), Law on Telecommunications (2011)

Regulation Status: Latvia applies the EU AI Act directly, with prohibitions, general-purpose AI rules and Article 50 transparency obligations applying and Annex III high-risk duties postponed to December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). National legislation adds the Law on the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre, amended on 14 May 2026, and the Financial Market Digital Operational Resilience and Artificial Intelligence Use Law in force since 1 October 2025, alongside Criminal Law deepfake provisions. Competent authorities were allocated by Cabinet-level informative report rather than by a general implementing statute, and sandbox secondary rules and Centre operations lag.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through binding EU and national instruments — the AI Act, the AI Centre Law and the financial market AI law — with the AI Centre's special regulatory environment as the main innovation tool. Guidance remains thin and institutions hold AI mandates that have not yet been used in compliance practice.
Governance Type: Latvia governs AI through a lead ministry, VARAM, plus a wide spread of sectoral market surveillance authorities, with Latvijas Banka supervising financial-sector AI and the Data State Inspectorate covering prohibited practices. The Ombudsman supplies independent fundamental rights oversight; no subnational tier has a role.
Actor Involvement: The Artificial Intelligence Centre institutionalises industry and university participation through LIKTA and the Latvian Universities Association as co-founders with VARAM, while civil society input comes through public consultation on draft laws. External engagement runs through EU structures, Baltic digital cooperation and OECD reporting.
Enforcement Level: Penalty ceilings exist in EU and national law and supervisors are named, but no AI-specific enforcement decision or routine AI monitoring has been published in Latvia.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, 2024), Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, 2026), Law on the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre (Mākslīgā intelekta centra likums, 2025) with amendments of 14 May 2026, Financial Market Digital Operational Resilience and Artificial Intelligence Use Law (Finanšu tirgus digitālās darbības noturības un mākslīgā intelekta izmantošanas likums, 2025), Criminal Law Section 90.1 on influencing the election process using deepfake technology (2024), Digital Transformation Guidelines 2021-2027 (2020), National AI Strategy 'Par mākslīgā intelekta risinājumu attīstību' (2020)

Regulation Status: Lebanon has no binding AI legislation. Governance rests on the National Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched on 7 November 2025 by the Office of the Minister of State for Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence, a Cabinet-approved draft law to create a Ministry of Technology and Artificial Intelligence referred to joint parliamentary committees in July 2026, and a draft Digital Authority law. AI-related conduct falls under general instruments, principally Law No. 81/2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data, which contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through non-binding strategy, ministerial memoranda of understanding with advisory firms such as Roland Berger and Sofrecom, and funded capacity-building programmes including NUMŪ and the UAE-supported AI training initiative, supported by the World Bank Digital Acceleration Project approved in January 2026. No AI-specific binding instrument, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and the lead office has no legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in a single ministerial office that drafts strategy and legislation, with sectoral regulators holding no AI mandate and coordination confined to interministerial committees announced in the roadmap. Parliament's joint committees are reviewing the MITAI bill, but no independent or judicial body shapes AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led and event-based: industry, donors and academia are convened at MITAI summits and through advisory memoranda, while digital-rights organisations such as SMEX comment publicly without a formal seat. Internationally Lebanon works with the Digital Cooperation Organisation, UNESCO, UN ESCWA, the World Bank and the United Arab Emirates rather than in treaty or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and the only penalties that could reach AI use are those of general law, with no authority, audit or monitoring practice in place.
Specific Laws: National Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025), Draft Law establishing the Ministry of Technology and Artificial Intelligence (MITAI) (2025, pending before Parliament), Draft Digital Authority Law (2025, pending before Parliament), Law No. 81/2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data

Regulation Status: Lesotho governs AI through a non-binding national policy instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (2025), led by the Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation, alongside general law in the Data Protection Act 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012) and sector powers of the Lesotho Communications Authority. In August 2026 the Ministry and the United Nations ran a five-day Maseru workshop to develop a National AI Strategy and Data Centre Blueprint, and in September 2026 Lesotho became the first country to apply the United Nations Blueprint for National AI and Data Strategies. No binding AI obligation, high-risk duty or AI regulator exists in law, and the Cybercrime Bill 2026 and Cybersecurity Bill 2026 remain in stakeholder consultation.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through a ministry-led national AI policy, UN-supported strategy and compute roadmap work, and capacity-building workshops. No AI-specific binding instrument, funded program, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule is in place, and digital governance capacity rests with the Lesotho Communications Authority under a general ICT mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation, which authored the Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (2025), with sectoral powers held only by the Lesotho Communications Authority. Coordination is project-based around UN-supported workshops, and there is no subnational, judicial or independent-review involvement in AI governance.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement of industry, civil society and academia occurs through occasional UN- and UNDP-supported events rather than formal consultation or standing bodies. Internationally Lesotho is an active participant, piloting the UN Blueprint for National AI and Data Strategies and drawing on the African Union Continental AI Strategy and the EU AI Act as reference points.
