Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI-specific obligation is in force, leaving only untested general data-protection penalties and a planned monitoring framework on paper.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Implementation Plan (2025, draft), Data Protection Act 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012), Lesotho Communications Authority Act (2012), ICT Policy (2005), Cybercrime Bill 2026 (pending), Cybersecurity Bill 2026 (pending)

Regulation Status: Liberia has no dedicated AI legislation, no national AI strategy and no binding AI-specific instrument. The legal base built in 2026 is general: President Joseph Boakai signed the Cybercrime Act and the Data Protection Act of Liberia, and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued the "Whole of Government" National Digital Strategy (2025-2029) and a Draft National Data Governance Policy (2026), none of which regulates AI systems, models or outputs.
Policy Lever: Policy activity on AI consists of UNDP-supported capacity building: the AI Training Programme for ministries and public institutions, the UNDP AI Sprint, a UNDP-Intel AI capacity partnership, and work with the University of Liberia on a first Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence. No binding AI instrument, published AI guidance, sandbox, procurement rule or designated AI body exists.
Governance Type: AI-adjacent oversight defaults to the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications and the Liberia Telecommunications Authority under general ICT law, a single centralized channel with no AI remit. There is no multi-body coordination, no subnational function and no independent or judicial review touching AI.
Actor Involvement: Involvement in AI is driven by UNDP and partners such as Intel rather than by domestic stakeholders, with the University of Liberia as the main national counterpart. Industry and civil society have no structured role because no domestic AI policy process has been opened.
Enforcement Level: Liberia has no AI-specific enforcement framework, sanctions, designated authority or monitoring practice.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act of Liberia (2026), Cybercrime Act (2026), "Whole of Government" National Digital Strategy (2025-2029), Draft National Data Governance Policy (2026), National Cybersecurity Strategy (2025-2029)

Regulation Status: Libya has no binding AI legislation. Governance rests on two non-binding instruments: the National Artificial Intelligence Policy launched by the General Authority for Communications and Informatics on 17 May 2024, and the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 with the National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics adopted in Tripoli on 1 June 2026, whose legislation-and-ethics pillar only promises a future legal framework.
Policy Lever: Policy runs entirely through soft instruments: the National Artificial Intelligence Policy (2024), the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 and the National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics. Institutional capacity is a ministerial portfolio created without an autonomous structure, and the strategy's 35 initiatives, including a National Artificial Intelligence Authority and a National Academy for Artificial Intelligence, remain unfunded plans.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Government of National Unity's Prime Minister's Office through the Minister of State for Digital Economy and Artificial Intelligence, with the General Authority for Communications and Informatics as the other state actor. Coordination is ad hoc through ministerial consultation, no sub-national tier is involved, and no independent review mechanism exists.
Actor Involvement: Consultation on the 2026-2030 strategy was conducted inside the state apparatus, with all thirteen participating bodies being ministries, state regulators or state-linked companies, and civil society, independent academia and private industry excluded. Externally, Libya attends United Nations and International Telecommunication Union AI governance dialogues and is an African Union and UNESCO member.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI-specific obligation is in force, no authority owns AI oversight, and the strategy's monitoring pillar remains unimplemented.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 (2026), National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Policy of the State of Libya (2024), Law No. 5 of 2022 Regarding Combating Cybercrimes, Law No. 6 of 2022 Concerning Electronic Transactions

Regulation Status: Liechtenstein has no AI-specific binding legislation in force: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and its amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, 8 July 2026) are marked EEA-relevant but remain under scrutiny by the EEA EFTA states, and the government states in BuA Nr. 34/2026 that both the AI Act and the Digital Services Act will apply directly only after EEA incorporation. The sole domestic AI-specific instrument is the non-binding KI-Strategie der Liechtensteinischen Landesverwaltung adopted on 14 April 2026, which governs the administration's own use and imposes mandatory staff training. AI in the market is reached only through general instruments: the Datenschutzgesetz, financial-market rules, and the criminal, media and personality law catalogue described in the deepfake Postulat response.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments: the Datenschutzstelle's AI chatbot guidance under data protection law, the Stabsstelle für Digitale Innovation's AI Act information material, and the April 2026 public-administration AI strategy prepared by the Task Force Künstliche Intelligenz. The Datenschutzstelle and the Finanzmarktaufsicht act on AI within existing mandates, without a dedicated AI remit, AI sandbox or AI procurement rules.
Governance Type: Competence is spread thinly across the Datenschutzstelle, the Finanzmarktaufsicht and the Stabsstelle für Digitale Innovation, which represented Liechtenstein at the EU AI Board through the Office for Financial Market Innovation and Digitalisation, with the Task Force Künstliche Intelligenz providing the only standing cross-office coordination. There is no subnational layer and no AI-specific judicial or ombudsman practice.
Actor Involvement: International engagement dominates: participation in drafting and signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, observer presence at EU AI Board meetings, and EEA EFTA scrutiny of the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus on AI. Domestic industry, civil society and academic input remains informal and case-by-case, without a standing AI consultation body.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is limited to general data protection, criminal and civil law, with no AI-specific sanctions, no designated AI authority and no AI enforcement decisions on record.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024, pending EEA incorporation), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Digital Omnibus on AI (2026, under EEA EFTA scrutiny), KI-Strategie der Liechtensteinischen Landesverwaltung (2026, non-binding), Postulatsbeantwortung betreffend Massnahmen gegen Missbrauch durch Deepfakes BuA Nr. 34/2026 (2026), Interpellationsbeantwortung betreffend Künstliche Intelligenz, Cloud-Computing und technologische Infrastruktur BuA Nr. 59/2026 (2026), Datenschutzgesetz (2019), Cyber-Sicherheitsgesetz LGBl. 2025/111 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence CETS 225 (signed 2025)

Regulation Status: Lithuania governs AI through the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI literacy, GPAI and Article 50 transparency and marking obligations apply, while Annex III high-risk obligations were pushed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). National implementation rests on the January 2025 amendments to the Law on Technology and Innovation (XV-105) and the Law on Information Society Services (XV-106), effective 1 April 2025, which named the Communications Regulatory Authority (RRT) as market surveillance authority and single point of contact and the Innovation Agency as notifying authority. A dedicated Law on Implementation of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, distributing high-risk supervision across eleven bodies and setting complaint, investigation and liability procedures, remains in the Seimas.
Policy Lever: Binding force comes from the EU AI Act and the two January 2025 implementing laws, supplemented by RRT guidance, the Seimas resolution on public-sector AI use and the 2026–2035 National AI Strategic Guidelines. Economic levers are substantial: an operating €3 million AI regulatory sandbox at the Innovation Agency, Lithuanian-language AI resources exceeding €42 million, an SME adoption programme and the LitAI innovation hub, plus a GovAI competence centre set up in February 2026 for the public sector.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised around RRT as single coordinating authority with the Innovation Agency as notifying authority and sandbox operator, and the pending implementation law would extend sectoral supervision to eleven bodies including the Bank of Lithuania, the Lithuanian Transport Safety Administration and the National Agency for Education. Sub-national bodies have no role, and non-governmental checks are limited to general administrative judicial review.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed in through the National AI Governance Forum, ministry consultations on the draft implementation law and the Innovation Agency sandbox, while domestic civil society takes part only episodically and holds no standing role. International engagement is active through the EU AI Board, EU standardisation work and Council of Europe and OECD processes.
Enforcement Level: The EU AI Act's penalty ceilings apply and RRT answers queries and publishes guidance on the transparency rules in force, but no AI-specific investigation, decision or audit programme has been documented pending adoption of the national implementation law.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Law on Technology and Innovation amendments No. XV-105 (2025), Law on Information Society Services amendments No. XV-106 (2025), Draft Law on Implementation of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategic Guidelines 2026-2035 (2026), Lithuanian Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), AI Strategy Action Plan 2023-2026

Regulation Status: Luxembourg's binding AI framework is the directly applicable EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), whose prohibitions and AI literacy duty have applied since February 2025 and general-purpose AI obligations since August 2025, while Annex III high-risk requirements were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). The national implementing instrument, Bill of Law 8476 filed on 23 December 2024, designating competent authorities and national penalties, remains in committee after Conseil d'État objections on arbitration between authorities. The CNPD acts as de facto coordinator pending that adoption.
Policy Lever: The binding lever is the EU AI Act, supplemented by CNPD soft law (AI literacy guidance, sandbox materials, training) and ILNAS standardisation work. Economic levers are substantial: the MeluXina-AI AI Factory, the June 2025 Mistral AI partnership, the Accelerating Digital Sovereignty 2030 national AI strategy and the ReMI regulatory sandbox, whose pilot ran in 2025-2026 with a new submission round from August 2026.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-plus-sectoral model: the CNPD is the proposed national coordinator, single contact point and default market surveillance authority, with roughly a dozen sectoral regulators each holding their own remit, and ALIA additionally named a fundamental rights authority. Coordination is currently informal because the statutory arbitration rules are still being revised in committee; there is no subnational layer.
Actor Involvement: Industry input is channelled through Luxembourg's statutory professional chambers and federations, which formally opined on Bill 8476, while academic actors engage through LIST, the University of Luxembourg, the AI Factory and the ReMI sandbox. Domestic civil society participation in AI policy is marginal; internationally Luxembourg is active in the EU AI Board, the EU AI Office network, OECD work and European AI standardisation.
Enforcement Level: EU-level fines are available in principle but Luxembourg has designated no final enforcement authorities, published no AI-specific decisions and runs no AI audit programme, leaving enforcement preparatory.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Bill of Law No. 8476 implementing the AI Act (2024, pending), Accelerating Digital Sovereignty 2030 – National AI Strategy (2025), Law of 4 April 2025 implementing the Digital Services Act, Law of 28 February 2025 implementing the General Product Safety Regulation, Bill of Law No. 8364 transposing NIS2 (2024)

Regulation Status: No dedicated AI statute, adopted national AI strategy or binding AI rule exists; AI is governed indirectly through the GDPR-aligned Law on Personal Data Protection (2020) and framed by the non-binding ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK 2030 (2025). A first draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy was discussed by the Ministry of Digital Transformation working group on 18 September 2026 for publication on the ENER consultation portal, with adoption targeted for end-2026 and a separate law on AI use announced as a follow-up activity. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225), signed on 8 May 2026, is not yet ratified or transposed.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through non-binding strategy documents and funded infrastructure rather than regulation: SMART/MK 2030, the draft AI strategy, and the Vezilka National Centre for Artificial Intelligence linked to the European AI Factory network. No regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rules, or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised: the AZLP enforces data protection and the Ministry of Digital Transformation leads AI strategy through an ad hoc working group, with no sectoral AI regulators and no municipal role. Independent scrutiny is limited to the State Audit Office audit of AI readiness in the public sector and the parliamentary hearing on it.
Actor Involvement: Domestic input is channelled through an ad hoc ministerial working group of experts and the academic sector, with FINKI running the national AI centre; civil society and industry associations have no standing role. International engagement is the strongest channel: the CETS No. 225 signature, EuroHPC participation, and EU accession alignment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through general data-protection supervision by the AZLP, with no AI-specific sanctions, decisions, authority or recurring monitoring.
Specific Laws: Law on Personal Data Protection / ZZLP (2020), ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK 2030 (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS No. 225 (signed 8 May 2026), draft National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2026), State Audit Office performance audit report on the possibility of using artificial intelligence in the public sector (2025)

Regulation Status: Madagascar has no AI-specific legislation and none in the legislative process. Governance of AI falls back on general instruments — Loi n° 2014-038 du 9 janvier 2015 sur la protection des données à caractère personnel with its Décret d'application n° 2023-1541, and Loi n° 2014-006 sur la lutte contre la cybercriminalité — none of which addresses AI systems, and the data protection authority they establish is not yet operational.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to broad digital transformation under the Plan Stratégique Numérique 2023-2028 and sectoral AI deployments such as the Malagasy customs digital strategy to 2029 and civil-registry digitisation. No AI strategy, guidance, sandbox or AI-mandated institution has been created.
Governance Type: AI matters sit entirely with the Ministère du Développement Numérique, des Postes et des Télécommunications, with no sectoral regulator, coordination body or subnational authority holding an AI remit. Independent review is absent, the data protection authority CMIL still being set up.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is almost entirely external and ministerial: participation in the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI, the World AI Conference in Shanghai and African Union digital frameworks. Domestic industry involvement runs through bilateral and donor projects rather than policy processes, and civil society and academia have no consultative role.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, and the general data protection and cybercrime penalties that could reach AI remain unused with the CMIL not yet operational.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 2014-038 du 9 janvier 2015 sur la protection des données à caractère personnel (2014), Décret n° 2023-1541 d'application de la loi n° 2014-038 (2023), Loi n° 2014-006 sur la lutte contre la cybercriminalité (2014), Plan Stratégique Numérique 2023-2028

Regulation Status: Malawi has no AI-specific binding instrument; the Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (2016) and the Data Protection Act (2024), in force since 3 June 2024 with MACRA as data protection authority, are the only laws reaching AI and contain no AI provisions. A National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and an accompanying AI Bill covering government and private-sector AI use are in drafting under the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, with the bill announced for tabling before December 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of preparatory instruments: a draft National AI Strategy under validation, a UNESCO-supported AI Readiness Assessment Report validated in July 2026, and MACRA's regulatory sandbox that accepts AI projects. No funded national AI programme, AI procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology, with MACRA as the only regulator applying law to AI use and no inter-agency AI mechanism. Oversight comes from parliamentary committee briefings and civil society and investigative-journalism pressure rather than from courts or an independent AI review body.
Actor Involvement: Consultation on AI has begun through national strategy workshops, the UNESCO readiness assessment and the COMESA regional process, drawing in government, industry, academia and development partners. Domestic civil society engages mainly by challenging MACRA's surveillance and monitoring activity rather than through standing consultative roles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on general communications, cybercrime and data protection powers exercised by MACRA, amounting so far to public warnings and police cooperation rather than decisions under AI-specific rules.
Specific Laws: Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (2016), Data Protection Act (2024), Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), draft Artificial Intelligence Bill (2026)

Regulation Status: Malaysia has no binding AI-specific legislation in force. The AI Governance Bill, drafted by the Ministry of Digital and the National AI Office, went through public consultation from 10 to 31 July 2026 and is now expected in the Dewan Rakyat in early 2027 with a risk-based design; the Cybercrimes Bill 2026, passed by the Dewan Rakyat on 1 July 2026 and the Dewan Negara on 20 July 2026, creates offences for deepfakes and digitally manipulated intimate images but awaits royal assent and a commencement date. AI is otherwise governed by general law and by the non-binding National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (2024) and MY-AI Standards platform.
Policy Lever: Malaysia governs AI through soft law and economic levers: the AIGE guidelines, MY-AI Standards platform, National AI Action Plan 2026-2030, startup and talent funding, and Bank Negara Malaysia's discussion paper on AI in the financial sector. Institutional capacity sits with AI Malaysia Berhad, MDEC, CyberSecurity Malaysia and the Department of Personal Data Protection, none of which holds an AI-specific legal mandate pending the AI Governance Bill.
Governance Type: Policy is centralised in the Ministry of Digital through AI Malaysia Berhad, which institutionalised the National AI Office in July 2026, with sectoral regulators applying their own remits to AI. Subnational governments have no regulatory role and independent or judicial review of AI matters is undeveloped.
Actor Involvement: Consultation on the AI Governance Bill in July 2026 was open to industry, academia, civil society and the public through the National AI Office and the Unified Public Consultation portal, but no group holds a standing formal role. Internationally Malaysia is active in ASEAN AI governance work, bilateral AI partnerships and international standards alignment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under general communications, online safety and data protection law, with no AI-specific sanctions, authority or audit regime pending the AI Governance Bill.
Specific Laws: National AI Roadmap (AI-Rmap 2021-2025), National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE 2024), Cybersecurity Act 2024, Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024, Online Safety Act (Act 866, in force 1 January 2026), MY-AI Standards Platform (2026), National AI Action Plan 2026-2030, Cybercrimes Bill 2026 (passed by both Houses July 2026, not yet in operation), proposed AI Governance Bill (public consultation July 2026)

Regulation Status: Maldives has no binding AI-specific legislation; the National AI Masterplan 2025–2035, announced by President Mohamed Muizzu in October 2024 and recommended for finalisation by the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report of 31 July 2025, is still in draft. Legislative activity in 2026 under the Maldives 2.0 agenda covers data protection, digital identity and digital transformation rather than AI systems, leaving AI addressed only incidentally through general digital and media law.
Policy Lever: The instruments used are strategy drafting, international ethics alignment and capacity-building ventures such as the Maldives AI Lab created with Bank of Maldives in 2026. No binding AI instrument, regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rule or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Homeland Security, Labour and Technology, executed by the Maldives Digital Service and the state-owned Maldives Innovation and Digital Company (MINDCo). Coordination with other agencies has been project-based through the UNESCO readiness assessment, and no subnational or independent-review layer exists.
Actor Involvement: Engagement has been driven by UNESCO's readiness assessment, which drew in government agencies, academics and some stakeholders, and by a public-private AI Lab with Bank of Maldives. Domestic industry and civil society hold no standing formal role in AI policymaking.
Enforcement Level: Nothing in Maldivian law creates AI obligations to enforce, and no authority has opened an AI case or conducted AI audits.
Specific Laws: National AI Masterplan 2025–2035 (draft, announced 2024), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report for Maldives (2025), Maldives Communications Authority / ICT Act (2017), Privacy and Personal Data Protection Bill (submitted to the People's Majlis, 2026), Maldives 2.0 Digital Transformation Bill (2026), Digital Identity Bill (2026), Maldives Media and Broadcasting Regulation Act (Act No. 16/2025)

Regulation Status: Mali's only AI-specific legal text is Ordonnance n°2023-022/PT-RM of 4 August 2023 creating the Centre d'Intelligence Artificielle et de Robotique du Mali (CIAR-Mali) as a public scientific and technological establishment, ratified by the Conseil national de Transition in October 2023 and implemented by a decree on the centre's organisation and functioning. That text establishes a training and research body and imposes no obligations on AI developers or users, and no AI bill, decree or regulation governing AI systems has been tabled. General law, chiefly Loi n°2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on personal data protection, contains no provision written for AI.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through institution-building and public investment rather than regulation: CIAR-Mali, created by ordinance in 2023, received a CFA 3.3 billion campus inaugurated in September 2026 and begins degree training in AI, robotics and data science. The government also decided in April 2026 to hold an annual national AI forum, while the Politique Nationale de Développement de l'Économie Numérique validated in October 2024 provides the broader digital framework without AI-specific guidance or standards.
Governance Type: AI matters are handled executively by transition-government ministries, with the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research supervising CIAR-Mali and the Ministry of Communication and Digital Economy owning digital policy; no AI regulator exists. Regional and local authorities have no role, and courts and independent bodies have not reviewed AI measures.
Actor Involvement: Involvement is state-led and narrow: public research and training institutions carry AI activity, industry and diaspora experts are to be convened through an annual national AI forum announced in April 2026, and domestic civil society has no formal channel. International engagement runs through the Alliance des États du Sahel and UN membership rather than AI-specific governance processes, Mali being suspended from the African Union and outside ECOWAS.
Enforcement Level: AI is unenforced in Mali: no AI-specific obligations, penalties, enforcement authority or audit programme exist, and only the data protection regime offers incidental reach.
Specific Laws: Ordonnance n°2023-022/PT-RM du 04 août 2023 portant création du Centre d'Intelligence Artificielle et de Robotique du Mali (2023), Décret n°2023-0420/PT-RM fixant l'organisation et les modalités de fonctionnement du CIAR-Mali (2023), Loi n°2013-015 du 21 mai 2013 portant protection des données à caractère personnel (2013, amended 2017), Politique Nationale de Développement de l'Économie Numérique (2024)

Regulation Status: Malta's binding framework is the EU AI Act, operationalised nationally by Legal Notice 226 of 2025 (Artificial Intelligence Regulations) and Legal Notice 227 of 2025 designating the Information and Data Protection Commissioner. Prohibitions, general-purpose AI duties, AI literacy and Article 50 transparency obligations apply, while stand-alone high-risk obligations were pushed to 2 December 2027 by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). Coverage is horizontal and cross-sectoral, with the national sandbox and high-risk supervision still being built out.
Policy Lever: Malta combines the EU AI Act with two 2025 legal notices allocating supervisory roles, MDIA voluntary certification and guidance, and the regulator-issued AI Gaming Charter. Economic levers include the Technology Assurance Sandbox, Digital Europe-funded AI pilots and a €100 million digitalisation allocation in the 2026 Budget, but no AI-specific procurement rules or operating AI Act sandbox.
Governance Type: Governance rests on a dual-authority model: MDIA as default market surveillance authority, notifying authority and single point of contact, and the IDPC for data-sensitive and fundamental-rights-related high-risk systems, with statutory coordination toward the MFSA and MGA. No sub-national tier regulates AI, and independent review of AI decisions has not yet been exercised.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia engage through MDIA and MGA consultations, certification schemes and strategy workstreams, while civil society has no standing formal role. Internationally Malta is a Council of Europe AI convention signatory, an EU AI Board member and, since February 2026, a GPAI member.
Enforcement Level: Penalties are legislated and authorities designated, but no AI-specific enforcement decision or monitoring report has been published since the AI Act began applying on 2 August 2026.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Artificial Intelligence Regulations – Legal Notice 226 of 2025 (S.L. 591.05), Artificial Intelligence (Designation of the Information and Data Protection Commissioner for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Regulations – Legal Notice 227 of 2025, Malta Digital Innovation Authority (Amendment) Act XIX (2024), Malta Digital Innovation Authority Act (Cap. 592, 2018), The Ultimate AI Launchpad: A Strategy and Vision for Artificial Intelligence in Malta 2030 (2019), MGA–MDIA AI Gaming Charter (2026)

Regulation Status: The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no AI-specific legislation in force or in the legislative process. Technology-related statutes on the Nitijela register are general in character: the Cybercrimes Act 2025 (31 MIRC Ch. 5) criminalises computer-related forgery and offences involving adapted or modified depictions without naming artificial intelligence, and there is no general personal data protection law or data protection authority. Leaders endorsed regional AI principles in September 2026, but nothing binding has followed domestically.
Policy Lever: The only AI policy instrument touching the Marshall Islands is the regional Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles endorsed by Forum Leaders in September 2026, a high-level statement with no domestic implementing measure. Government digital activity is concentrated on connectivity and cybersecurity, with no AI funding, procurement rules, sandbox or dedicated institutional capacity.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralized in a small-state executive, with the Ministry of Transportation, Communications and Information Technology leading digital matters and no AI remit assigned anywhere. Neither local councils nor courts nor independent review bodies have engaged with AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI governance involves no structured participation by industry, civil society or academia because no national process has been established. External engagement is at declaration level: co-sponsorship of the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution on safe, secure and trustworthy AI, remote accession to the Lagatoi Declaration on Digital Transformation of the Pacific in 2023, and endorsement of the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in 2026.
Enforcement Level: AI is not enforced against in any form; only generic Cybercrimes Act 2025 penalties could reach AI-assisted offences, and no authority, action or monitoring exists.
Specific Laws: Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional instrument endorsed by the Republic of the Marshall Islands at the Fifty-Fifth Pacific Islands Forum), Cybercrimes Act 2025 (31 MIRC Ch. 5, general cybercrime law with no AI provision)

Regulation Status: Mauritania governs AI through the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Mauritania 2024-2029, prepared by the Ministry of Digital Transformation, Innovation and Modernization of Administration, which sets five priorities including data governance and ethical AI but creates no obligations. No AI-specific statute, decree or regulation is in force or before the National Assembly, and Law No. 2017-020 on the protection of personal data addresses automated processing without any AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to the National AI Strategy 2024-2029 and donor-funded capacity building, notably the expansion of the $60 million Mauritanian component of the West Africa Regional Digital Integration Program to AI data infrastructure, skills and sectoral deployment agreed with the World Bank in June 2026. No AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and AI work sits inside a ministry without a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in one ministry, with implementation support from the World Bank, and no sectoral regulator, interministerial committee or independent review body involved. Regional and local authorities have no role, and the data protection authority under Law No. 2017-020 is not independently structured.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led and episodic: ministry events around the National AI Strategy drew universities and firms, and an AI advocacy initiative in Nouakchott campaigns publicly without a formal seat. International involvement consists of attendance at the Paris AI Action Summit and African Union frameworks rather than treaty or standards work.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced, since the only binding exposure is the general penalty regime of the personal data protection law and no body has been given an AI remit.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Mauritania 2024-2029 (2024), Law No. 2017-020 on the Protection of Personal Data (2017)

Regulation Status: Mauritius has no horizontal binding AI legislation; the National AI Strategy 2025-2029 and the FAIR Guidelines launched on 10 April 2026 are explicitly non-binding. The only binding AI-specific instrument remains the Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021, supplemented by the Financial Services Commission's non-binding Fintech Series Guidance Notes No. 4 on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services of September 2025. The Data Protection Act 2017 applies to AI only incidentally, and the Economic and Financial Measures (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 addresses AI through an investment scheme rather than conduct rules.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law and fiscal incentives: the National AI Strategy 2025-2029 and FAIR Guidelines developed with UNDP support, FSC guidance for financial services, and budget measures including the Public Sector AI Programme, start-up tax deductions and the AI City Scheme legislated in August 2026. Institutional capacity rests on a newly created ministerial AI Unit without statutory powers alongside the National Computer Board, the Data Protection Office and the FSC.
Governance Type: Governance combines a central ministerial AI Unit at MITCI with sectoral regulators, principally the Financial Services Commission for AI in non-bank finance and the Data Protection Office for data aspects. There is no sub-national tier, and independent review of AI has not been exercised by courts or the ombudsman.
Actor Involvement: The National AI Strategy 2025-2029 and FAIR Guidelines emerged from one-off multi-stakeholder consultations involving industry, start-ups, academia and civil society rather than standing advisory bodies. International engagement runs through UNDP cooperation and African Union and Smart Africa membership.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity exists only in financial services through the FSC's licensing and sanctioning powers, and no AI-specific action or audit has been made public.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy (2018), Data Protection Act (2017), Financial Services (Robotic and Artificial Intelligence Enabled Advisory Services) Rules (2021), Digital Transformation Blueprint 2025-2029, FSC Fintech Series Guidance Notes No. 4 on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services (2025), National AI Strategy 2025-2029, FAIR Guidelines (2026), Economic and Financial Measures (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 (AI City Scheme)

Regulation Status: No general AI law is in force: the Ley Nacional para Regular el Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (11 February 2026) and the Senate Science and Technology Committee's draft general AI law announced on 30 April 2026 remain in committee. Binding AI provisions exist only inside adapted general law—the 14 May 2026 reforms to the Ley Federal del Trabajo and Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor against voice and image cloning, and the 2025 LFPDPPP rules on automated decision-making—supplemented by Instituto Nacional Electoral guidelines restricting AI and deepfakes in electoral propaganda.
Policy Lever: Mexico relies mainly on programmatic and soft-law levers—the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2026, Principios Chapultepec and the ATDT's AI Factory and training school—with one enacted AI-specific binding reform in labour and copyright law. No body holds statutory AI compliance powers and no AI procurement rules or regulatory sandbox exist.
Governance Type: AI oversight is dispersed across the ATDT, the Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno, telecom, financial and consumer regulators and the autonomous INE, coordinated informally rather than through a statutory mechanism. States legislate on AI independently of any federal framework, and electoral courts have directly compelled AI rulemaking.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through Senate roundtables, UNAM forums and the Agenda Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2024-2030, while domestic civil society is consulted only occasionally and was not built into the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2026. International engagement runs through the Santiago Declaration and OECD AI forums rather than binding treaties.
Enforcement Level: Penalties reach AI conduct through copyright, labour, data protection and electoral rules, but no AI enforcement authority, published AI sanction decision or systematic auditing regime exists.
Specific Laws: Reformas a la Ley Federal del Trabajo y a la Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor en materia de inteligencia artificial (2026), Ley Federal de Protección de Datos Personales en Posesión de los Particulares (2025), Ley Federal de Telecomunicaciones y Radiodifusión (2025), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Principios Chapultepec (2026), Propuesta de Agenda Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2024-2030, Lineamientos y principios para el desarrollo estratégico y uso regulado de la inteligencia artificial en el Instituto Nacional Electoral (INE/JGE175/2025), Ley Nacional para Regular el Uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (draft, 2026)

Regulation Status: The Federated States of Micronesia has no AI-specific legislation, no binding AI rules, and no formal AI governance framework in force or under active consideration as of mid-2026. The country remains focused on foundational connectivity and digital infrastructure challenges rather than AI regulation.
Policy Lever: No binding AI instruments, soft-law guidance, economic tools such as sandboxes or AI-focused funding programs, or dedicated institutional bodies for AI policy exist in Micronesia.
Governance Type: There is no AI governance structure of any kind; no regulatory body, inter-agency coordination mechanism, subnational role, or nongovernmental check on AI has been established.
Actor Involvement: No structured engagement with industry, civil society, or academia on AI policy exists domestically; Micronesia has limited participation in international AI governance forums as a UN member and party to some broader Pacific regional dialogues, placing it marginally above complete absence on the international dimension.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI enforcement framework, no designated authority, no penalties defined, and no monitoring or auditing activity of any kind.

Regulation Status: Moldova has no dedicated AI law; the only binding rules written for AI are the Framework Regulation on Academic Integrity in Higher Education Institutions approved on 24 June 2026, which defines unauthorised use of generative AI as misconduct and requires students to declare AI use, together with the Ministry of Education and Research anti-plagiarism methodological standards. Law No. 195/2024 on Personal Data Protection, in force since 23 August 2026, applies to AI only indirectly, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS No. 225) remains signed but unratified. The National Programme on Artificial Intelligence and Data Management 2026–2030 and Central Electoral Commission amendments covering AI in online campaigns are still drafts.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments and funding: the 2024 White Paper on Data Management and Artificial Intelligence, the draft National Programme on Artificial Intelligence and Data Management 2026–2030 consulted publicly to 12 May 2026, the Moldova AI Hub consortium, and the EU-funded FAIMA AI antenna. Institutional machinery consists of the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization and the consultative Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research, neither holding AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalization, with the Ministry of Education and Research owning academic AI rules, the National Centre for Personal Data Protection owning data issues, and the Central Electoral Commission drafting rules on AI in online campaigning. Coordination runs through the Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research; there is no subnational tier and no judicial or ombudsman practice on AI.
Actor Involvement: The Sub-Council for Artificial Intelligence and Applied Research and the Moldova AI Hub consortium give industry, universities, United Nations agencies and civil society standing consultative roles alongside ministries. Internationally, Moldova signed but has not ratified the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, aligns with the EU acquis as an accession candidate, and completed the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nominal: sanctions exist only for unauthorised AI use in universities, no authority holds an AI mandate, and no AI-specific decision has been published.
Specific Laws: White Paper on Data Management and Artificial Intelligence (2024), Framework Regulation on Academic Integrity in Higher Education Institutions (2026), Methodological Anti-Plagiarism Standards for Higher Education Institutions (2026), Law No. 195/2024 on Personal Data Protection (in force 23 August 2026), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225) – signature 2024, draft National Programme on Artificial Intelligence and Data Management 2026–2030, National Smart Specialisation Programme "Smart Moldova" 2024–2027 (Government Decision No. 588/2024)

Regulation Status: Monaco has no AI statute in force; AI is reached only through Law No. 1.565 of 3 December 2024 on the protection of personal data, enforced by the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles. Two AI-relevant texts are in the legislative pipeline: Projet de loi n° 1.087 on video protection and remote biometric identification, which expressly builds on artificial-intelligence image processing and was still awaiting debate in 2026, and Proposition de loi n° 281 on online hate content, adopted by the Conseil National on 29 June 2026, which defines deepfakes.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through non-binding strategy and state-funded digital programmes: Extended Monaco (2019), Extended Monaco Enterprises with Digital FlashUp, and sovereign cloud infrastructure. The reorganisation of state digital services into the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique on 2 October 2026 gives a ministry-level unit responsibility for an administration AI strategy, while the APDP's statutory powers remain confined to personal data.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralised: the Prince's Government sets digital policy through the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique, and the APDP is the only independent authority with powers touching AI. Judicial review before the Tribunal Suprême and institutional opinions on the biometric identification bill provide the only external checks.
Actor Involvement: Participation is government-led, with business involvement channelled through the Extended Monaco Enterprises programme and no formal seats for civil society or universities. International engagement runs through Council of Europe data protection instruments rather than AI-specific treaties or summits.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only under personal data law through the APDP, with no AI-specific sanction, audit or published decision.
Specific Laws: Law No. 1.565 on the Protection of Personal Data (2024), Act No. 1.566 approving ratification of the Protocol amending Convention 108 (2024), Law No. 1.383 for a Digital Principality (2011, as amended), Projet de loi n° 1.087 on video protection and remote biometric identification (pending before the Conseil National), Proposition de loi n° 281 on strengthening measures against online hate content (adopted by the Conseil National, 2026), Sovereign Ordinance creating the Délégation Interministérielle au Numérique (2026), Extended Monaco digital transformation programme (2019)

Regulation Status: Mongolia governs AI through policy rather than law: the National Strategy on Big Data and Artificial Intelligence was adopted by Government Resolution No. 108 in September 2025 alongside the Digital First policy, and 2026 was declared the Year of Big Data and AI. No binding AI-specific instrument is in force; a Law on Artificial Intelligence is being drafted jointly by the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Communications and the Ministry of Justice and Home Affairs but has not reached the State Great Khural. AI use is reached only by general law, principally the Law on Personal Data Protection (2021).
Policy Lever: Policy runs on non-binding levers: an adopted national AI strategy, a Digital First policy, skills and infrastructure programs including the Oracle training partnership and a planned GPU-cluster AI Centre. Institutional work sits with the ministry's Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Department and the new National Council on Artificial Intelligence, neither of which has a legal mandate to impose obligations; no regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rules operate.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Communications, with a cross-ministry National Council on Artificial Intelligence created in 2026 and a parliamentary group on AI and big data active since August 2024. Sub-national authorities and independent review bodies play no part in shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Strategy development drew structured but ad hoc input from industry, academia and civil society through UNDP-facilitated workshops and the February 2025 national conference, with no standing statutory consultative bodies. International engagement runs through UNDP, the Oxford Global Cyber Security Capacity Centre, the United Kingdom and a corporate partnership with Oracle rather than binding AI treaties.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement exists: there are no AI-specific obligations, penalties, enforcement decisions or audits, and oversight is limited to one-off readiness assessments.
Specific Laws: National Strategy on Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (2025, Government Resolution No. 108), Digital First policy (2025), Digital Nation Strategy, Law of Mongolia on Personal Data Protection (2021), Five-Year Development Guidelines of Mongolia for 2026-2030 (2025), draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (in preparation, 2025-2026)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific binding instrument is in force, and the National AI Strategy 2026-2030 with its 2026 Action Plan is still being drafted by the Working Group coordinated by the Ministry of Public Administration. The Ministry of Justice has announced separate legislation on the misuse of AI, drafted with Italian assistance, with no text before Parliament. Personal data protection, copyright and criminal law apply to AI only incidentally.
Policy Lever: Montenegro works exclusively through soft and economic instruments: the UNDP assessment, the strategy drafting process, MontEDIH, EuroCC/NCC high-performance computing support and donor-funded AI infrastructure for the judiciary. No binding AI instrument, compliance guidance or regulatory sandbox exists, and no body holds a legal AI mandate.
Governance Type: Policy is centralised in the Ministry of Public Administration, with the Ministry of Justice recently taking the lead on criminal-law aspects of AI misuse and the Agency for Personal Data Protection covering data issues under general law. Coordination is through an ad hoc strategy working group, there is no subnational role, and independent review of AI occurs only incidentally.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society participate through consultative sessions and thematic workshops of the AI Strategy Working Group rather than standing statutory roles. Internationally Montenegro is a signatory of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and participates in Council of Europe expert committee work, EU Digital Europe programmes and UNDP cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced: sanctions reach AI only through data protection and criminal law, no AI enforcement decision has been issued, and oversight is limited to a single donor-supported readiness study.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection Law (2008, amended 2024, Official Gazette Nos. 79/2008 and 77/2024), Personal Data Protection Act (2023), Criminal Code of Montenegro, Copyright and Related Rights Act, Digital Transformation Strategy 2022-2026, Education Reform Strategy 2025-2035, Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225, signed 2025), draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 with Action Plan for 2026

Regulation Status: Morocco's only binding AI rules sit inside electoral law: Organic Law 53.25 amending Organic Law 27.11 introduced article 51-bis penalising dissemination of falsified or AI-generated content and banning electoral material on AI tools on polling day, and HACA's Superior Council decision 50-26 of 16 June 2026 prohibits deceptive AI-generated electoral content and requires permanent labelling of AI-generated broadcast material. Outside elections, AI is governed by general law — Law No. 09-08 on personal data applied by the CNDP and Law No. 05-20 on cybersecurity applied by the DGSSI. The cross-sector Digital X.0 framework law remains under review at the General Secretariat of the Government and the bill creating a National AI Agency has not been adopted.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by soft instruments — the Maroc IA 2030 roadmap, the Maroc Digital 2030 strategy, CNDP and HACA election guidance — supported by funded skills, research and infrastructure programmes such as the JAZARI ROOT Institute. Binding levers are confined to the electoral AI provisions, and no institution yet holds a statutory AI compliance mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform, with CNDP, HACA and DGSSI exercising AI-relevant powers inside their own remits and coordination handled case by case during drafting of the Digital X.0 law. No sub-national authority has any role, and judicial and independent oversight of AI is occasional, visible in the election-related prosecutions and in CNDH interventions.
Actor Involvement: Industry and universities are consulted through conferences, roadmap workshops and JAZARI ROOT Institute agreements, while domestic civil society is engaged only sporadically. International engagement is the most developed channel, spanning the UNESCO ethics recommendation, African Union continental AI work and bilateral digital partnerships with the EU, France and Gulf states.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only through election-period rules carrying criminal penalties and HACA content monitoring, plus CNDP action under Law No. 09-08, with no dedicated AI authority or published AI-specific sanction decisions.
Specific Laws: Organic Law No. 53.25 amending Organic Law No. 27.11 on the Election of Members of the House of Representatives (2026), HACA Superior Council of Audiovisual Communication Decision No. 50-26 (2026), Law No. 09-08 on the Protection of Individuals with Regard to the Processing of Personal Data (2009), Law No. 05-20 on Cybersecurity (2020), Digital X.0 Framework Law (draft, 2025), Maroc IA 2030 National AI Roadmap (2026), Maroc Digital 2030 Strategy (2024), Bill for the Establishment of the National Agency for Artificial Intelligence (2024, retabled 2026)

Regulation Status: Mozambique's only binding AI-specific instrument is Decree No. 14/2026 of 17 April 2026, which creates the National Commission for Artificial Intelligence (CNIA) as a consultative and technical advisory body reporting to the Council of Ministers; it imposes no duties on developers or users of AI. The National AI Strategy (ENIA) remains a draft after public consultation from 4 May to 4 June 2026 and continued stakeholder engagement through October 2026, and the Ministry of Education and Culture is drafting rules on AI in education for submission to the Council of Ministers before the end of 2026. The Cybersecurity Law and Cybercrime Law approved in 2026 and the Personal Data Protection Bill approved by the Council of Ministers on 3 March 2026 contain no AI-specific provisions.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by one institutional decree (Decree No. 14/2026), a draft national strategy, and donor-backed experimentation, with ITU support for a national AI regulatory sandbox and a health-sector sandbox agreed with the Instituto Nacional de Saúde but not yet operating. INTIC leads delivery with UNESCO, ITU, the European Union, the African Union and the World Bank, while CNIA provides advice rather than compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralized in INTIC under the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation, with CNIA providing decree-based interministerial coordination directly under the Council of Ministers. Provincial structures participate only through consultation, and no independent or judicial body reviews AI decisions.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: industry, civil society and academia contributed to the ENIA public consultation and provincial workshops, and the Mozambican AI Association (AMIA) was launched in August 2026 without a formal policy role. Internationally the country works with UNESCO, ITU, the European Union, the African Union and the World Bank, and joined the World AI Cooperation Organization as a founding member.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, penalty or enforcement action exists, and oversight is limited to INTIC's general ICT remit and CNIA's advisory opinions.
Specific Laws: Decreto n.º 14/2026, de 17 de Abril – Cria a Comissão Nacional de Inteligência Artificial (CNIA) (2026), Estratégia Nacional de Inteligência Artificial / National AI Strategy – ENIA (draft, 2026), Cybersecurity Law (2026), Cybercrime Law (2026), Proposta de Lei do Regime Jurídico de Protecção de Dados Pessoais (bill before Parliament, 2026), Electronic Transactions Law No. 3/2017, Decree No. 71/2025 – Data Centers Regulations, Decree No. 70/2025 – Cloud Computing Regulations

Regulation Status: Myanmar has no AI-specific legislation in force and none in the legislative process; the National AI Strategy (2025-2030) and National AI Policy drafted by the Ministry of Science and Technology since 2025 remain unpublished and unadopted. Cybersecurity Law No. 1/2025, in force since 30 July 2025, defines artificial intelligence and licenses digital platforms and cybersecurity service providers, but imposes no duty on AI developers or deployers. Regional assessments place Myanmar, with Cambodia and Lao PDR, among ASEAN members without a dedicated national AI strategy or agency.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to a ministry-led drafting process and announced university research centres; no AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists. Institutional work sits inside the Ministry of Science and Technology without statutory powers over AI.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralized in one ministry under an executive dominated by the military leadership, with coordination limited to occasional drafting meetings. Regions and states play no part, and no independent or judicial check on AI-related policy operates.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-internal, with limited industry and university presence at drafting meetings and donor-run training, and civil society excluded. International involvement runs through ASEAN soft-law alignment and bilateral cooperation with China rather than treaty or standards bodies; reported founding membership of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization is not officially confirmed.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is limited to general cybersecurity and platform licensing powers, with no AI-specific obligation, authority, case or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Cybersecurity Law No. 1/2025, draft National AI Strategy (2025-2030) and National AI Policy, Digital Economy Development Master Plan (2021-2025)

Regulation Status: Namibia has no binding AI-specific instrument; the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025) confirms the absence of AI legislation, and the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology has stated an Artificial Intelligence Act is being developed but not yet tabled. The draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, prepared by the National Commission on Research, Science and Technology with UNESCO, the United Nations Development Programme and the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung, was at national validation stage in September 2026. AI-related harms such as deepfake scams are handled through general communications and criminal law and public advisories rather than AI-written rules.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through non-binding diagnostics and institution-building: the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025), a draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, and the National Artificial Intelligence Institute launched on 23 September 2026 with centres for research, software development, innovation and data. There is no AI-specific binding instrument, regulatory sandbox, or AI procurement rule, and the Institute holds a research and skills remit rather than compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in national bodies: the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology on digital policy and legislation, the National Commission on Research, Science and Technology hosting the National Artificial Intelligence Institute, and the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia on communications matters, with coordination that the national readiness assessment describes as fragmented. Regional and local government play no AI role, and no court or independent oversight body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is episodic and workshop-based: the 2023 UNESCO ethics engagement with over 80 participants from government, academia, civil society and the private sector, the 2025 Readiness Assessment launch, the 215-expert strategy process, and industry meetings including Deloitte & Touche Namibia. International engagement is the strongest channel, through the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the ITU AI for Good Global Commission, African Union and SADC processes and the Smart Africa Alliance.
Enforcement Level: With no AI-specific obligations in force, enforcement is limited to general communications and criminal law applied by the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia and Nam-CSIRT, alongside public awareness work on deepfakes and AI-enabled scams.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report (2025), draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2026), National Digital Strategy, Cybercrime Bill (2026, draft), Data Protection Bill (draft), Communications Act (2009), National Digital Economy Roadmap (2022)

Regulation Status: Nauru has no AI-specific legislation, bill or national AI strategy; the Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030 addresses connectivity, digital services, planned data-protection and cybersecurity legislation, without AI provisions. Artificial intelligence is touched only incidentally by the Cybercrime Act 2015 and the Communications and Broadcasting Act 2018, neither of which contains any AI-written rule.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to connectivity and e-government delivery under the Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030, which schedules data-protection, cybersecurity and electronic-transactions legislation rather than AI measures. No AI guidance, funding line, sandbox or mandated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in a unitary micro-state administration where the Department of Information and Communications Technology leads digital policy alone. No sectoral regulator, sub-national authority or independent review body plays any role in AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy involvement is absent across industry, civil society and academia. Nauru's engagement is through regional and multilateral membership: it joined Pacific Islands Forum Leaders in endorsing the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026, which are to feed a regional AI governance framework for consideration in 2027, and it is bound as a UNESCO member to the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: No AI obligations, penalties, enforcement authority or monitoring arrangements exist in Nauru.
Specific Laws: Nauru National Digital Transformation Strategy 2025-2030 (2025), Cybercrime Act 2015, Communications and Broadcasting Act 2018, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional, endorsed by Pacific Islands Forum Leaders)

Regulation Status: Nepal governs AI chiefly through the cabinet-approved National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy 2082 of August 2025, a non-binding strategy that promises AI legislation and an AI Regulation Council. The only binding AI-written rules sit inside the Election Code of Conduct 2082, in force since 18 January 2026, which prohibits AI-generated misinformation and deepfakes in election campaigning and carries fines and candidacy cancellation. A dedicated AI bill appears in the government's legislative plan for fiscal year 2026-27 and the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation has approved a concept paper for an umbrella Science, Technology and Innovation Bill covering AI and robotics, but neither has reached parliament.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through a non-binding national strategy plus a ministry unit: the National AI Policy 2082 and the National AI Center under the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, joined by the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation created in May 2026. Promised levers, including an AI Regulation Council, regulatory sandboxes and provincial AI Excellence Centres, have no legal basis, dedicated budget or operations.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, which drafted the policy and hosts the National AI Center, with the Election Commission and the new Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation acting in their own remits. Formal coordination machinery and any provincial role remain on paper, and oversight by courts or independent bodies is limited to election observers' reporting on AI-generated misinformation.
Actor Involvement: Industry bodies, digital rights organisations and academics engage through commentary, seminars and donor projects rather than institutionalised consultation, and participation remains concentrated in Kathmandu. International engagement is development-partner based, mainly with UNDP and UN forums, without accession to AI treaties or standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI exists only in the electoral sphere, where the Election Commission monitored and warned about AI-generated deepfakes and imposed a handful of code-of-conduct fines, while no authority enforces AI obligations outside elections.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy 2082 (2025), Election Code of Conduct 2082 (2026), National Advertising Policy 2026, Individual Privacy Act 2075 (2018), E-commerce Act 2081 (2025)

Regulation Status: The directly applicable EU AI Act governs AI in the Netherlands, with prohibited-practice and AI literacy rules applying since February 2025, general-purpose AI obligations since August 2025, and high-risk obligations deferred to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI that entered into force on 27 July 2026. National implementation is incomplete: the Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening, which designates the market surveillance authorities, penalties and the joint regulatory sandbox, closed consultation on 1 June 2026 and has not been enacted. Beyond the AI Act, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens' Directorate for Coordination of Algorithms exercises algorithm-specific oversight under the GDPR and the UAVG.
Policy Lever: The Netherlands combines the directly applicable EU AI Act with an unusually dense layer of soft law—periodic AI and algorithm risk reports, AP guidance on human intervention and generative AI, the mandatory government Algorithm Register and impact assessments—plus funded AI investment programmes. Supervisory institutions exist and are resourced, but their statutory AI Act powers, penalties and the single multi-sectoral regulatory sandbox await adoption of the implementing act.
Governance Type: Supervision is decentralised and hybrid: the AP and RDI coordinate while eight to ten sectoral market surveillance authorities keep their own remits, cooperating through the Digital Regulation Cooperation Platform pending statutory anchoring. Sub-national bodies implement national transparency rules rather than legislate, and courts, the Raad van State and the National Ombudsman exert substantive independent control over public-sector AI.
Actor Involvement: Policy input runs through open internet consultations, AP stakeholder seminars and the Nederlandse AI Coalitie, which gives industry and knowledge institutions standing partnership roles, while civil society is consulted rather than seated. The country is a highly active participant in EU, OECD, UNESCO, Council of Europe and European standardisation processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity and published cross-sector monitoring are well developed, but concluded sanction decisions so far rest on the GDPR rather than the AI Act, whose national enforcement architecture is still in the legislative pipeline.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI amending the AI Act (2026), General Data Protection Regulation (2018), Dutch GDPR Implementation Act / UAVG (2018), Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening draft bill (2026, in consultation), Nationaal AI Deltaplan (2025), Government Algorithm Register policy (2022)

Regulation Status: New Zealand regulates AI through existing law and voluntary frameworks: the July 2025 Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with Confidence, the Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand and the Public Service AI Framework carry no legal force, while the only binding rules touching AI are the Privacy Act 2020, the Privacy Amendment Act 2025 (IPP3A from 1 May 2026) and the Biometric Processing Privacy Code, which became fully applicable to pre-existing biometric processing on 3 August 2026. The one AI-specific legislative proposal, the Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill, passed first reading and received submissions to 19 June 2026 but lapsed when Parliament was dissolved on 1 October 2026 ahead of the 7 November election.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on soft law plus money: voluntary guidance for business and the public service sits alongside the $231 million New Zealand Institute for Advanced Technology (independent from July 2026), AI research funding and a small-business AI pilot. Binding levers remain general data and consumer law, and institutional responsibility is distributed without any statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Responsibility for AI is dispersed among general and sectoral regulators coordinated informally through Cabinet and the AI Strategy, with no single AI authority and no subnational layer. Independent scrutiny comes from courts, the Human Rights Review Tribunal and the GCDO's AI Expert Advisory Panel rather than from AI-specific oversight institutions.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is consultative: business groups and the AI Forum New Zealand feed into strategy and guidance, civil society and researchers participate through consultations and select committee submissions, and academics hold a standing advisory role on the GCDO's AI Expert Advisory Panel. Internationally New Zealand works through OECD principles, GPAI and summit declarations rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on Privacy Act complaints and the Biometric Processing Privacy Code handled by the Privacy Commissioner, with no AI-specific penalties, dedicated AI enforcement body or routine AI auditing.
Specific Laws: Privacy Act 2020, Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand (2020), Public Service AI Framework (2025), New Zealand's Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with Confidence (2025), Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses (2025), Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (2025), Privacy Amendment Act 2025, Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, Customer and Product Data Act 2025, Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill (2025, lapsed on dissolution of Parliament in October 2026)

Regulation Status: As of mid-2026, Nicaragua has no binding AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill under formal legislative consideration, and no AI-focused executive orders in force. The only AI-relevant activity was a June 2023 National Assembly task force agreement to develop proposals, which produced no enacted instrument; existing laws such as the Special Cybercrime Law (No. 1042, 2020) and the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020–2025 touch digital activity incidentally but contain no AI provisions.
Policy Lever: No binding AI instruments, published AI guidance, sandboxes, funding programs, or dedicated AI institutional bodies exist; Nicaragua relies entirely on pre-existing general ICT and cybercrime frameworks with no AI-specific policy infrastructure.
Governance Type: There is no dedicated AI regulator or multi-body coordination structure; AI oversight would theoretically fall to general telecommunications and cybercrime authorities under a highly centralized state, with no subnational AI role and no active independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI matters.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society, and academic actors have no structured role in AI governance; Nicaragua's only international AI engagement is marginal participation in regional forums (e.g., CELAC), and it signed the Santiago Declaration, placing it at the lowest tier of international involvement.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanctions, enforcement actions, dedicated enforcement authority, or monitoring mechanisms exist in Nicaragua.
Specific Laws: Special Law on Cybercrimes No. 1042 (2020), National Cybersecurity Strategy 2020–2025 (Presidential Decree No. 24-2020)

Regulation Status: Niger has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no adopted national AI strategy; the Ministry of Communication, Posts and Digital Economy announced at the second Semaine de l'Intelligence Artificielle et des Technologies Géospatiales in July 2025 that a national AI and geospatial strategy would be elaborated through an inclusive process, and no such instrument has been published. AI-related activity falls under general instruments, chiefly Loi n° 2017-28 of 3 May 2017 on personal data protection as amended by Loi n° 2019-71, which is not written for AI. The country remains under military rule following the July 2023 coup, with the Charter of Refoundation replacing the suspended constitutional order.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of convening and capacity-building rather than instruments: ANSI runs the annual Semaine de l'Intelligence Artificielle et des Technologies Géospatiales, whose third edition was held in Niamey on 23-24 July 2026, and the UN Resident Coordinator's Illimi Niger programme trained 140 officials in AI for human security in June 2026. No national AI strategy, guidance, procurement rule, sandbox or funded AI programme of the Nigerien state exists.
Governance Type: AI sits with the executive: the Ministry of Communication, Posts and Digital Economy sets direction and ANSI implements digital programmes, with the independent HAPDP confined to personal data under Loi n° 2017-28. There is no designated AI regulator, no inter-agency coordination body, no sub-national competence and no exercised judicial or independent review of AI.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is event-based: SIATeG 2026 in Niamey brought government, academia and private-sector participants together, and UN agencies deliver AI training to officials, while domestic civil society has no documented role. Niger's suspension from the African Union and its withdrawal from ECOWAS confine international AI involvement to United Nations and Alliance des États du Sahel channels; it has ratified the African Union Malabo Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, which is not an AI instrument.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligation, sanction, enforcement action or monitoring programme exists, and HAPDP's limited and under-resourced supervision reaches AI only through general personal data rules.
Specific Laws: Loi n° 2017-28 du 3 mai 2017 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, amended by Loi n° 2019-71 (2019); Niger 2.0 digital strategy (2017). No AI-specific law, regulation or national AI strategy has been adopted.

Regulation Status: Nigeria has no standalone AI law: the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, which would give NITDA risk-tiered powers over AI systems, was still in the legislative process in mid-2026, and separate National Artificial Intelligence Commission and Nigerian Artificial Intelligence bills remain at committee stage. Binding AI-specific obligations exist only in narrow instruments — Chapter Five of the NITDA Internet Code of Practice 2026 for internet access service providers and the 2025 Guidelines for Clearance of IT Projects covering federal procurement of AI-enabled systems valued at NGN 10 million or more. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and its General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 carry the bulk of practical AI oversight as general law.
Policy Lever: Nigeria leans on soft law and funding: the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025), NITDA guidance and research and skills programmes, with a single binding AI chapter in the NITDA Internet Code of Practice 2026. A multi-agency National Regulatory Sandbox is under construction through a Technical Working Group inaugurated in May 2026 and is not yet admitting participants, and the bodies holding AI responsibility lack a statutory AI remit.
Governance Type: Governance is a lead-body-plus-sectoral-regulator model, with NITDA and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy setting AI policy and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, Nigerian Communications Commission and Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission acting within existing mandates. Coordination is organised through working groups and the National AI Trust, states have no regulatory role, and judicial review of AI rules has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making draws on industry through public hearings, the National AI Trust and the regulatory sandbox working group, while civil society and academic input is consultative and occasional. Internationally Nigeria is an active participant, having adopted the African Union Continental AI Strategy and completed a UNESCO readiness assessment, and aligned with multilateral AI safety declarations.
Enforcement Level: AI-specific enforcement has not occurred: sanctions reach AI only through the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and NITDA Act, and the statutory AI penalty regime awaits passage of the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill.
Specific Laws: Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023), Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive (2025), Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act (2024), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy — NAIS (2025), NITDA Guidelines for Clearance of Information Technology Projects for Federal Public Institutions (2025), NITDA Internet Code of Practice (2026), NITDA Code of Practice for Artificial Intelligence (draft, 2025), National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill (2025, pending), National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill (2025, pending)

Regulation Status: North Korea has no AI-specific legislation, regulation or formal governance instrument. Technology is governed through general sectoral statutes — the Science and Technology Law, the Law on the Introduction of New Technology (revised 2026), the Information Security Law, the Telecommunications Law and the Electronic Authentication Law — none of which contains provisions written for AI systems, while the 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan adopted at the Ninth Workers' Party Congress in February 2026 lists information technology and AI as development priorities.
Policy Lever: State direction of AI runs through party economic planning and state research institutions rather than policy instruments: the 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan designates AI a priority, and AI research capacity sits in bodies such as Kim Il Sung University's Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and military research units. No strategy document, guidance, standard, sandbox or AI-mandated institution has been published.
Governance Type: Authority over technology is concentrated in the Korean Workers' Party, the Cabinet and the security apparatus, with no independent regulators, no subnational competence and no judicial or independent review. Governance is entirely centralized and opaque.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academia are state-controlled and have no structured input into technology policy. International engagement is limited to UN General Assembly voting, where North Korea opposed the 2024 resolution on autonomous weapons systems, and the country joins no AI declarations, standards bodies or multilateral AI initiatives.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, authority, sanction or monitoring practice exists, and any control over technology use is exercised through opaque party and security channels.
