Specific Laws: Five-Year Plan for National Economic Development 2026-2030 (2026, names information technology and artificial intelligence as priority areas), Law on the Introduction of New Technology (revised 2026), Science and Technology Law, Information Security Law

Regulation Status: Norway has no AI-specific binding instrument in force. The draft KI-loven, which would make the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) applicable through a reference provision, completed public consultation in autumn 2025 with close to 150 responses, but entry into force originally targeted for late summer 2026 has slipped: the government will consult on the EU simplification package in autumn 2026 and present a bill in spring 2027, and the EEA Joint Committee has not yet incorporated the Regulation. The new Public Administration Act adopted 20 June 2025 contains binding rules on automated decisions and documentation of decision logic for public bodies, but no commencement date has been set.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft instruments and funding rather than binding rules: Datatilsynet's regulatory sandbox, Digdir's and Nkom's published AI guidance, and KI-Norge, launched 12 June 2026 under director Hans Christian Holte as the national arena for responsible AI and host of the forthcoming AI Act sandbox built with Nkom and Datatilsynet. A renewed national AI strategy was announced on 5 October 2026, building on the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020) and the National Digitalisation Strategy (2024).
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-body-plus-sectoral model, with Nkom as coordinating market surveillance authority and national contact point, Datatilsynet covering data protection, and sectoral supervisors to be designated in the KI-lov. Oversight is exclusively national, with independent review supplied by courts and the parliamentary ombudsman.
Actor Involvement: Domestic involvement runs through the Norwegian consultation and corporatist tradition: the 2025 KI-lov høring was open to all actors, KI-Norge partners with business, academia and the public sector, and an October 2026 letter of intent with employer and union confederations covers AI in working life. Internationally Norway acts through the EEA/EFTA track, the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and the OECD.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement against AI rests entirely on general data protection law pending entry into force of the KI-lov, with Nkom designated but not yet empowered.
Specific Laws: Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence (KI-loven) (2025 consultation draft, bill announced for spring 2027), Public Administration Act (forvaltningsloven, LOV-2025-06-20-81, adopted 2025, not in force), Personal Data Act (2018), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020), National Digitalisation Strategy (2024), renewed national AI strategy announced October 2026, EU AI Act Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EEA incorporation pending), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (signed 2024)

Regulation Status: Oman regulates AI through the General Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems, issued by the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology on 1 April 2025 and effective 9 April 2025, a risk-based policy instrument rather than a statute. Royal Decree No. 50/2026 of 30 April 2026 is binding and AI-titled but establishes an Artificial Intelligence Special Zone in Muscat Governorate under the Law of Special Economic Zones and Free Zones rather than imposing duties on AI systems. General law, principally the Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree 6/2022), reaches AI processing without containing provisions written for AI.
Policy Lever: Policy levers are a non-binding ethics-and-governance policy, the National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Digital Technologies, and economic incentives delivered through the Artificial Intelligence Special Zone created by Royal Decree No. 50/2026. No regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule has been published, and institutional capacity rests in a ministry programme unit without legal compliance powers.
Governance Type: MTCIT is the lead AI authority through the National Programme, with sector-specific regulators expected to apply the 2025 General Policy in their domains and the Public Authority for Special Economic Zones and Free Zones managing the AI Special Zone. Governance is centralized: no statutory inter-agency AI coordination body, no subnational competence, and no independent or judicial oversight specific to AI.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed into AI policy through MTCIT consultations, the National Programme and the Green AI Alliance, while domestic civil society has no structured role. Internationally Oman is a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, participated in the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, hosts a World Economic Forum Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution partnership, and is assessed under UNESCO's AI Ethics Observatory.
Enforcement Level: Compliance rests on self-assessment and reporting to MTCIT under a policy that carries no sanctions, and no AI-specific enforcement action has been taken.
Specific Laws: National Programme for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Digital Technologies (2024), General Policy for the Safe and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems (2025), Royal Decree No. 50/2026 Establishing the Artificial Intelligence Special Zone in the Governorate of Muscat (2026), Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree No. 6/2022)

Regulation Status: Pakistan has no binding AI legislation; the National AI Policy 2025, the Islamabad AI Declaration 2026 and the National Data Governance Policy 2026 are executive policy documents, and the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2024 remains in Senate committee. AI-specific duties on transparency, human review of automated decisions and generative-AI controls apply only to federal public bodies through policy, while private-sector AI is touched only incidentally by the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 as amended in 2025. No personal data protection statute has been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven through soft-law instruments and funding: the National AI Policy 2025, the Islamabad AI Declaration 2026, the National Data Governance Policy 2026, the National AI Fund and Ignite-backed programmes. The Pakistan Digital Authority is the designated AI governance and supervisory body but has not issued binding AI instruments or used compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centred on the Pakistan Digital Authority under the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, with the National Digital Commission and the AI Council providing coordination and sectoral regulators covering telecoms and banking. Provincial governments participate in national councils without independent AI powers, and judicial or independent review of AI decisions is not institutionalised.
Actor Involvement: Policy development drew on industry, academic and public-sector consultation, with the Indus AI Summit 2026 and Indus AI Week bringing in startups, students and foreign participants. Domestic civil society input was episodic and criticised as limited, and international engagement is declaratory and bilateral rather than treaty-based.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanction, enforcement decision or audit regime exists, and the Pakistan Digital Authority's supervisory framework remains unoperationalised.
Specific Laws: National AI Policy (2025), Islamabad AI Declaration on Sovereign, Responsible, and Capability-Driven Artificial Intelligence (2026), National Data Governance Policy (2026, draft), Digital Nation Pakistan Act (2025), Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill (2024, Senate, not enacted), Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (2016), Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act (2025)

Regulation Status: Palau has no statute, regulation, executive order or national strategy whose subject is artificial intelligence. AI falls only under general instruments such as the Privacy Act provisions of the Palau National Code and the Cybersecurity Act passed by the Olbiil Era Kelulau on 20 July 2026, neither of which contains AI-specific provisions, and no competent authority for AI exists.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is directed at cybersecurity and government IT consolidation rather than AI: Executive Order No. 500 (2026) created the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy inside the Office of the President, and the National Cybersecurity Strategy and Policy 2026-2030 was signed with ITU support. No AI guidance, funding program, sandbox or AI procurement rule has been issued.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent; executive technology functions sit with the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy under the President and, once the Cybersecurity Act is implemented, a Bureau of Cybersecurity under the Ministry of Public Infrastructure and Industries. Neither has an AI mandate, and no sub-national or independent review body is involved.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academic actors have no structured role in AI policy-making, and technical engagement comes from external partners such as the International Telecommunication Union and MITRE on cybersecurity. International involvement is limited to general UN and UNESCO membership.
Enforcement Level: Nothing specific to AI is enforced in Palau, and only general cybersecurity and privacy penalties could reach AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: Executive Order No. 500 (2026) establishing the Office of Applied Technology and Strategy, Cybersecurity Act / Senate Bill No. 12-9, SD1, HD2 (2026), National Cybersecurity Strategy and Policy 2026-2030, Privacy Act provisions of the Palau National Code (Title 6) - none of which are AI-specific

Regulation Status: Panama has no binding AI law imposing obligations on AI systems; the unified Bill 588 establishing adaptive AI governance, based on risk management and regulatory experimentation, passed first debate on 15 April 2026 and remains in committee, while Anteproyecto 51 of 2026 would add Penal Code penalties for malicious AI-generated content. Binding instruments that explicitly mention AI are institutional: Executive Decree 36 of 7 May 2026 declares critical and emerging technologies a national priority and creates the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies with an AI Subcommission. General instruments — Law 81 of 2019 on personal data protection and Law 144 of 2020 on government digital transformation — remain the operative rules touching AI.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy and coordination rather than regulation: the National AI Strategy 2026-2036 adopted by Cabinet Resolution No. 89-26, the National Advanced Technologies Agenda with USD 105 million behind the semiconductor strand, SENACYT-funded talent programs, and the AI Subcommission created by Executive Decree 36 of 2026. A regulatory sandbox and AI procurement rules exist only as provisions of the pending Bill 588.
Governance Type: AI governance is coordinated through the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies chaired by the Ministry of the Presidency, with SENACYT, the National Authority for Government Innovation and ANTAI contributing from existing mandates and ministries designating representatives through published resolutions. There is no subnational layer and no AI-specific judicial or independent review.
Actor Involvement: Government, universities and business participate through the CNTCE and the consultative process that produced the National AI Strategy, with civil society involved episodically through SENACYT workshops rather than any standing seat. Internationally Panama joined Pax Silica in 2026, adheres to the UNESCO Recommendation on AI Ethics and the Santiago Declaration, and engages with the IDB and SICA on regional AI work.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific penalty, authority or audit exists, leaving ANTAI's data-protection powers under Law 81 of 2019 and criminal law as the only enforcement routes touching AI.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy of the Republic of Panama approved by Cabinet Resolution No. 89-26 (2026), National Advanced Technologies Agenda including the National Semiconductor and Microelectronics Strategy (2026), Executive Decree 36 of 7 May 2026 creating the National Commission for Critical and Emerging Technologies and its AI Subcommission, National AI Strategy / ENIA (2021), Law 81 on Personal Data Protection (2019), Executive Decree 285 (2021), Law 144 on Government Digital Transformation (2020), Law 478 on Cybercrime Amendments (2025), Bill 588 on Adaptive Governance of Artificial Intelligence (2026, approved in first debate), Anteproyecto 51 on Penal Code reform for malicious AI use (2026, pending)

Regulation Status: Papua New Guinea has no dedicated AI legislation, no AI-specific binding instruments proposed or enacted as of mid-2026. The Digital Government Act (2022) provides general digital governance provisions but contains no AI-specific rules, leaving all regulation sub-indicators at the minimum level.
Policy Lever: No binding AI instruments, soft-law AI guidance, dedicated AI funding programs, sandboxes, or institutional bodies with AI mandates exist; the Digital Government Act (2022) is the sole operative digital governance instrument and does not establish any AI-specific policy levers.
Governance Type: AI governance responsibilities are unassigned in Papua New Guinea; there is no lead AI regulator, no inter-agency coordination mechanism, no subnational AI regulatory role, and no independent review body or court practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society, and academia are not engaged in any structured AI policy process; Papua New Guinea participates marginally in regional digital cooperation through the Pacific Islands Forum, which provides a minimal international AI governance connection and represents the only above-minimum score.
Enforcement Level: There is no AI enforcement framework, no designated enforcement authority, no sanctions for AI-related conduct, and no monitoring or auditing practice in Papua New Guinea.
Specific Laws: Digital Government Act (2022)

Regulation Status: Paraguay has no cross-sector AI statute; a Senate bill regulating and promoting AI systems, which would create an AI regulatory authority, has been socialised in public hearing but not enacted. Binding AI-specific texts in force are institutional: Corte Suprema de Justicia Resolución N° 12.677/2026 on AI use in the judiciary and Resolución DINAVISA N° 047/2026 creating an AI unit in health regulation. Ley N° 7593/2025 on personal data protection grants rights against automated and semi-automated individual decisions and profiling, but takes effect only in November 2027.
Policy Lever: Policy effort concentrates on promotion and internal state use: Decreto N° 5306/2026 grants preferential electricity tariffs to AI, cloud and data-centre industries, while the Hoja de Ruta Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial and the UNESCO RAM assessment provide non-binding direction. No regulatory sandbox, AI procurement rules or body with a statutory AI compliance mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is centred on MITIC as policy lead, with individual state institutions issuing their own AI rules and a narrow bi-ministerial commission for industry accreditation. No designated AI regulator, standing inter-agency mechanism, sub-national competence or independent review body with an AI mandate exists.
Actor Involvement: The UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise coordinated by MITIC and CONACYT, presented in 2025, brought public bodies, companies, universities and civil society organisations into a one-off multisectoral process, repeated in the Senate public hearing on the AI bill. International engagement runs through UNESCO ethics processes, regional ministerial summits, the Pax Silica Joint Declaration and bilateral cooperation with Taiwan on AI compute.
Enforcement Level: AI rules are not enforced against third parties: there is no AI sanctions regime, no competent authority and no audit practice, only internal compliance duties in the judiciary and the health regulator.
Specific Laws: Ley N° 7593/2025 de Protección de Datos Personales (2025), Ley N° 6534/2020 de Protección de Datos Personales Crediticios (2020), Corte Suprema de Justicia Resolución N° 12.677 sobre directrices para el uso de sistemas de inteligencia artificial en el Poder Judicial (2026), Resolución DINAVISA N° 047/2026 (2026), Decreto N° 5306/2026 sobre industrias convergentes de inteligencia artificial, computación en la nube y data centers (2026), Hoja de Ruta Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Informe de Metodología de Evaluación del Estado de Preparación en Inteligencia Artificial - UNESCO RAM Paraguay (2025)

Regulation Status: Peru governs AI through Law No. 31814 (2023) and its implementing Reglamento, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM, which took effect in January 2026 and imposes risk classification, algorithmic transparency, human oversight, internal policies and traceability registers on developers and deployers. The first adequacy deadline expired on 10 September 2026 for public powers, autonomous bodies and private operators in health, education, justice, security, economy and finance, while transport, commerce, labour, production, agriculture, energy, mining, remaining sectors and smaller firms have until 2027-2029.
Policy Lever: Peru combines binding instruments (Law No. 31814, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM, Law No. 32314) with a strategy-based promotional layer in ENIA 2026-2030, obligatory for public entities and state enterprises. Economic levers such as the regulatory sandbox, CNIDIA and the national AI platform are foreseen in the Reglamento and ENIA but not yet operating, and the SGTD leads with limited resources.
Governance Type: The Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros, through the SGTD, is the national AI authority, issuing lineamientos, technical standards and binding opinions, while the data protection authority, Indecopi, Concytec and sectoral ministries apply their own regimes to AI. Coordination is structured by the Sistema Nacional de Transformación Digital and by ENIA's AI Officer and quarterly reporting duties; subnational governments only implement national rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia took part in the 2024 public consultations on the draft Reglamento and in preparing ENIA 2026-2030, but none holds a standing formal role in AI policy-making. Peru aligns its framework with OECD and UNESCO instruments and the EU risk-based model, and participates in regional Latin American AI declarations.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is indirect: the SGTD monitors and refers cases while the data protection authority, Indecopi and criminal courts apply pre-existing penalties, and no decision under the AI framework has been published since the first obligations became applicable on 10 September 2026.
Specific Laws: Law No. 31814 - Ley que promueve el uso de la inteligencia artificial en favor del desarrollo económico y social del país (2023), Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM - Reglamento de la Ley N° 31814 (2025), Law No. 32314 - modifies the Penal Code and the Computer Crimes Law to treat the use of artificial intelligence as an aggravating factor (2025), Resolución Ministerial N° 152-2026-PCM - Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2026-2030 (2026), Resolución N° 0844-2025-JNE - Reglamento sobre propaganda electoral, publicidad estatal y neutralidad en periodo electoral (2026), Emergency Decree No. 007-2020 (2020)

Regulation Status: The Philippines has no enacted horizontal AI statute; about 40 House bills and 7 Senate bills in the 20th Congress, including House Bill 7396 and Senate Bill 25 (Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act), are being consolidated by a House technical working group into a risk-based Artificial Intelligence Development and Regulation Act. Binding AI-specific rules cover only election campaign content under COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 and public-sector AI use under DICT-CSC Joint Memorandum Circular No. 003, Series of 2026, while NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 applies the Data Privacy Act of 2012 to AI systems processing personal data.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft instruments - national roadmaps, NPC and BSP guidance, and sector memoranda - backed by two narrow binding issuances for elections and government use. Funding and research capacity are concentrated in CAIR, NAICRI and the AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan 2026-2033, with no operating AI sandbox or AI-specific procurement rules.
Governance Type: AI governance is spread across DICT and the Civil Service Commission for public-sector use, DOST and NAICRI for research, NPC for data protection, BSP for finance, CHED for higher education and COMELEC for elections, with DEPDev preparing a national AI governance framework. Coordination rests on joint circulars and inter-agency processes rather than a statutory council, and sub-national and judicial roles are marginal.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia take part through congressional technical working groups, agency consultations and roadmap validation rather than standing statutory bodies. Internationally the country is highly active, using its 2026 ASEAN chairmanship to push a regional AI legal framework and participating in UNESCO AI ethics processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is episodic and remit-bound, resting on COMELEC's election task force, NPC action under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and administrative discipline for government AI use, with no published AI-specific sanction decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy Roadmap 2.0 / NAISR 2.0 (2024), National AI Strategy for the Philippines – NAIS-PH (2025), COMELEC Resolution No. 11064 on Social Media and AI in Election Campaigns (2024), NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 on Application of the Data Privacy Act to AI Systems Processing Personal Data (2024), DICT-CSC Joint Memorandum Circular No. 003, Series of 2026 on Ethical and Responsible Development, Deployment and Use of AI in Government (2026), Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Memorandum No. M-2026-031 on AI Governance Principles (2026), Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Memorandum No. M-2026-034 on Frontier AI Cybersecurity Risks (2026), CHED Memorandum Order No. 21, Series of 2026 on Responsible AI Use in Higher Education (2026), Philippines AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan 2026–2033 (2026), Data Privacy Act (Republic Act No. 10173, 2012), House Bill 7396 – Artificial Intelligence Development and Regulation Act of the Philippines (pending, 2023), Senate Bill 25 – Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act (pending, 2025)

Regulation Status: Poland combines the directly applicable EU AI Act, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), with its own Act of 3 July 2026 on Artificial Intelligence Systems, published 27 July 2026 and in force since 11 August 2026. Coverage is horizontal and AI-specific, but the national supervision, inspection and penalty chapters apply only from 28 October 2026 and the AI Act's high-risk obligations were postponed to December 2027 and August 2028.
Policy Lever: Poland relies on directly applicable EU rules plus a national implementing statute, supported by regulator guidance from UODO and the Ministry of Digital Affairs. Economic levers include the PLN 1 billion AI Fund, publicly funded Polish language models and a statutory regulatory sandbox at KRiBSI that is free for SMEs and charges large firms a one-off fee, which has not yet begun operating.
Governance Type: Supervision is centralised in one new authority, KRiBSI, an outlier design within the EU, though its collegiate membership drawn from UOKiK, KNF, KRRiT and UKE and the attached Social Council for Artificial Intelligence build coordination into the body itself. Judicial review runs through the Warsaw competition and consumer protection court, and UODO retains independent GDPR oversight.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society were consulted on successive drafts of the AI Systems Act and the AI Policy until 2030 and are represented in the PL/AI advisory group, while the statutory Social Council for Artificial Intelligence attached to KRiBSI is not yet constituted and business and NGOs were excluded from the Commission's own membership. Internationally Poland is a Council of Europe AI convention signatory and an active participant in the EU AI Board and OECD AI work.
Enforcement Level: Penalties are defined in both EU and national law and a complaint channel is open to any person, but KRiBSI gains inspection and sanctioning powers only on 28 October 2026, so no AI-specific decision has been taken.
Specific Laws: Act of 3 July 2026 on Artificial Intelligence Systems (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003); EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, 2024); Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, 2026); Policy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Poland from 2020 (Council of Ministers Resolution No. 196, 2020); Policy for AI Development in Poland until 2030 (draft Council of Ministers resolution, 2026); Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (2024, signed)

Regulation Status: Portugal has not enacted a dedicated national AI statute and does not plan one; the directly applicable EU AI Act is the regulatory backbone, supplemented by Lei n.º 58/2019 (GDPR implementation), Lei n.º 24/96 (consumer protection), Decreto-Lei n.º 57/2008 and Lei n.º 125/2025 (NIS2). Prohibited-practice, AI-literacy, general-purpose AI and transparency obligations apply, while high-risk obligations were pushed to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026. National implementation remains partial: ANACOM acts as market surveillance authority and single point of contact, but national penalty rules and an AI sandbox are outstanding.
Policy Lever: Portugal governs AI mainly through the directly applicable EU AI Act, administrative designation of ANACOM as supervisor, and funding instruments: the Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial and its Action Plan 2026-2030 (Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 2/2026), the AMALIA national large language model, and AI Portugal 2030. Guidance is published by ANACOM and the government's digital portal, while the Technological Free Zones regime (Decreto-Lei n.º 67/2021) has not yet been converted into an AI Act regulatory sandbox.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-plus-sectoral model: ANACOM supervises the AI Act and acts as national contact point, coordinating fourteen sectoral and fundamental-rights authorities, with ANIA implementation monitored under the governance model set by Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 2/2026. No subnational tier regulates AI, and independent oversight comes mainly from the CNPD and the courts.
Actor Involvement: Stakeholder involvement runs through consultations and project consortia rather than standing statutory roles: the Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial went to public consultation in January 2025 with an accompanying committee of industry, academic and civil-society representatives, and public universities build the AMALIA model under FCT and ARTE coordination. Internationally, Portugal acts through the EU AI Board, the EU Coordinated Plan on AI, European research infrastructures and Lusophone digital cooperation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement remains preparatory: ANACOM holds the supervisory mandate and informs the market about obligations applying since 2 August 2026, but national penalty rules are not enacted and no AI-specific enforcement decision or audit programme has been published.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 2/2026 - Agenda Nacional de Inteligência Artificial e Plano de Ação 2026-2030 (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 178/2026 - AMALIA (2026), Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 201/2024 - AMALIA (2024), Lei n.º 12-A/2026 - execution of the Digital Services Act (2026), Lei n.º 125/2025 - NIS2 cybersecurity (2025), Lei n.º 58/2019 - GDPR Implementation (2019), Lei n.º 24/96 - Consumer Protection Law (1996, applicable to AI), Decreto-Lei n.º 57/2008 - Unfair Commercial Practices (2008, applicable to AI), Decreto-Lei n.º 67/2021 - Technological Free Zones (2021), Estratégia Digital Nacional (2024), AI Portugal 2030 National Strategy (2019)

Regulation Status: Qatar has no horizontal AI statute; binding rules are the Qatar Central Bank Artificial Intelligence Guideline (September 2024) for licensed financial institutions and QICDRC Practice Direction No. 1 of 2026 governing AI use before the QFC Court and Regulatory Tribunal. The Qatar Financial Markets Authority's draft AI regulations consulted in May 2025 are still unenacted, and the Shura Council on 27 April 2026 referred a proposal for a general debate on AI governance to committee rather than a bill. Everything else — the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), MCIT ethical AI principles and NCSA secure-AI guidelines — is non-binding.
Policy Lever: Qatar combines two binding sectoral AI instruments with a growing soft-law layer (MCIT ethics principles, NCSA secure-AI guidelines) and funding and capability programmes such as AIQAT, the ALIF government training programme with Scale AI, and the Fanar platform. Institutional structures — the Artificial Intelligence Committee and the newly approved National Center for Artificial Intelligence — coordinate strategy, while compliance powers over AI sit with the Qatar Central Bank inside its existing supervisory machinery.
Governance Type: Governance follows a lead-plus-sectoral pattern: MCIT and its Artificial Intelligence Committee set national direction, while the Qatar Central Bank, Qatar Financial Markets Authority, National Cyber Security Agency and the Qatar Financial Centre regulate AI within their own perimeters. There is no subnational tier, and independent checks come from the QFC courts and the National Data Privacy Office rather than from broad judicial review of AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Industry input flows through regulator consultations, QFC sandboxes and summit partnerships, and academia has a formal seat via QCRI's vice-chairmanship of the Artificial Intelligence Committee plus the MCIT-QRDI AIQAT research programme. Domestic civil society is absent from the process, while international engagement runs through GCC and UNESCO channels and Doha's hosting of World Summit AI.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is sector-confined: the Qatar Central Bank can act against licensed firms under its AI guideline and the National Data Privacy Office issues binding data-protection decisions, but no AI-specific enforcement action has been published and monitoring is neither cross-sectoral nor publicly reported.
Specific Laws: Qatar National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2019), Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2021 establishing the Artificial Intelligence Committee, Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016), Qatar Central Bank Artificial Intelligence Guideline (2024), NCSA Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence (2024), MCIT Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Development and Deployment of Artificial Intelligence (2024), QFC Practice Direction No. 1 of 2026 on the Use of Artificial Intelligence

Regulation Status: Romania's binding AI rules come entirely from the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), which has applied directly since 1 August 2024 with prohibitions from February 2025, general-purpose AI duties from August 2025 and transparency plus high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026. No standalone domestic AI statute exists: national competent authorities were named by a Government memorandum of 12 March 2026, and the implementing law that would confer control procedures and the national penalty regime remains in preparation. Obligations therefore bind operators across sectors while the domestic supervisory machinery is incomplete.
Policy Lever: Romania relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Government Decision 832/2024), with no domestic binding AI instrument and no maintained national guidance suite. Economic levers are EU-funded programmes channelled through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan and the Digital Europe Programme, and the AI regulatory sandbox required by Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is not operating.
Governance Type: Governance is centred on ANCOM as national market surveillance authority and single point of contact, with the National Bank of Romania, the Financial Supervisory Authority, ANSPDCP, the consumer protection authority ANPC and the Labour Inspection covering their own domains. Coordination is set out in a Government memorandum rather than statute, sub-national bodies have no role, and the Ombudsman together with audiovisual and electoral authorities exercise fundamental-rights oversight powers.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation runs mainly through the consultative Romanian Committee for Artificial Intelligence established by MCID Order 20484/2023, which draws on industry and academic experts, while NGOs take part only through general public consultation on draft acts. Internationally Romania is represented on the European AI Board, adheres to the OECD AI Principles and is a signatory of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: AI Act penalties are formally available in Romania but cannot be applied because the national act conferring control procedures and the sanctions regime has not been adopted, and no AI enforcement decision or monitoring report exists.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 approved by Government Decision No. 832/2024, MCID Order No. 20484/2023 establishing the Romanian Committee for Artificial Intelligence, Government memorandum of 12 March 2026 designating national competent authorities and the single point of contact for the AI Act, Law No. 190/2018 implementing the GDPR

Regulation Status: Russia moved from strategy to statute with Federal Law No. 243-FZ of 26 July 2026 On Supporting the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation, in force since 1 September 2026, which defines artificial intelligence and large foundation models and creates the sovereign and national model statuses. Core obligations - developer duties, machine-readable labelling tools on platforms with over 500,000 daily users, and copyright rules for training - apply only from 1 March 2027, with a transition to 2032 for foreign systems already deployed in sensitive areas. Supporting instruments remain Presidential Decree No. 490 (National AI Strategy to 2030, updated 2024) and the experimental legal regime laws FZ-123 and FZ-258.
Policy Lever: Policy combines a framework statute with industrial-policy levers: support measures, tax and financing incentives for developers of sovereign and national models, state-funded compute, and operating regulatory sandboxes under FZ-258 and the Moscow regime under FZ-123. Soft law runs through the AI Ethics Code and its sectoral codes and through Rosstandart AI standards, while the content of binding duties has been delegated almost entirely to secondary acts not yet issued.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in federal executive hands, with the Presidential Commission on the Development of AI Technologies coordinating the Government, the Ministry of Digital Development, sectoral regulators and the Bank of Russia. Sub-national bodies implement national experimental regimes, and independent judicial or civil-society oversight of AI is absent apart from the industry-led AI ethics commission.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is a state-industry affair: the largest technology companies and the AI Alliance shaped both the 2026 statute and the ethics code, academia contributes occasionally, and domestic civil society is absent. International engagement runs through BRICS and CIS channels and the promotion of a sovereign-AI model abroad rather than through multilateral treaty frameworks.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is nominal: the duties that could be sanctioned under FZ-243 only become applicable on 1 March 2027, no AI-specific penalties are in the Code of Administrative Offences, and no authority has yet exercised compliance powers over AI.
Specific Laws: Federal Law No. 243-FZ On Supporting the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation (2026), National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence until 2030 approved by Presidential Decree No. 490 (2019, updated 2024), Presidential Decree No. 116 establishing the Presidential Commission on the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2026), Federal Law No. 123-FZ on the experimental legal regime for artificial intelligence in Moscow (2020, updated 2024), Federal Law No. 258-FZ on experimental legal regimes in the sphere of digital innovation (2020), National Code of Ethics in the Field of Artificial Intelligence (2021)

Regulation Status: Rwanda governs AI through a dedicated but non-binding framework: the Cabinet-approved National AI Policy of April 2023, the AI Readiness and Maturity Framework, and RURA's Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence. Legal effect comes only from general instruments, chiefly Law No. 058/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy and Law No. 24/2016 Governing Information and Communication Technologies. The Cabinet decision of 8 June 2026 creating a National Artificial Intelligence Agency moves governance toward institutional form without creating enforceable AI obligations.
Policy Lever: Rwanda relies on soft law and investment: the National AI Policy, the AI Readiness and Maturity Framework, RURA ethical guidelines, the National Data Sharing Policy (2025), and funded vehicles such as the Rwanda AI Scaling Hub and C4IR Rwanda. Institutional capacity is being consolidated in the Cabinet-approved National Artificial Intelligence Agency, which has a coordination rather than a regulatory enforcement mandate.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive, with MINICT and the Cabinet-approved National Artificial Intelligence Agency leading and sectoral regulators (RURA, National Cyber Security Authority, National Bank of Rwanda) acting within existing remits. There is no subnational tier and no judicial or ombudsman review shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed in through drafting workshops, C4IR Rwanda and UNESCO-supported processes rather than standing formal bodies, and domestic civil society input has not recurred since the 2023 policy drafting. Internationally Rwanda is a convenor and norm-entrepreneur: Global AI Summit on Africa host, Africa Declaration on Artificial Intelligence sponsor, Smart Africa Alliance leader, and participant in the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI runs solely through data-protection powers of the National Cyber Security Authority, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or published enforcement decisions.
Specific Laws: National AI Policy (2023), AI Readiness and Maturity Framework for Rwanda (2023), Guidelines on the Ethical Development and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (RURA), Cabinet decision establishing the National Artificial Intelligence Agency (2026), National Data Sharing Policy (2025), Law No. 058/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy, Law No. 24/2016 Governing Information and Communication Technologies

Regulation Status: South Sudan has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or national AI strategy; the country's first comprehensive digital statute, the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, was signed on 18 February 2026 and addresses hacking, critical infrastructure, online content and investigative powers without any AI provision. A first Data Protection Bill was announced by the Ministry of Information, Communication Technology and Postal Services for 2026 but has not been introduced, and comparative legal reviews place South Sudan as the only East African state with neither AI legislation nor AI soft law.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to general digital law and connectivity work, including the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, the SUDESA Strategic Framework for the Digital Transformation of South Sudan's Government and Public Sector, and a National Spectrum Management and 5G Strategy begun in July 2026. AI appears only in capacity-building events such as the National Communication Authority's AI app development bootcamp and UNESCO-supported training, not in any rule, guidance or funding instrument.
Governance Type: AI governance is absent rather than centralized: the Ministry of Information, Communication Technology and Postal Services and the National Communication Authority lead digital policy without any AI remit, and no coordination body, state-level institution or independent review mechanism addresses AI. Judicial and oversight engagement with digital law is limited to the contested enforcement of the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026.
Actor Involvement: There is no structured domestic engagement by industry, civil society or academia on AI policy, and AI activity in Juba is limited to community events such as IndabaX South Sudan 2026 and donor-run training. International involvement rests on African Union and UNESCO membership rather than national participation in AI governance processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement activity is confined to the general Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, under which a specialised unit and criminal penalties operate, while no AI-specific obligation, authority or monitoring exists.
Specific Laws: Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 (signed 18 February 2026), Cybercrimes and Computer Misuse Provisional Order 2021, SUDESA Strategic Framework for the Digital Transformation of South Sudan's Government and Public Sector, National Spectrum Management and 5G Strategy (under development, 2026), Data Protection Bill (announced for 2026, not introduced) — none AI-specific

Regulation Status: Saint Kitts and Nevis has no AI-specific legislation, no AI bill before the National Assembly, and no national AI strategy. The applicable framework is general technology and consumer law: the Electronic Transactions Act (Cap. 18.44), the Consumer Protection Act, 2023 adopted from the CARICOM model, and the Data Protection Act, 2018, which was passed on 4 May 2018 but has never been commenced. Government statements present consumer protection law as the vehicle for fair and responsible AI, which is the only link between binding law and AI.
Policy Lever: The policy toolkit contains no AI-specific binding or soft-law instrument, no AI funding line, sandbox or procurement rule, and no body with an AI mandate. Activity is limited to the state's own adoption of AI tools, notably the Ministry of Justice and Legal Affairs' AI assistant for public legal information and planned AI-based traffic management.
Governance Type: Governance of technology in this unitary microstate is concentrated in central government ministries, with nothing assigned to or contested by other bodies on AI. The Nevis Island Administration plays no AI role, and courts and independent oversight bodies have not reviewed AI matters, although the judiciary itself has begun using digital and AI-assisted services.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy-making involves no structured input from industry, civil society or academia, as no AI policy process has been opened. Engagement is confined to the international level, through statements at the United Nations and participation in UN and regional Caribbean AI discussions.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced or monitored, and only generic consumer-law penalties could reach AI-related conduct.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, 2018 (passed 4 May 2018, not in force), Electronic Transactions Act (Cap. 18.44, 2011), Consumer Protection Act (2023)

Regulation Status: Saint Lucia has no AI-specific legislation, no draft AI bill and no AI provisions inside its general statutes; the partially proclaimed Data Protection Act, Cap 8.18 is the main general instrument that touches automated processing. The Minister for Education and Digital Transformation called in January 2026 for legislation on AI use in school-based assessments, but no text has been introduced. Cullen International's September 2026 regional benchmark confirms that no Caribbean country covered, Saint Lucia included, has adopted an AI-specific regulatory framework.
Policy Lever: Policy action is confined to broader digital transformation work: the DigiGov e-services platform, the National Authentication Framework digital ID launched in 2026, and a planned ECLAC-supported regulatory sandbox for digital identity and fintech. No AI funding scheme, AI procurement rule, AI guidance document or AI-mandated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance of AI is centralised and informal: one ministerial portfolio touches the subject, with no dedicated regulator, no statutory coordination body and no role for courts or independent oversight bodies in shaping AI rules. Regional bodies, in particular CARICOM and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union Caribbean AI Task Force, provide the only structured forums in which Saint Lucia takes part.
Actor Involvement: Structured participation in AI policy is international rather than domestic: Saint Lucia joins UNESCO regional ethics forums, CARICOM digital processes and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union Caribbean AI Task Force, while no national consultation, working group or advisory council brings in domestic industry, civil society or universities. Business interest surfaces through the Saint Lucia Chamber of Commerce rather than through government process.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capacity for AI is absent: no AI-specific duties, no designated authority, no recorded action and no monitoring beyond regional readiness reviews.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act, Cap 8.18 (2011, partially in force 2023)

Regulation Status: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has no AI-specific legislation, bill or subsidiary regulation; AI is touched only incidentally by the Electronic Transactions Act (2007), Cybercrime Act (2016) and Telecommunications Act (2001), none of which contain a provision written for AI systems. The Privacy Act (2003), which would cover processing of personal data by public authorities, remains un-commenced, leaving no data-protection baseline for automated decision-making.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is confined to general digital transformation: a five-year digital transformation strategy process and the Caribbean Digital Transformation Project deliver connectivity, e-government and skills work without AI-specific guidance, funding windows, procurement rules or a sandbox. Regionally endorsed material such as the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean AI Task Force Final Report (2026) is advisory and has not been translated into national instruments.
Governance Type: Governance is highly centralized: the NTRC is the only standing authority touching AI-adjacent matters, supported by the regional ECTEL treaty structure, and the Ministry responsible for digital transformation sets policy direction without a coordination mechanism. There is no subnational tier and no court or independent-review practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is almost entirely external: participation in the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's AI and data-governance ministerial dialogues, the CARICOM-level Caribbean AI Task Force process and the 4th UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI. Domestically there is no structured consultation channel for industry, civil society or academia on AI policy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement capability is limited to general criminal and electronic-transactions penalties, with no AI-specific obligations, no designated enforcer and no monitoring or audit practice.
Specific Laws: Electronic Transactions Act (2007), Cybercrime Act (2016), Telecommunications Act (2001), Privacy Act (2003, not in force)

Regulation Status: Samoa has no dedicated AI legislation, no binding AI rules and no AI bill before the Legislative Assembly. The National Communications & Information Technology Policy 2025/26-2030/31 and the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31, launched by the Deputy Prime Minister on 17 April 2026, define artificial intelligence and treat trust, safety and responsible data use as principles, but impose no legal duties. AI activity remains governed incidentally by general instruments including the National Digital Identification Act 2024 and telecommunications law.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to soft framing: the National ICT Policy 2025/26-2030/31 and National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31 reference artificial intelligence as an emerging risk and opportunity, and MCIT ran a UNDP-supported AI trust and safety workshop in Apia on 13-14 November 2025. No funded AI programme, sandbox, procurement rule or body with a legal AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: AI matters sit entirely with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, whose Digital Transformation and Innovation Division leads digital and cybersecurity policy. Sectoral regulators, subnational authorities and independent review bodies have no AI role.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI runs through ministry-led consultation events rather than standing structures: private sector and community actors took part in the National ICT Policy validation and Samoa Digital Week 2026, and experts joined the MCIT-UNDP AI workshop. International partners, chiefly UNDP and Pacific regional forums, supply most AI governance input.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, penalty, authority or monitoring practice exists, leaving only general telecommunications, digital identity and cybercrime penalties incidentally applicable.
Specific Laws: National Communications & Information Technology Policy Samoa 2025/26-2030/31 (2026), Samoa National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26-2030/31 (2026), Pathway for the Development of Samoa 2025/26-2030/31, National Digital Identification Act 2024

Regulation Status: San Marino has no dedicated AI legislation in force or in the legislative pipeline; AI falls incidentally under Law No. 171/2018 on personal data protection. The Republic signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law on 5 September 2024 as one of its first signatories, but has not ratified it and the treaty remains outside domestic law. The EU–Andorra–San Marino Association Agreement, whose signature and provisional application the Council of the European Union authorised on 16 July 2026, is the channel through which internal-market rules would later reach San Marino.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is limited to a general data-protection law and a generic high-technology enterprise incentive regime administered by San Marino Innovation, updated by Decreto Delegato n. 91 of 20 July 2026. There is no AI strategy, AI guidance, AI funding programme, regulatory sandbox or body holding a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is fully centralised: one general data-protection authority carries whatever AI-adjacent oversight exists, alongside the executive Secretariats of State and San Marino Innovation. There is no coordination mechanism, no sub-national layer and no judicial or independent-review practice shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is predominantly external, through the Council of Europe treaty process and International Monetary Fund and European Union fora, with the University of San Marino hosting occasional academic debate. Domestic industry contact occurs through innovation events rather than AI consultations, and civil society has no role.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only indirectly through the data-protection powers of the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Law No. 171/2018 (Data Protection Law), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed 5 September 2024, not ratified), Decreto Delegato n. 101/2019 on high-technology enterprises as amended by Decreto Delegato n. 91 of 20 July 2026

Regulation Status: São Tomé and Príncipe has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or sectoral AI rule. The applicable framework is general: Law No. 3/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data, Law No. 7/2017 establishing the National Personal Data Protection Agency (ANPDP), and the Cybercrime Law of 2017, none of which contains provisions written for AI systems. The UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology country report places the country at a consumption stage of AI with regulation and oversight identified as a priority still to be addressed.
Policy Lever: Policy activity on AI is limited to a UNESCO-supported readiness diagnostic; the country uses no AI-specific binding instruments, guidance, funding programmes or sandboxes. Digital policy is carried by the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2028 and the digital governance strategy work supported by United Nations University, neither of which creates AI obligations or an AI mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in a single national government with no AI-specific authority, coordination body or independent review role. The ANPDP is the one operational independent digital regulator, and its powers under Law No. 7/2017 do not extend to AI as such.
Actor Involvement: International organisations drive what AI engagement exists: UNESCO conducted and published the AI readiness assessment presented in São Tomé in June 2025, and African Union membership brings the Continental AI Strategy. Domestic industry, civil society and universities have no structured role in AI policy-making.
Enforcement Level: No AI rules exist to enforce, and the only oversight touching AI is the general data protection mandate of the ANPDP, which has taken no recorded AI-related action.
Specific Laws: Law No. 3/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (2016), Law No. 7/2017 on the Organisation and Functioning of the National Personal Data Protection Agency (2017), Cybercrime Law (2017), National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2028 (2023), UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology country report for São Tomé and Príncipe (2025)

Regulation Status: Saudi Arabia governs AI mainly through non-binding SDAIA instruments, with binding AI-written provisions confined to the Copyright Law (Royal Decree M/169) in force since 12 August 2026 and its Implementing Regulations, which set conditions on using copyrighted works to develop AI. The Personal Data Protection Law applies to automated processing and profiling without AI-specific duties, and the Draft Responsible AI Policy and Draft Global AI Hub Law remain unenacted after public consultations.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through SDAIA's maintained soft-law suite—AI Ethics Principles, Generative AI Guidelines, AI Adoption Framework and the National AI Risk Management Framework (SDAIA-P145, 2026)—supported by funded programmes, sandboxes and public-sector adoption leverage. Binding levers are limited to the PDPL and the AI-training provisions of the 2026 Copyright Law.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in SDAIA, which sets strategy, issues frameworks and enforces the PDPL, with sectoral bodies such as CST, DGA and the Saudi Authority for Intellectual Property acting inside their existing mandates. There is no subnational tier and no independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultation-based through the Istitlaa platform, used for the draft Global AI Hub Law (2025) and the draft Responsible AI Policy (April–May 2026), without standing roles for industry, civil society or academia. Internationally the Kingdom is active in UN and G20 AI governance work and hosts major AI events while signing no binding AI instrument.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement operates under the PDPL through SDAIA's violation-review committees, with 48 decisions reported in January 2026, while no AI-specific obligation carries its own sanction or published enforcement record.
Specific Laws: National Strategy for Data and AI – NSDAI (2020), Personal Data Protection Law – Royal Decree M/19 (2021, in force 2023), AI Ethics Principles – SDAIA (2023), Generative AI Guidelines – SDAIA (2024), AI Adoption Framework – SDAIA (2025), National Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework – SDAIA-P145 (2026), Copyright Law – Royal Decree M/169 (2026, in force 12 August 2026) and its Implementing Regulations (2026), Cabinet decision designating 2026 the Year of Artificial Intelligence (2026), Draft Responsible AI Policy – SDAIA (consultation closed May 2026), Draft Global AI Hub Law – CST (2025)

Regulation Status: Senegal has no binding AI-specific legislation; governance rests on the non-binding Stratégie Nationale pour le Développement de l'Intelligence Artificielle (2023) and the New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034 launched in February 2025. Recent digital legislating has been general rather than AI-written: the National Assembly adopted Law No. 25/2026 on the protection of critical information infrastructures and digital security on 20 August 2026, and Law No. 2008-12 on personal data remains the main instrument the regulator applies to AI processing. A regional parliamentary workshop on AI regulation hosted in Dakar from 16 to 18 September 2026 discussed future rules without producing a national bill.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven by non-binding strategy and public investment rather than regulation: the SNDIA (2023) and the New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034 (2025) set objectives for AI skills, data infrastructure and a Cluster Sénégal IA, while a joint Ministry of Public Service and Ministry of Telecommunications plan announced in September 2026 targets AI training for more than 35,000 civil servants. The Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles holds data-protection powers applicable to AI, but no body has a statutory AI mandate.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Communication, Telecommunications and Digital Economy, with the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles covering data protection and ARTP covering telecoms and emerging-technology infrastructure. Coordination between them is ad hoc, sub-national authorities have no role, and independent review of AI decisions is confined to data-protection supervision.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia were consulted in the SNDIA process, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology exercise and events such as Afrik'IA and the 2026 Internet governance forum, but none holds a standing formal role. International engagement is the strongest channel, through the African Union, Smart Africa, UNESCO and United Nations discussions on autonomous weapons.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaching AI occurs only under data-protection and cybersecurity law, with no AI-specific obligation, penalty or dedicated supervisor in place.
Specific Laws: National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Senegal (SNDIA) (2023), New Deal Technologique Horizon 2034 (2025), Law No. 2008-12 on the Protection of Personal Data (2008), Law No. 25/2026 on the Protection of Critical Information Infrastructures and Digital Security (2026), African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention) (ratified 2016)

Regulation Status: Serbia has no binding AI law in force; artificial intelligence is governed by the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence 2025-2030, the 2023 Ethical Guidelines for reliable and responsible AI, and general legislation on personal data protection, electronic commerce and information security. A working group of the Ministry of Science, Technological Development and Innovation is drafting a first Law on Artificial Intelligence closely modelled on the EU AI Act, providing risk classification, prohibited practices, labelling of AI-generated content, an Artificial Intelligence Agency and a register of high-risk systems; adoption is targeted for December 2026 and the draft has not been submitted to the National Assembly. A draft Law on Personal Data Protection published for consultation on 30 July 2026 would add AI-specific duties, including mandatory impact assessments and prior opinions for high-risk AI processing, but remains a draft.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through strategy, soft law and spending: the AI Strategy 2025-2030 with its action plan, the 2023 Ethical Guidelines, the state-funded Institute for Artificial Intelligence of Serbia and the national AI computing platform. Coordination rests with the Council for Artificial Intelligence, which holds no compliance powers, and the regulatory sandbox and compliance-assessment bodies remain plans tied to the pending draft AI law.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Science, Technological Development and Innovation, supported by the cross-ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and a drafting working group; no independent AI regulator exists and the planned Artificial Intelligence Agency awaits the draft law. Subnational authorities have no role, and independent review of AI-related matters is limited to isolated data protection complaints that produced no decision.
Actor Involvement: Participation is invitation-based: industry bodies, NALED, law firms and academic researchers sit in the ministry's AI law working group, while digital-rights groups comment largely from outside the process and the draft text has not been opened to general public consultation. Internationally Serbia is highly active, having chaired the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence, hosted the Belgrade Ministerial Declaration and aligned its draft law with the EU AI Act as an accession candidate.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligations, penalties, supervisory authority or audit regime are in force, and the only AI-related complaint before the Data Protection Commissioner closed without action for lack of enforcement capacity.
Specific Laws: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2025-2030 (Official Gazette RS No. 5/2025), Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia 2020-2025 (Official Gazette RS No. 73/2019), Ethical Guidelines for the Development, Application and Use of Reliable and Responsible Artificial Intelligence (2023), Law on Personal Data Protection (2018), Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (2026, in preparation), Draft Law on Personal Data Protection (2026, public consultation 30 July-10 September 2026)

Regulation Status: Seychelles has no dedicated AI legislation and no AI bill in the National Assembly; the Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), in force since 22 December 2023 and enforced by the Information Commission, reaches AI only as general data law. The single AI-specific instrument is the National Artificial Intelligence in Education Framework 2026-2030, published in March 2026 and approved by Cabinet on 22 July 2026, a non-binding policy limited to state schools that sets expectations on data privacy, child protection, academic integrity, cybersecurity and procurement. The National Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation Act, 2025 (Act 24 of 2025) names artificial intelligence among the institute's promotional functions but has not commenced.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through a Cabinet-approved sectoral framework and ministry-led capacity building, including a national workshop on digital competencies for teachers delivered with the Commonwealth of Learning and technical support from the World Bank. No AI-specific binding instrument, dedicated funding line, sandbox or AI procurement rule is in place, and the National Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation Act, 2025, which would give a statutory body an AI promotion remit, has not commenced.
Governance Type: AI governance is handled by central executive bodies: the Ministry of Education and Human Resource Development for the education framework, the Department of Information Communications Technology for digital policy, with the Information and Communications Technologies Authority and the Information Commission applying general communications and data law. There is no AI coordination structure, no district-level role and no judicial or independent-review activity on AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement on AI is occasional and event-based: a National Assembly seminar on artificial intelligence in March 2024 with university, ministry and citizen speakers, and the 2026 National Innovation Fair bringing together government, academia, private sector and civil society. External linkage comes from the World Bank's technical support for the education framework, the Commonwealth of Learning teacher-competency work, and membership of UNESCO and the African Union.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI rests entirely on general data protection and communications law, with no AI-specific penalties, no recorded actions and only framework-level monitoring commitments in schools.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence in Education Framework 2026-2030 (2026), Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023), National Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation Act, 2025 (Act 24 of 2025)

Regulation Status: Sierra Leone has no enacted AI-specific legislation and none before Parliament. The Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation, with the World Bank Group, produced a Draft Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic Report and held three days of stakeholder consultation in May 2026 toward a first National AI Strategy, which remains unadopted. AI-adjacent conduct falls under general law such as the Cyber Security and Crime Act 2021, and a Cabinet-approved National Data Protection Policy (April 2026) awaits a merged data protection and access-to-information law.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through donor-funded programmes rather than law: the Sierra Leone Digital Transformation Project finances the AI readiness diagnostic, a civil-service digital and AI literacy programme, and the National AI and Deepfake Awareness Campaign launched in Freetown in September 2026. The Bank of Sierra Leone operates a fintech regulatory sandbox, but it is not AI-specific, and no AI procurement rules or AI-specific binding instruments exist.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in central government, with the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation as lead and the Directorate of Science, Technology and Innovation as implementing partner alongside the Ministry of Information and Civic Education. Cooperation occurs through individual projects financed by the World Bank, without a statutory coordination mechanism, subnational competence or independent oversight.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is limited to one-off consultation: government, media, civil society and private sector took part in the May 2026 engagement on the Draft AI Readiness Diagnostic Report, and no body holds a standing advisory seat. International engagement is more active, combining World Bank partnership, African Union Continental AI Strategy membership, endorsement of the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models, and presidential advocacy at the 81st UN General Assembly.
Enforcement Level: With no AI rules in force, there is nothing to enforce, no penalties, no designated authority and no monitoring of AI systems.
Specific Laws: Cyber Security and Crime Act (2021), National Communications Authority Act (2022), National Innovation and Digital Strategy (2019-2029), National Data Protection Policy (2026) [Cabinet-approved], Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill (2025) [draft, not enacted], Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic Report (2026) [draft, non-binding], National AI Strategy [under development], National AI and Deepfake Awareness Campaign (2026)

Regulation Status: Singapore governs AI mainly through voluntary, AI-explicit instruments—the Model AI Governance Framework family, AI Verify, and the National AI Strategy Update of 20 May 2026—with binding obligations confined to AI-generated content under the Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025. The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 supplies the general legal base, now read through the PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in Generative AI, which make AI-specific notification mandatory. The MAS Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management are still in preparation following the consultation that closed on 31 January 2026.
Policy Lever: Policy runs on voluntary frameworks, testing tools and funding: the Model AI Governance Frameworks, AI Verify, the MAS AI Risk Management Toolkit and the PDPC generative AI guidelines, backed by National AI Missions, R&D funding, tax incentives and sandboxes. Binding levers remain limited to the electoral deepfake ban and general statutes applied by existing regulators.
Governance Type: IMDA under MDDI leads AI governance with the AI Verify Foundation, while MAS, PDPC, the Online Safety Commission and the Elections Department cover their own sectors, coordinated through the National AI Council chaired by the Prime Minister. There is no subnational layer, and independent review of AI decisions is limited to ordinary court remedies.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold structured, continuing roles through the AI Verify Foundation, the MAS–industry MindForge work and the NTU-hosted AI Safety Institute, while domestic civil society is limited to occasional public consultations. Internationally Singapore is highly active, from the AI Safety Institute network and OECD work to ASEAN leadership and bilateral AI agreements.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to narrow content rules and general statutes, with penalties defined under ELIONA and the online safety regime but no published sanction imposed under an AI-specific provision.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy (2019), National AI Strategy 2.0 (2023), National AI Strategy Update (2026), Model AI Governance Framework (2019, updated 2024 for Generative AI), Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI version 1.5 (2026), Personal Data Protection Act (2012, amended 2020), PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in Generative AI (2026), Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act (2024), Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act (2025), Online Criminal Harms Act (2023), Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act (2022), MAS Consultation Paper on Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (2025), MAS AI Risk Management Toolkit (2026), Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Act (2026)

Regulation Status: Slovakia is covered by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions, AI-literacy and general-purpose AI duties already apply and whose Article 50 transparency rules apply from 2 August 2026, while Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed high-risk obligations to December 2027. Nationally, Act No. 56/2018 Coll. on conformity assessment of products was amended by Act No. 318/2025 Coll. from 1 January 2026 to anchor AI Act enforcement and penalties, and the Act on State Administration in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and European Data Regulation, approved by the government on 26 August 2026, is in second reading with effect from 1 January 2027. No standalone Slovak AI statute is yet in force.
Policy Lever: Slovakia relies on the directly applicable EU AI Act plus the conformity-assessment amendment of Act No. 318/2025 Coll., supplemented by MIRRI's AI information hub, CERAI advice and EU codes of practice. Economic levers are EDIHs, national supercomputing and AI-skills funding, with a regulatory sandbox and dedicated staffing provided for only in the pending state-administration bill.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in MIRRI as coordinator and prospective general AI market surveillance authority, with the Office for Personal Data Protection, National Security Authority, Slovak Trade Inspection and the Office for Standardisation as notifying authority holding sectoral remits. A separate Digital Integrity Office was dropped on budgetary grounds, there is no subnational layer, and independent scrutiny is limited to CERAI's advisory opinions.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and trade unions feed into AI policy through the AIslovakIA platform, CERAI, interdepartmental consultation and a 2026 memorandum with the Technology Trade Union, while NGOs have no standing statutory seat. Internationally Slovakia acts through the EU AI Board, OECD and GPAI and has signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist on paper through the AI Act and Act No. 318/2025 Coll., but no Slovak authority has yet been fully empowered or resourced and no AI enforcement decisions have been taken.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Digital Omnibus on AI (2026), Act No. 56/2018 Coll. on Conformity Assessment of Products as amended by Act No. 318/2025 Coll. (2025), Draft Act on State Administration in the Field of Artificial Intelligence and European Data Regulation (2026), Act No. 18/2018 Coll. on Personal Data Protection (2018), Act No. 69/2018 Coll. on Cybersecurity (2018), Government Plenipotentiary for Artificial Intelligence (2025), Action Plan for Digital Transformation of Slovakia 2023–2026 (2023), CERAI Standing Commission on Ethics and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (2020)

Regulation Status: Slovenia regulates AI through directly applicable Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and the national Act on the Implementation of the EU Regulation on Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (ZIUDHPUI), in force since 21 November 2025, which designates competent authorities, offences and fines. Prohibited practices, general-purpose AI, penalty and Article 50 transparency provisions apply, while high-risk obligations were postponed to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I) by the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Sector-specific AI duties exist in the Media Act (ZMed-1, 2025), which requires visible labelling of generative-AI media content and places AI-assisted content under editorial responsibility.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 operationalised by ZIUDHPUI, with AI-content labelling duties in ZMed-1; soft law comprises the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 (adopted 5 March 2026), AKOS guidance and Information Commissioner opinions. Economic levers include NpUI and recovery-fund financing, the Slovenian AI Factory supercomputer, the AI Competence Centre and European Digital Innovation Hubs, with the statutory AI regulatory sandbox at AKOS prepared but not yet operating.
Governance Type: The Ministry for Digital Transformation steers policy while supervision is split among AKOS, the Information Commissioner, the Bank of Slovenia, the Insurance Supervision Agency, the Market Inspectorate and the Information Society Inspectorate, linked by the coordination council of supervisory authorities created by ZIUDHPUI. Oversight is wholly national; independent input comes from the Information Commissioner and the National Council for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence rather than from courts or sub-national bodies.
Actor Involvement: Preparation of the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 involved ministries, the research community, business, the public sector and civil society through several public consultations and unanimous endorsement by the Economic and Social Council. Academic experts hold formal seats on the National Council for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence, while international engagement runs through the EU AI Board, OECD work and signature of Council of Europe Framework Convention CETS 225.
Enforcement Level: Penalties mirroring the AI Act's tiered fines are legislated in ZIUDHPUI and supervisory powers became applicable in August 2026, but enforcement so far consists of guidance and opinions rather than decisions or sanctions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence – Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Act on the Implementation of the EU Regulation on Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence – ZIUDHPUI (2025), Media Act – ZMed-1 (2025), National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence until 2030 – NsUI 2030 (2026), National Programme to Promote the Development and Use of AI in the Republic of Slovenia by 2025 – NpUI (2021), Digital Slovenia 2030 Strategy (2023)

Regulation Status: Solomon Islands has no AI-specific legislation, regulation or bill; AI appears only in planning documents, namely the SIG ICT Services Digital - Data, People, Technology and Cyber Strategy 2026-2030, which lists an AI for Government project and an intention to develop ethical AI guidelines, and the ICT for Education Master Plan 2026-2030 launched by the Ministry of Education and Human Resources Development. The Data Protection and Privacy Bill drafted with UNCTAD support remains unenacted, leaving even general data law absent.
Policy Lever: Policy action runs through strategy documents and donor-supported projects rather than instruments: the SIG ICT Services Digital Strategy 2026-2030 foresees AI for Government work and ethical AI guidelines, while the ICT for Education Master Plan 2026-2030 covers AI literacy. No funded AI program, sandbox, procurement rule or dedicated institution exists.
Governance Type: Governance of digital matters is centralized in national ministries, with no AI function assigned to any regulator, no cross-agency coordination body, and no provincial or independent-review role. The Telecommunications Commission of Solomon Islands regulates telecoms only.
Actor Involvement: Engagement on AI is almost entirely external: Solomon Islands acts through the Pacific Islands Forum, where leaders endorsed the non-binding Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles in September 2026, and through donor partners such as UNCTAD, UNDP and the World Bank. Domestic industry, civil society and academia have no structured role in AI policy.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent because no AI-specific obligation, penalty or supervisory authority exists.
