Specific Laws: SIG ICT Services Digital - Data, People, Technology and Cyber Strategy 2026-2030, Solomon Islands ICT for Education Master Plan 2026-2030, National Cyber Security Policy (2024), National ICT Policy (2017), draft Data Protection and Privacy Bill (2024)

Regulation Status: Somalia has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or national AI strategy; artificial intelligence reaches the statute book only through the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), whose Article 23 gives a right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and whose transparency duties cover automated decision-making and profiling. Governmental engagement with AI is confined to convening activity, principally the National Communications Authority's AI Summit Somalia 2026 in Mogadishu, which discussed AI governance and regulation without producing a binding instrument.
Policy Lever: Policy action on AI is limited to convening and research: the National Communications Authority hosts the annual AI Summit Somalia with World Bank SCALE-UP support, and Somali National University opened the Somali National Artificial Intelligence Centre in July 2026 for research and policy input. No AI guidance, standard, sandbox, procurement rule or statutory AI mandate has been created.
Governance Type: AI matters sit informally with the National Communications Authority, with the Data Protection Authority handling automated-processing rights under the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023). Coordination is occasional and event-driven, federal member states play no part, and no judicial or independent oversight of AI has occurred.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is strongest from academia, with Somali National University and Zamzam University co-organising the national AI summit and SNU hosting the Somali National Artificial Intelligence Centre; industry and civil society take part as summit attendees rather than through formal consultation. Internationally, Somalia is an African Union member covered by the Continental AI Strategy, cooperates with Saudi Arabia's CST on AI regulation, and hosts UNESCO work on the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI is confined to general data protection measures, such as the Data Protection Authority's June 2026 mandatory registration directive under Article 32 of the Data Protection Act, with no AI-specific penalties, authority or monitoring.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), Communications Act (2017)

Regulation Status: South Africa has no AI-specific binding legislation. The Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy, gazetted on 10 April 2026 with a 60-day comment period, was withdrawn after fictitious AI-generated citations were found, and Minister Solly Malatsi confirmed in September 2026 that a revised draft will reach Cabinet by the end of the 2026/27 financial year. Governance of AI therefore rests on general law, principally the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) and its automated decision-making provision, plus the Electoral Commission's July 2026 draft code requiring labelling of AI-generated campaign content.
Policy Lever: Policy is driven through soft instruments and capacity programmes: the National AI Policy Framework (2024), DCDT summit documents, and the DCDT-funded Artificial Intelligence Institute of South Africa hubs at TUT and UJ. Institutional capacity is advisory only, the National AI Expert Review Panel having been appointed to rebuild the withdrawn draft policy rather than to exercise compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is centred on the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies, with the Information Regulator the nearest thing to an operative AI-adjacent regulator and sectoral bodies such as ICASA, the Competition Commission and the FSCA acting within existing mandates. Coordination is episodic, provinces play no regulatory role, and courts and Parliament have intervened on AI matters only occasionally.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative and episodic: a gazetted comment window in April 2026 cut short by withdrawal, summit-based engagement with industry, and academic experts given a prominent review role through the National AI Expert Review Panel. Internationally South Africa was active through its 2025 G20 presidency AI Task Force, the African Union continental AI agenda and a UNESCO AI readiness assessment published in 2025.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through POPIA, where the Information Regulator issues enforcement notices and administrative fines, while section 71 on automated decision-making has produced no published guidance or cases.
Specific Laws: Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) No. 4 of 2013 (fully effective 2021), National AI Policy Framework (2024), National AI Government Summit Discussion Document (2024), Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy (gazetted 10 April 2026, withdrawn 2026), Electoral Commission Draft Code of Conduct on Disinformation and AI-generated election content (2026)

Regulation Status: South Korea regulates AI through the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness, in force since 22 January 2026 with its Enforcement Decree, covering high-impact AI in ten designated domains, generative AI transparency, high-performance AI above 10^26 FLOPs and foreign providers via a domestic representative duty whose filings fall due in October 2026. MSIT has issued five guidelines and two notices, but a grace period of at least one year defers administrative fines of up to KRW 30 million and routine fact-finding investigations except for serious harm, and secondary rules are still being refined by a public-private task force.
Policy Lever: Korea combines a binding core — the AI Basic Act and Decree, deepfake provisions in the Public Official Election Act and the sexual crimes punishment statute, and AI training-data rules in the Personal Information Protection Act amended with effect from 11 September 2026 — with a maintained body of ministry and regulator guidance. Economic levers are large and operating: a KRW 10.1 trillion 2026 AI budget, National Growth Fund allocations, the Haenam National AI Computing Center run through Korea AI Computing Center Co., an ICT regulatory sandbox and AI-oriented public procurement, while MSIT's compliance powers remain unused during the grace period.
Governance Type: MSIT leads implementation of the AI Basic Act while the Personal Information Protection Commission, Korea Communications Commission and sector regulators apply their own remits to AI, with the presidential National AI Strategy Committee serving as the statutory cross-government control tower that met in plenary in February 2026. Sub-national bodies only implement national promotion plans, and independent review comes mainly from the PIPC and the courts rather than from AI-specific adjudication.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academic experts hold seats on the presidential National AI Strategy Committee and on the 40-plus-member AI Basic Act institutional improvement task force convened in March 2026, while civil society participates through public comment rounds and task force membership rather than standing statutory roles. Internationally Korea is a frontrunner, having co-hosted the Seoul AI Safety Summit and participating in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, OECD, GPAI and APEC AI work.
Enforcement Level: Sanctions exist on paper across the AI Basic Act but are suspended during the grace period, so active enforcement touching AI runs through election deepfake takedowns, criminal deepfake prosecutions and PIPC action under data protection law rather than the AI statute.
Specific Laws: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness / AI Basic Act (2025, effective 2026), AI Basic Act partial amendment (Act No. 21311, 2026), AI Basic Act Enforcement Decree (2026), Personal Information Protection Act as amended (Act No. 21445, 2026), Public Official Election Act deepfake provisions (2023), Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes as amended (2024), Presidential Decree on the Establishment and Operation of the National AI Strategy Committee (2025), Korea AI Action Plan 2026-2028 (2026), National AI Strategy (2019)

Regulation Status: Spain is governed by the directly applicable EU AI Act, whose prohibitions and AI-literacy duties have applied since 2 February 2025, general-purpose AI model obligations since 2 August 2025 and Article 50 transparency duties since 2 August 2026, while the Digital Omnibus on AI that entered into force on 27 July 2026 postponed Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded obligations to 2 August 2028. Nationally, the Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la inteligencia artificial, approved by the Council of Ministers on 26 May 2026 and published in the Boletín Oficial de las Cortes Generales on 12 June 2026, is still at the amendments stage in the Congress Committee on Economy, Trade and Digital Transformation. Dedicated AI instruments already in force domestically are Royal Decree 729/2023 creating AESIA and Royal Decree 817/2023 on the AI regulatory sandbox.
Policy Lever: The binding layer is the EU AI Act plus the two Spanish royal decrees creating AESIA and the pre-AI Act sandbox, supplemented by a maintained national guidance pack that AESIA updated in July 2026. Economic levers include the national AI strategy, Cátedras ENIA chairs, Digital Spain 2026 funding and an operating regulatory sandbox, while AESIA is staffed and mandated but has not yet exercised compliance powers.
Governance Type: AESIA leads as national AI supervisor while AEPD, CNMC and financial regulators retain adjacent remits, with coordination through an interministerial working group and the AI Advisory Council pending the statutory architecture in the bill before Congress. Autonomous communities implement and fund AI programmes without independent regulatory powers, and judicial review of algorithmic decisions is occasional.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society feed into policy through public consultations, the sandbox and the AI Advisory Council, with academia holding the most institutionalised role via the Council and the Cátedras ENIA. Internationally Spain is highly active, in the EU AI Board, OECD, UNESCO and Council of Europe processes, and hosted the Council of Europe AI Convention anniversary conference in Madrid in September 2025.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist in the EU AI Act and are drafted in the pending Organic Law, but AESIA has published no AI Act enforcement decisions, leaving data-protection fines by the AEPD as the only AI-related sanctions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act – Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2026, in force 27 July 2026), Royal Decree 729/2023 on the AESIA Statute (2023), Royal Decree 817/2023 establishing the controlled testing environment for artificial intelligence (2023), Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial (2026, in Parliament), Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial – ENIA (2020), Digital Spain 2026 Agenda (2021), Order ETD/1180/2022 on Cátedras ENIA (2022), Order TDF/304/2025 (2025)

Regulation Status: AI governance rests on the non-binding National AI Strategy 2024-2028 (AI Sri Lanka 2028) and, since May 2026, a non-binding AI Policy Framework for State Universities; no AI-specific legislation is enacted or tabled in Parliament. The Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, as amended by Act No. 22 of 2025, binds data processing and addresses solely automated decisions, but Parts I and III commence only on 1 January 2027 and the penalty regime awaits a further order. The Online Safety Act No. 9 of 2024 reaches online content generally without AI-written provisions.
Policy Lever: Sri Lanka relies on voluntary strategy documents, sectoral frameworks and funding or capacity-building programmes rather than binding AI instruments. The Central Bank FinTech regulatory sandbox and the Personal Data Protection Act operate under general mandates, and no AI procurement rules or AI-specific regulatory body are in force.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in the Ministry of Digital Economy and the Presidential Secretariat's digital economy advisory structure, with sectoral regulators acting only inside their existing mandates and no dedicated AI regulator. Governance is centralised, nationally driven and coordinated informally through conferences and ad hoc committees.
Actor Involvement: Industry, academia and civil society take part through consultations, drafting committees and national events such as Sri Lanka AI Week 2026, but none hold standing statutory roles. International engagement is bilateral and declaratory, covering the UNESCO ethics recommendation, cooperation with Singapore and the United States, and summit participation.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific sanctions, authority or monitoring exist, and the Data Protection Authority's general data powers are not yet in operation.
Specific Laws: National AI Strategy 2024-2028 (AI Sri Lanka 2028) (2024), AI Policy Framework for State Universities (2026), Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 2025, Online Safety Act No. 9 of 2024

Regulation Status: Sudan has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or data protection statute in force, and general telecommunications and informatics-offences law contains nothing written for AI. The single AI-specific legal act is the decree signed by Prime Minister Kamil Idris on 5 November 2025 creating the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority alongside a Digital Transformation Authority and a Cybersecurity Authority, an institutional measure that places no duties on developers or deployers. Armed conflict since April 2023 continues to limit state capacity and territorial reach.
Policy Lever: Policy activity is institutional rather than regulatory: three authorities for digital transformation, data and AI, and cybersecurity were created by decree in November 2025 under the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation, with no accompanying AI guidance, funding instrument or sandbox. A UNESCO-supported project on a national strategy for the use of AI and information technology in the education system is the main external input.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in the Ministry of Communications and Digital Transformation, which oversees the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, the Digital Transformation Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority created on 5 November 2025. Civil conflict leaves parts of the territory outside government administration, and no independent or judicial check on AI governance operates.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is made inside government without structured input from industry, universities or civil society. External engagement runs through UNESCO project support and African Union membership rather than through Sudanese participation in international AI standard-setting.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is absent: there are no AI obligations, penalties, cases or monitoring, and the newly created authority has not exercised any power.
Specific Laws: Prime Ministerial Decree establishing the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, the Digital Transformation Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority (2025)

Regulation Status: Suriname has no AI-specific legislation and no AI bill before De Nationale Assemblée; AI is touched only by general instruments such as the Wet Elektronisch Rechtsverkeer (2017) and by the pending Ontwerpwet Bescherming Privacy en Persoonsgegevens. The Suriname National Digital Strategy 2023-2030 discusses artificial intelligence as an emerging driver in education, public services and finance without creating obligations. Government activity in 2026 centres on the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology 2.0 exercise, which is intended to inform a future integrated national AI strategy.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of a ministry-led diagnostic and capacity work: the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Entrepreneurship and Technological Innovation runs the UNESCO RAM 2.0 assessment with the Ministry of Education, Science and Culture and has delivered internal AI training for its staff. No binding instrument, published AI guidance, funded AI programme, sandbox or body with a statutory AI mandate exists.
Governance Type: Governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Entrepreneurship and Technological Innovation, working with the Ministry of Education, Science and Culture and the e-Government directorate on the UNESCO readiness assessment. No independent regulator, subnational authority or judicial body has an AI remit.
Actor Involvement: International engagement drives Suriname's AI agenda: participation in the Santiago Declaration, the India AI Impact Summit Declaration of February 2026 and UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology 2.0. Domestic involvement is limited to the RAM consultation process, where industry, civil society and academic institutions were invited but hold no standing role.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, sanction or supervisory authority exists, and the only oversight-type activity is the one-off UNESCO readiness assessment.
Specific Laws: Suriname National Digital Strategy 2023-2030, Wet Elektronisch Rechtsverkeer (2017), Ontwerpwet Bescherming Privacy en Persoonsgegevens (draft, pending before De Nationale Assemblée)

Regulation Status: Eswatini has no AI-specific binding legislation. The Data Protection Act 5 of 2022, the Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 6 of 2022 and the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 2022 govern data and digital conduct generally, with the Data Protection Act's automated decision-making clause the closest provision to AI. A National AI Strategy and a combined Fourth and Fifth Industrial Revolution Strategy are being prepared under the Ministry of Information, Communications and Technology, neither published.
Policy Lever: Policy action consists of strategy drafting, conferences and donor-supported studies rather than instruments; the Eswatini Communications Commission and the Eswatini Data Protection Authority exercise data-protection powers with no AI remit. Funding, procurement rules and sandboxes for AI are absent.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the executive: the Ministry of Information, Communications and Technology drives strategy while the Eswatini Communications Commission applies data-protection law. Coordination happens through occasional national and regional events, and no subnational or independent review layer exists.
Actor Involvement: Engagement runs through international and academic channels: UN Eswatini, COMESA, the World Bank, the ITU and the Kingdom of Eswatini Academy of Sciences. Structured domestic consultation of industry and civil society on AI policy has not been documented.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI exists only through data-protection and cybercrime powers exercised by the Eswatini Communications Commission and Data Protection Authority, with no AI-specific obligations, sanctions or audits.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act 5 of 2022, Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 6 of 2022, Electronic Communications and Transactions Act (2022), Eswatini Digitalisation Strategy (2024–2028), Eswatini National Cybersecurity Strategy (2022–2027), National FinTech Strategy for the Kingdom of Eswatini (2025–2030)

Regulation Status: Sweden is bound by the EU AI Act, whose prohibitions (February 2025), GPAI rules (August 2025) and Article 50 transparency duties (August 2026) apply, while the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027. Nationally the Riksdag adopted a dedicated law allowing police use of real-time facial recognition AI, in force 1 July 2026, while the complementary AI Act act and ordinance proposed in SOU 2025:101 remain under preparation after the consultation closed on 23 February 2026. Competent authorities are designated only temporarily, through 31 December 2026, keeping implementation in transition.
Policy Lever: Sweden's main lever is the directly applicable EU AI Act, supplemented by the national facial-recognition act, GDPR supervision by IMY and sectoral regimes, with soft law in the 2026 AI strategy action plan and PTS guidance. Economic levers include Vinnova and AI Sweden funding, an IMY–eSam regulatory sandbox pilot completed in February 2026, and a PTS assignment to establish the statutory AI sandbox required by 2 August 2027.
Governance Type: Governance is plural: PTS leads coordination and acts as EU contact point, IMY covers biometrics, law enforcement, migration and prohibited practices, Finansinspektionen covers finance, and further sectoral authorities are designated in the pending complementary legislation. Independent oversight comes from courts and the ombudsman institutions, while municipalities and regions implement rather than legislate.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making runs through the Swedish inquiry and remiss system, which gave industry, unions, human-rights bodies and universities published roles on SOU 2025:101 and SOU 2025:12. Internationally Sweden acts through the EU AI Board and Council negotiations, OECD work and European AI standardisation.
Enforcement Level: EU-level penalties apply but Sweden has issued no AI Act enforcement decision, has only temporarily designated competent authorities, and has not enacted its national sanction provisions.
Specific Laws: EU AI Act / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (2024), Digital Omnibus on AI / Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (2026), Lag om användning av AI-system för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid för brottsbekämpande ändamål (2026), Proposition 2025/26:150 Polisens användning av AI för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid (2026), SOU 2025:101 Anpassningar till AI-förordningen (2025, proposed), SOU 2025:12 AI Commission Roadmap for Sweden (2025), Handlingsplan för Sveriges AI-strategi (2026), Swedish Data Protection Act (2018:218), National Approach to Artificial Intelligence (2018)

Regulation Status: Switzerland has no cross-sector AI statute; the Federal Council decided on 12 February 2025 to ratify the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed on 27 March 2025, and to implement it through mainly sector-specific amendments, with a consultation draft from the Federal Office of Justice due by the end of 2026. Operative rules come from the revised Federal Act on Data Protection (2023), whose Article 21 covers automated individual decisions, and from the Ordinance on Automated Driving in force since 1 March 2025, alongside supervisory guidance from FINMA and the FDPIC.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through general law plus published guidance (FINMA Guidance 08/2024, FDPIC guidance on the Federal Act on Data Protection, Federal Council AI Guidelines for the Confederation) and substantial research funding via the Swiss AI Initiative, the Swiss National AI Institute and CSCS. Institutional capacity rests with the Competence Network for Artificial Intelligence and sectoral regulators, none of which holds an AI-specific legal mandate.
Governance Type: Governance is deliberately sectoral: FINMA, Swissmedic, OFCOM, the Federal Roads Office and the FDPIC act within existing remits, with the Competence Network for Artificial Intelligence at the Federal Chancellery as the administration's contact point and the Federal Office of Justice leading the implementing bill with DETEC and the FDFA. Cantons implement data-protection rules and run initiatives such as the Zurich AI sandbox, and judicial review proceeds under ordinary law.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia contribute through the ordinary consultation procedure, expert reports and cantonal sandbox projects rather than standing AI bodies, and the implementing bill's consultation has not yet opened. Internationally Switzerland is highly active, having signed the Council of Europe AI Convention and engaging in OECD and Geneva-based AI governance processes.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement relies on pre-existing data-protection and prudential powers, with FINMA's supervisory reviews of AI governance in finance the only systematic monitoring and no sanctions or decisions under AI-specific law.
Specific Laws: Federal Act on Data Protection / FADP (2023), Ordinance on Automated Driving / VAF (2025), FINMA Guidance 08/2024 on Governance and Risk Management when using Artificial Intelligence (2024), Federal Council Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (2020), Digital Switzerland Strategy (2025), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence – signed by Switzerland (2025)

Regulation Status: Syria has no AI-specific binding instrument; the only legal texts touching AI are Law No. 25 of 2024, which lists artificial intelligence among the emerging technologies within the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology's policy remit, and the Personal Data Protection Law No. 12 of 2024 with its executive instructions, which regulate data processing generally. The transitional government formed after December 2024 has prioritised fibre and data-centre reconstruction and published a technology foresight roadmap for 2026-2045, without tabling AI legislation.
Policy Lever: Policy action on AI is confined to ministry-level promotion—an AI forum in April 2025, the 'Mujtama Thakaa' digital-community project, and a 2026-2045 technology foresight roadmap—without any binding AI instrument, funding line or sandbox. General data protection law supplies the only binding rules that reach AI systems.
Governance Type: AI-related policy sits entirely with one central ministry, with no sectoral regulators, no coordination body and no independent or judicial review of AI. Territory outside Damascus's control, including the northeast administration, has likewise produced no AI governance institution.
Actor Involvement: Domestic engagement with AI is organised by newly licensed associations and foundations—the Syrian Association for Artificial Intelligence and Entrepreneurship and the Syria AI Foundation—rather than through any government consultation process. Internationally, Syria has only its nominal 2024 endorsement of China's Global AI Governance Initiative.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement on AI is absent: only general data protection penalties could reach AI uses, and no authority, case or monitoring programme exists.
Specific Laws: Law No. 25 of 2024 establishing the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (defines emerging technologies including artificial intelligence), Personal Data Protection Law No. 12 of 2024 and its Executive Instructions (2024), Constitutional Declaration of the Syrian Arab Republic (2025), Global AI Governance Initiative endorsement (2024)

Regulation Status: The Artificial Intelligence Basic Act, in force since 14 January 2026, is a horizontal, principles-based statute that sets seven governance principles, designates the National Science and Technology Council as central competent authority and obliges government bodies to complete AI risk assessments by July 2026 and adopt internal AI control rules by January 2027. Private-sector obligations are delegated to sector regulators using the Ministry of Digital Affairs AI Risk Classification Framework published 7 July 2026, so cross-sector operational duties do not yet apply. Binding sanctions reaching AI outputs today come from the 2023 deepfake amendments to the Public Officials Election and Recall Act and the Criminal Code.
Policy Lever: Taiwan combines one horizontal statute with narrow criminal and election provisions on synthetic media, a growing body of sectoral soft law from MODA, the Financial Supervisory Commission and the Ministry of Health and Welfare, and large state funding for AI infrastructure and talent. Institutional mandates are legally grounded in the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act but carry no inspection or sanctioning powers.
Governance Type: Governance is centrally organised: NSTC is the statutory lead, MODA owns the risk classification architecture, and sectoral ministries translate it into their own guidance, coordinated through the Premier-chaired National AI Strategy Special Committee created in March 2026. There is no subnational regulatory tier and independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI rules is incidental.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia hold statutory places in the National AI Strategy Special Committee, while civil society participates through episodic consultation rather than a standing role. International engagement is active but constrained to declarations and multistakeholder fora because Taiwan cannot accede to treaty-based AI instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to criminal deepfake provisions and public-sector self-assessment, since the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act sets no penalties and no authority holds AI compliance powers.
Specific Laws: Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (2026), AI Risk Classification Framework (2026), Executive Yuan Implementation Plan for the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (2026), Guidelines for Medical Institutions Applying Generative Artificial Intelligence (2026), Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Applications in the Financial Industry (2024, revised 2025), Public Officials Election and Recall Act deepfake amendments (2023), Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act deepfake amendments (2023), Taiwan AI Action Plan 2.0 (2023-2026), AI Technology R&D Guidelines (2019)

Regulation Status: The only AI-specific instruments are the Strategy for AI Development of the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040 (Government Resolution No. 483, amended by Resolution No. 83 of 31 January 2025) and AI components of the Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030, both non-binding planning documents. The Strategy mandates preparation of a draft Law "On Artificial Intelligence" setting the basis of state regulation, which has not been introduced in the Majlisi Namoyandagon. Tajikistan is revising the Strategy to raise the AI contribution target from 5% to 8% of GDP across 17 sectors.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through planning documents and investment incentives: the Strategy until 2040, the Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030, the designation of 2025-2030 as Years of Development of the Digital Economy and Innovation, and IT Park/IT Hub Dushanbe incentives. The Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies under the President coordinates this work but holds no compliance powers over AI.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies under the President, which drafts strategy and monitors programme delivery. Sectoral regulators, subnational authorities and independent review bodies play no role in AI.
Actor Involvement: Domestic AI policy is made within government, with no structured industry, civil society or academic consultation; academia participates only as a training and research partner. Internationally Tajikistan is highly active, sponsoring two UN General Assembly AI resolutions and proposing a coordinated AI legal framework within the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and a Central Asian regional AI centre.
Enforcement Level: With no binding AI rules in force, nothing is enforced and oversight is limited to programme-delivery monitoring by the Agency for Innovation and Digital Technologies.
Specific Laws: Strategy for AI Development of the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040 (Government Resolution No. 483, 2021, amended by Resolution No. 83 of 31 January 2025), Medium-Term Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2030 (2025)

Regulation Status: Tanzania has no AI-specific legislation in force and no AI bill in the legislative pipeline; AI deployment is governed by general law, principally the Personal Data Protection Act 2022 with the Personal Data Protection (Personal Data Collection and Processing) Regulations GN No. 449C of 2023, the Cybercrimes Act 2015, the Electronic Transactions Act 2015 and the Electronic and Postal Communications Act 2010. AI-specific activity is confined to non-binding instruments: the National Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Education (2025), the Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania Health Sector (2022), the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology guidelines on secure and ethical AI use, and a draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Framework.
Policy Lever: Tanzania relies on soft-law levers: sectoral AI guidelines for education and health, draft cross-sector ethical AI guidelines, a draft national AI strategy informed by the UNESCO-supported Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report of June 2025, and the National Digital Economy Strategic Framework 2024-2034. Binding leverage comes only from general data protection, cybercrime and communications law, and no body holds a statutory AI mandate or dedicated AI budget line.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology and the Tanzania ICT Commission, with the Personal Data Protection Commission, TCRA and the education and health ministries acting separately in their own fields and no formal inter-agency AI coordination mechanism. Independent review of AI governance is absent, and Zanzibar's separate administration has taken no AI-specific role.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia participated in the UNESCO-supported AI Readiness Assessment consultations, the National AI Forum held in Dar es Salaam in July 2025 and the stakeholder review of the draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, but hold no standing formal role. Internationally Tanzania works through UNESCO's ethics framework, the African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Smart Africa rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI occurs only through general data protection, cybercrime and online content powers, with no AI-specific sanction, designated AI authority or recurring AI audit programme.
Specific Laws: Personal Data Protection Act (2022), Personal Data Protection (Personal Data Collection and Processing) Regulations GN No. 449C (2023), Cybercrimes Act (2015), Electronic Transactions Act (2015), Electronic and Postal Communications Act (2010), National Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Education (2025), Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence (draft, 2025), Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania Health Sector (2022), Tanzania National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Framework (draft), Artificial Intelligence Readiness Assessment Report: Tanzania (2025), National Digital Economy Strategic Framework 2024-2034

Regulation Status: Thailand has no enacted comprehensive AI statute: ETDA published the Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence for public consultation on 2/9 July 2026, comments closed 14 August 2026, and no Cabinet or parliamentary enactment has followed. Binding AI-specific obligations in force are confined to two narrow areas - the Office of the Consumer Protection Board notification requiring disclosure labels on AI-generated or AI-edited advertising images and video, and the Civil Court regulation of 17 November 2025 on disclosure and verification of AI-generated content in pleadings. Financial-sector instruments from the Bank of Thailand and the Securities and Exchange Commission set expectations rather than enforceable AI duties.
Policy Lever: Thailand governs AI mainly through soft law and capacity-building - ETDA generative AI and executive governance guidelines, Bank of Thailand and SEC sector frameworks, PDPC and NCSA guidance - alongside two narrow binding instruments on AI advertising and AI-prepared court filings. Economic levers include large national compute and data investments approved in 2026, while the proposed AI regulatory sandbox and ETDA's statutory enforcement powers remain in draft.
Governance Type: Governance runs through ETDA as lead body under MDES, with sectoral regulators and the courts setting their own AI rules, coordinated by the Prime Minister-chaired National AI Committee and the National Digital Economy and Society Committee. No subnational tier regulates AI, and independent oversight is limited to the judiciary's own rules on AI use in proceedings.
Actor Involvement: Participation is consultative rather than institutionalised: industry, law firms and foreign tech associations submitted comments on the 2026 draft AI Act, academia contributes through strategy working groups, and civil society input is episodic. Internationally Thailand is prominent, hosting the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI and positioning the AI Governance Practice Centre as a regional hub.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is confined to general consumer-protection and court procedural sanctions attached to two narrow AI rules, with no AI-specific enforcement decisions reported and ETDA's statutory supervisory powers still in draft.
Specific Laws: Draft Act on Artificial Intelligence (2026, public consultation 2 July - 14 August 2026), Office of the Consumer Protection Board Notification on AI-Generated Advertising Content (2025), Civil Court Regulation on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Pleadings and Documents (2025), Guidance of the President of the Supreme Court on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Performance of Judicial Case Work B.E. 2568 (2025), Bank of Thailand Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (2025), SEC Governance Framework for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (2025), ETDA Guidelines for Application of Generative AI with Good Governance for Organizations (2024), AI Governance Guideline for Executives (2026), National AI Strategy and Action Plan (2022-2027), Digital Thailand - AI Ethics Guideline (2022), Draft Royal Decree on Business Operations Using AI Systems (2022), Draft Act on the Promotion and Support for National AI Innovations (2023)

Regulation Status: Togo has no binding AI legislation, no AI bill before the National Assembly, and no AI-specific provision in its digital statutes; the general data protection law Loi n°2019-014 of 29 October 2019 is the only instrument that incidentally reaches AI data processing. Government work is at strategy stage: preparation of a national AI strategy for public administration was launched at a Lomé forum in December 2025, and a projet de Code du numérique is being drafted with external legal counsel.
Policy Lever: Togo governs AI through programs rather than rules: the Togo AI Lab applies data science to public policy, a national AI and digital skills training program is running, and an AI-in-technical-education policy is being drafted with OIF support. No AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists, and the only enforceable instrument touching AI is the 2019 data protection law.
Governance Type: AI policy is concentrated in the ministry responsible for the digital economy and digital transformation, supported by the Togo AI Lab, with the sectoral regulators ARCEP, ANCy and the data protection authority IPDCP operating without any AI remit. Coordination takes place through ad hoc multi-stakeholder forums, there is no subnational tier, and no judicial or independent body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Domestic participation is occasional and event-driven: a December 2025 strategy forum with ministries, public bodies and civil society, a June 2026 ISOC-Togo forum on AI governance, and research partnerships with CEGA, Zindi and local startups. Internationally Togo engages through African Union and ECOWAS digital frameworks and multilateral events such as AI for Good, without treaty-level AI commitments.
Enforcement Level: Nothing AI-specific is enforced in Togo; the data protection authority IPDCP and ARCEP hold general powers that have not been exercised against AI systems.
Specific Laws: Loi n°2019-014 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel (2019), Stratégie nationale d'intelligence artificielle du Togo (in preparation since 2025), Stratégie Togo Digital 2025-2030 (in preparation)

Regulation Status: Tonga has no AI-specific legislation in force or in the legislative process, and its digital statute book—the Cybersecurity Act 2025, the electronic transactions legislation and the Tongan Data Exchange Policy and Framework—contains no provision written for AI systems. Government activity centres on connectivity, the TongaPass digital ID, government data-centre modernisation under a United States Trade and Development Agency feasibility agreement signed 2 September 2026, and climate resilience.
Policy Lever: Tonga deploys no AI-specific levers: no binding instrument, no national guidance, no AI funding line and no body with an AI remit. Its only relevant commitments are the regionally endorsed Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles and a finance-sector regulatory sandbox run by the National Reserve Bank of Tonga.
Governance Type: Governance is centralised in national ministries, principally MEIDECC, with no AI-specific regulator, coordination body or independent review role. Island divisions exercise no regulatory competence.
Actor Involvement: Domestic industry, civil society and academia have no structured role in AI policy, which does not exist as a national workstream. Tonga's engagement is external and declaratory, through the Pacific Islands Forum, where Leaders endorsed regional AI principles in September 2026 ahead of a regional AI governance framework due for consideration in 2027.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, sanction, competent authority or monitoring practice exists in Tonga.
Specific Laws: Cybersecurity Act 2025, Tonga National Cybersecurity Framework (2022), Digital Government Strategic Framework 2019-2024, Tongan Data Exchange Policy and Framework (2021), Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, regional endorsement)

Regulation Status: Trinidad and Tobago has no AI-specific legislation in force, no AI bill before Parliament, and no adopted national AI strategy; policy work remains at the diagnostic stage through the UNESCO Readiness Assessment Methodology and UNDP AI Landscape Assessment completed and validated in February 2026. The Data Protection Act 2011 is only partially proclaimed and contains no AI provisions, so AI systems are governed solely by incidental general law.
Policy Lever: Policy is pursued entirely through non-binding levers: readiness assessments with UNESCO and UNDP, the six-month AI Academy capacity-building pilot, the Anansi national AI assistant, an OpenAI education partnership and a memorandum of understanding with United Arab Emirates technology entities. The MPAAI is the institutional home for this work but carries no legal AI mandate, and no funding scheme, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule is in place.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Public Administration and Artificial Intelligence, with sectoral regulators such as the Telecommunications Authority of Trinidad and Tobago and the Office of the Information Commissioner holding no AI mandate and no formal coordination body linking them. Oversight by courts, an ombudsman or independent review bodies has not shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society and academia entered AI policy through one-off diagnostic channels: the UNESCO RAM survey, sector consultations in January 2026 and the UWI-hosted validation workshop, none of which created standing advisory roles. Internationally the country is active through UNESCO, UNDP, CARICOM and the Caribbean Telecommunications Union's Caribbean AI Task Force, and has signed partnerships with OpenAI and United Arab Emirates technology entities.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI rules does not exist, since there are no AI obligations, no designated AI authority, and the general data protection regime is itself unenforced for want of a fully resourced Information Commissioner.
Specific Laws: Data Protection Act (2011)

Regulation Status: AI governance rests on general instruments: Organic Act No. 2004-63 on Personal Data Protection, Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on cybercrime, and the Startup Act, none of which contain AI-specific obligations. The Organic Bill on Protection of Personal Data, which addresses profiling and automated decision-making, remained under committee hearings in the Assembly of the Representatives of the People through 2026, and the National AI Strategy (2026-2030) is a non-binding policy document.
Policy Lever: Tunisia relies on soft-law strategy documents and innovation-economy tools, notably the Startup Act framework and donor-supported programmes with GIZ, rather than binding instruments. INPDP and ANSI act only within data protection and cybersecurity mandates, with no AI compliance powers.
Governance Type: AI-relevant oversight is split between a lead ministry and two adjacent-domain regulators, INPDP and ANSI, coordinated only through periodic ministerial councils. Sub-national bodies play no role and judicial or independent review of AI decisions has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Industry and academia feed AI policy through consultations, workshops and the ATUGE white paper, while domestic civil society participates mainly through external advocacy rather than standing roles. International engagement is comparatively strong, resting on Convention 108 ratification, Arab ICT Organization and African Union AI readiness work, and EU and Gulf partnerships.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement reaches AI only indirectly through data protection and cybercrime law, with no AI-specific sanctions, decisions or audit regime on record.
Specific Laws: Organic Act No. 2004-63 on Personal Data Protection (2004), Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on Combating Cyber Offences (2022), Startup Act (Law No. 2018-20, amended), National AI Strategy and Roadmap (2021-2025), National AI Strategy (2026-2030), Organic Bill on Protection of Personal Data (2025, before the Assembly of the Representatives of the People)

Regulation Status: No dedicated AI law is in force; three AI bills remain in committee at the Grand National Assembly, including the horizontal Yapay Zeka Kanun Teklifi (Esas No. 2/2234) and the Bill on Amendments to Certain Laws Regarding Artificial Intelligence (Esas No. 2/3358). The binding instruments reaching AI are general: Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data and Law No. 5651 on internet publications. The AI-specific instruments in force, the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) enacted by Presidential Circular No. 2026/9 and Presidential Decree No. 119 restructuring the National Technology and Artificial Intelligence General Directorate, are policy and organisational measures addressed to public bodies.
Policy Lever: Turkey governs AI through strategy and guidance rather than binding instruments: the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030), its predecessor National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2021-2025), and KVKK's 2026 AI guidance documents. Funding, data-opening and computing-capacity programmes are set out in the Action Plan, while the only enforceable lever is data-protection law applied by KVKK.
Governance Type: AI policy is centralised in the Ministry of Industry and Technology through the National Technology and Artificial Intelligence General Directorate, with KVKK, BTK, RTÜK and BDDK covering slices of AI inside existing mandates. A presidentially chaired National Artificial Intelligence Board and Programme Office are being established as the formal coordination layer, there is no subnational role, and independent or judicial scrutiny of AI matters is marginal.
Actor Involvement: Industry, universities and civil society organisations fed into the Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) and the TBMM Artificial Intelligence Research Commission, but none holds a standing formal role in AI rule-making. Internationally Turkey engages through OECD and G20 channels and declaration-level commitments without acceding to the Council of Europe AI treaty.
Enforcement Level: Rules touching AI are enforced only through general data-protection and internet legislation, with no AI-specific sanctions, enforcement decisions or operating monitoring regime.
Specific Laws: Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan (2026-2030) enacted by Presidential Circular No. 2026/9 (2026), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2021-2025 (2021), Presidential Decree No. 119 establishing the National Technology and Artificial Intelligence General Directorate (2025), Yapay Zeka Kanun Teklifi / Draft Artificial Intelligence Law Bill (Esas No. 2/2234, 2024, in committee), Bill on Amendments to Certain Laws Regarding Artificial Intelligence (Esas No. 2/3358, 2025, in committee), TBMM Artificial Intelligence Research Commission Report No. 260 (2026), Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data (2016), Law No. 5651 on Regulation of Publications on the Internet (2007), KVKK Guidance on Agentic AI (2026), KVKK Guidance on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools in Workplaces (2026)

Regulation Status: No AI-specific legislation is in force in Turkmenistan. In April 2026 the Cabinet of Ministers directed preparation of a national legal framework for AI covering rules of use, allocation of responsibility, the powers of state agencies and national standards and technical regulations, and a National AI Strategy is being drafted by the Ministry of Communications with UNDP support as part of the State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2028. Nothing has reached the Mejlis, and existing data-protection and communications law addresses AI nowhere.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through state programmes and presidential resolutions rather than law: the State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy for 2026-2028 and its action plan drive AI pilots, a national data processing centre and a planned AI Competence Centre at Turkmentelecom. No binding AI instrument, published guidance, regulatory sandbox or AI procurement rule exists.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the President and Cabinet of Ministers, with the Ministry of Communications and the state operator Turkmentelecom as executing arms. Coordination is episodic and internal, sub-national bodies only implement, and independent review of technology policy is absent.
Actor Involvement: AI policy is made by state bodies working with the United Nations Development Programme; the main external input is international rather than domestic. State-owned enterprises and a state university take part in capacity-building, while independent industry and civil society have no channel into the process.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation, sanction or supervisory authority has been created.
Specific Laws: State Programme for the Development of the Digital Economy of Turkmenistan for 2026-2028 and its Action Plan (2026), Concept for the Development of the Digital Economy in Turkmenistan for 2026-2028 (2025), Law of Turkmenistan No. 519-V On Information about Private Life and its Protection (2017); a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy is in draft

Regulation Status: Tuvalu has no AI-specific legislation, draft bill or regulatory proposal; the Tuvalu National ICT Policy approved by Cabinet on 5 October 2023 sets connectivity, digital-government and cybersecurity priorities rather than technology-specific codes. Even foundational digital law is incomplete: a Cybercrime Bill remains pending and the Council of Europe records Tuvalu as having no cybercrime policy or strategy. Government attention centres on climate survival, the Digital Nation project and submarine-cable connectivity.
Policy Lever: Policy effort is confined to connectivity and digital-government delivery under the Tuvalu National ICT Policy (2023) and the Tuvalu National Broadband Plan (2024), neither of which creates AI obligations, guidance or funding. Public-sector capacity in a state of roughly 11,000 people is absorbed by climate resilience and basic service delivery.
Governance Type: Digital policy is centralised in the central-government ICT department and the state-owned Tuvalu Telecommunications Corporation, with no AI remit allocated anywhere. No coordination mechanism, sub-national tier or independent review body touches AI.
Actor Involvement: No domestic stakeholder process on AI exists for industry, civil society or academia. International engagement is limited to general UN and Pacific Islands Forum membership, where digital and climate issues are discussed, without participation in AI-specific standards or treaty processes.
Enforcement Level: No AI enforcement framework, penalty, authority or monitoring practice exists in Tuvalu.
Specific Laws: None recorded; the Tuvalu National ICT Policy (2023) and Tuvalu National Broadband Plan (2024) are the only national digital instruments and contain no AI provisions

Regulation Status: Uganda has no AI-specific binding instrument: the Artificial Intelligence Bill 2025 remains an unintroduced draft and the National AI and Emerging Technologies Strategy, originating in a Cabinet directive for an AI policy, was still being drafted after nationwide consultations concluded in March 2026. Regulation of AI runs entirely through horizontal law, principally the Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 9 of 2019 and the Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96), neither of which addresses algorithmic transparency or automated decision-making. The UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report validated on 26 May 2026 confirms the absence of a dedicated legal framework.
Policy Lever: Uganda's levers are preparatory: a strategy in drafting, the ITU-supported National AI Landscape Assessment, the UNESCO Readiness Assessment, and general-law guidance from the Personal Data Protection Office. Economic instruments exist only as non-AI-specific financial-sector sandboxes and donor-supported innovation funding in health, agriculture and public services.
Governance Type: AI governance is centred on the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance and NITA-U, with the Personal Data Protection Office, Uganda Communications Commission and Bank of Uganda touching AI inside existing remits and the Uganda Communications Commission and Ministry each preparing separate AI strategies. Coordination is informal through the National AI Focal Point, local governments have no role, and oversight by courts or independent review bodies is confined to general data-protection complaints.
Actor Involvement: Government, industry, academia and civil society met in structured but non-standing consultations during the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment process in February and May 2026 and the strategy stakeholder engagements that closed in March 2026. International engagement is the strongest axis, spanning UNESCO, ITU, UNDP, the African Union and a 30 September 2026 parliamentary exchange with Kenya on AI regulation.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI flows exclusively through general regulators applying data protection, communications and cybercrime law, as shown by the Personal Data Protection Office decision against WhatsApp LLC in February 2026, and no AI-specific sanction, authority or audit regime exists.
Specific Laws: Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 9 of 2019, Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96), Data Protection and Privacy Regulations 2021, Artificial Intelligence Bill 2025 (draft, not tabled), National Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies Strategy (in development, 2026), Uganda National AI Landscape Assessment (ITU, 2024), Uganda AI Readiness Assessment Report (UNESCO, validated 26 May 2026), National Information Security Framework 2026

Regulation Status: Ukraine remains in the voluntary first stage of its two-stage model: no AI-specific binding rules are in force, and the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI signed on 15 May 2025 awaits ratification by the Verkhovna Rada. A working group at the Ministry of Digital Transformation convened in June 2026 to draft a European-integration AI law aligned with the EU AI Act, with submission planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. Governance therefore rests on dedicated but non-binding AI documents plus general data-protection and cybersecurity law.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through soft law and economic tools: the White Paper, the voluntary Code of Conduct, sectoral guidance and labelling sit alongside an operating AI and Blockchain Sandbox run with the Ukrainian Startup Fund and the WINWIN AI Center of Excellence. Institutional capacity is concentrated in the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which holds policy leadership but no legal compliance mandate over AI.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Digital Transformation, which sets strategy, runs the sandbox and drafts the forthcoming law, with other agencies contributing through an inter-ministerial action plan and the 2026 working group. Independent review is limited to the Ombudsman's general human-rights mandate, and no subnational tier plays any role.
Actor Involvement: Consultation is broad but informal: companies, NGOs and academics take part in the Roadmap process, the Expert Committee, the 2026 legal-regulation working group and the public consultation on the AI Strategy to 2030, none of which confers a standing decision-making role. International engagement is substantial, including treaty signature, OECD principles, EU alignment workshops, and a proposal to open the national sandbox to European partners.
Enforcement Level: Compliance rests on voluntary and reputational incentives, with no AI-specific penalties, enforcement decisions, dedicated enforcement authority or audit regime in place.
Specific Laws: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Ukraine (Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 1556-р, 2020), Action Plan for Implementation of the Concept of AI Development in Ukraine for 2025-2026 (Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 457-р, 2025), Roadmap for AI Regulation in Ukraine (2023), White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Regulation (2024), Policy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in Priority Spheres of Economy until 2026 - Cabinet of Ministers Order (2024), Cabinet of Ministers resolution establishing the AI and Blockchain Sandbox experimental project (2024), Voluntary Code of Conduct on Ethical and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (2024), WINWIN 2030 Global Innovation Strategy (2024), draft National Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy until 2030 (2025, in public consultation), Law of Ukraine On Personal Data Protection No. 2297-VI (2010), Law of Ukraine On the Basic Principles of Ensuring Cybersecurity of Ukraine No. 2163-VIII (2017), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law CETS 225 (signed 2025, not ratified)

Regulation Status: The UAE has no horizontal federal AI statute; binding federal AI rules cover election campaigning and the use of AI inside government, while the Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021) and the Child Digital Safety Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2025) are general instruments applied to AI. Free-zone rules such as DIFC Data Protection Regulation 10, enforceable from January 2026, bind only within those jurisdictions. The Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, approved on 14 June 2026, is mandated to propose AI legislation that does not yet exist.
Policy Lever: Policy runs mainly through soft law (UAE AI Charter 2024, National AI Strategy 2031, CBUAE Guidance Note 2026) and very large state-backed investment and infrastructure programmes, with binding AI rules confined to elections, government use and free zones. Institutional capacity was consolidated in June 2026 into the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, which has yet to exercise compliance powers.
Governance Type: Governance combines a newly consolidated federal centre reporting to the Cabinet with emirate and free-zone jurisdictions that write and enforce their own AI rules. Courts, ombudsmen and independent review bodies play no visible role in shaping AI policy.
Actor Involvement: Industry is consulted through free-zone and sectoral processes while domestic civil society is absent from AI policy-making. International engagement is intense, spanning UN processes, multilateral declarations and bilateral government-to-government AI frameworks.
Enforcement Level: AI rules are backed mainly by general-law penalties and supervisory expectations, with no published AI-specific enforcement decision and a federal AI authority that has not yet used compliance powers.
Specific Laws: UAE National AI Strategy 2031 (2017), Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data (PDPL), UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (2024), Abu Dhabi Law No. 3 of 2024 establishing the Abu Dhabi Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council, DIFC Data Protection Regulations Regulation 10 (2023, enforceable January 2026), National Elections Committee Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (2025), Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2025 on Child Digital Safety, National AI System Cabinet integration decision (2026), CBUAE Guidance Note on Consumer Protection and the Responsible Adoption and Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning by Licensed Financial Institutions (2026), Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data establishment decision (2026)

Regulation Status: The UK has no enacted horizontal AI-specific legislation as of June 2026; the Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill [HL] (a private member's bill) was at final stages in Parliament as of April 2026 but is not government-sponsored law. AI is addressed through the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Royal Assent June 2025, core provisions in force February 2026) and sector-specific rules from ICO, FCA, Ofcom, CMA, and MHRA, applying five cross-sector principles via the DSIT pro-innovation framework. The Regulating for Growth Bill (King's Speech, May 2026) would put regulatory sandboxes onto a statutory footing but adds no binding AI-specific rules.
Policy Lever: The UK relies on soft-law instruments—five cross-sector AI principles, sector-regulator AI strategic frameworks (FCA Mills Review, PRA SS1/23, ICO ADM guidance), and the AI Security Institute's evaluation work—supported by economic programs such as the AI Growth Lab and AI Opportunities Action Plan (Jan 2025), with no binding horizontal AI statute; binding instruments are limited to sector-specific rules under existing legislation such as the DUAA 2025.
Governance Type: Seven sector regulators (ICO, FCA, PRA, CMA, Ofcom, MHRA, and others) each apply the five DSIT principles independently within their domains, with the Digital Regulation Co-operation Forum (DRCF) providing ad hoc cross-regulator coordination; there is no single AI authority, no subnational AI regulation, and judicial/independent review operates through existing administrative law channels.
Actor Involvement: Industry has structured input through consultations, working groups, and the AI Opportunities Action Plan process; civil society and academia are consulted occasionally (e.g., AISI evaluations, BCS engagement with AI Action Plan) but hold no standing formal roles; internationally, the UK hosted the Bletchley AI Safety Summit (2023) and participates in OECD and G7 AI governance forums but declined to sign the Paris AI Action Summit declaration (February 2025), signalling a more selective international alignment.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement relies on existing sector-regulator powers (e.g., ICO fines under UK GDPR, FCA supervisory actions) rather than a dedicated AI enforcement authority; the AI Security Institute conducts model evaluations and risk monitoring but has no enforcement remit, and published regulatory actions touching AI are occasional rather than routine.
Specific Laws: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, AI Opportunities Action Plan (2025), Regulating for Growth Bill (2026, introduced), Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill [HL] (2025-2026, private member's bill in final stages), UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018, Online Safety Act 2023, AI Safety Institute Framework (2024)

Regulation Status: The United States has no comprehensive federal AI statute; the TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) is the only federal AI-specific law binding private actors, and its platform notice-and-removal duties became enforceable on 19 May 2026. Other federal AI-specific obligations are executive instruments binding on agencies and contractors — Executive Order 14319 with OMB Memorandum M-26-04 on unbiased LLM procurement, OMB M-25-21 and M-25-22 on federal AI use and acquisition, and Executive Order 14409 (2 June 2026) on advanced AI innovation and security. Executive Order 14365 (11 December 2025) and the March 2026 National Policy Framework press for preemption of state AI laws, but no federal preemption statute has been enacted.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through a thin layer of binding AI instruments (TAKE IT DOWN Act, OMB procurement memoranda), a dense soft-law layer centred on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and large funding programmes such as the Genesis Mission and NAIRR. Federal AI procurement rules apply to agencies, but no federal regulatory sandbox is operating.
Governance Type: Governance is highly fragmented: federal agencies act in parallel under their own authorities while 45-plus states legislate independently, producing Texas, California and Colorado regimes that the federal executive is contesting. Coordination is executive-led through OSTP and the Chief AI Officer Council, and courts are a central arena for defining the limits of AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Industry has the deepest structured access through standards consultations, procurement engagement and the voluntary frontier-model framework under Executive Order 14409; civil society and academia contribute mainly through public comment. Internationally the country is active in standards bodies and bilateral AI agreements while avoiding binding multilateral commitments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement is real but narrow: the FTC polices the TAKE IT DOWN Act and uses general consumer-protection powers against deceptive AI claims, while state attorneys general enforce the state AI statutes.
Specific Laws: TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025), Executive Order 14179 Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence (2025), America's AI Action Plan (2025), Executive Order 14319 Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government (2025), Executive Order 14365 Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (2025), Executive Order on the Genesis Mission (2025), Executive Order 14409 Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (2026), National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (2026), OMB Memorandum M-25-21 (2025), OMB Memorandum M-25-22 (2025), OMB Memorandum M-26-04 Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles (2025), NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023), Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (2025), California SB 53 Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (2025), Colorado SB 26-189 (2026)

Regulation Status: Uruguay has no comprehensive AI statute; binding AI-relevant rules consist of Articles 74 and 75 of Law 20.212 (2023), which mandate a national data and AI strategy, and Decreto 276/025 of December 2025, which sets a governance scheme with impact assessments, time limits and supervision for controlled testing environments and data spaces used for data and AI projects. The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, signed in September 2025, has not been ratified and the treaty itself is not in force. Personal data processing by AI is covered by Law 18.331 (2008), which contains no AI-specific provision.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through Agesic's statutory strategy mandate, soft-law recommendations and strategy documents, and economic instruments: the Uruguay Innova sandbox launched jointly with MIEM, Agesic, ANII and URCDP, and the Instituto Vidart national AI centre financed by a US$10 million loan. Binding levers are confined to Decreto 276/025 and general data protection law.
Governance Type: Agesic is the lead body, coordinating through the Public Sector Strategic Committee for AI and Data and through the joint sandbox instrument run with MIEM, ANII, URCDP and Uruguay Innova. Governance is national and centralized, with departmental governments absent and external review limited to data protection complaints and ordinary courts.
Actor Involvement: Participation is strongest internationally: treaty negotiation and signature at the Council of Europe, adherence to the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, OECD AI work and the Montevideo Declaration. Domestically, industry, civil society and academia were consulted during strategy development and take part in the sandbox and observatory initiatives, without formal standing roles.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement of AI obligations is not operational: supervision exists only for projects admitted to sandboxes, and sanctions available against AI uses derive from the general data protection regime enforced by URCDP.
Specific Laws: Law 18.331 Personal Data Protection Law (2008), Law 20.212 Articles 74 and 75 (2023), Decreto 276/025 regulating controlled testing environments and data spaces for data and artificial intelligence (2025), National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2030, Agesic AI Regulatory Recommendations (2024), Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (signed September 2025), Artificial Intelligence Strategy for Digital Government (2020)

Regulation Status: Uzbekistan regulates AI through Law No. ZRU-1115 of 21 January 2026, which defines artificial intelligence, bans legally significant decisions taken solely by AI, requires labelling of AI-generated content and adds administrative fines for unlawful AI-based personal data processing, and through the Ethical Rules for the Creation, Implementation and Use of AI-Based Solutions (Order No. 3787, registered 14 March 2026, in force 17 June 2026), which bind every developer, implementer and user of AI in any sector. The framework is horizontal and principle-based rather than risk-tiered: it contains no high-risk classification, conformity assessment or registration regime, and the national AI standards foreseen by the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 have not been issued.
Policy Lever: Policy combines one horizontal binding law, a binding ministerial ethics order, and development instruments: Cabinet Resolution No. 425 of 10 July 2025 on priority AI projects, Decree PF-189 on AI procurement, GPU purchasing and investment allowances, and PP-320's $100 million allocation through the Reconstruction and Development Fund and venture funds. An AI regulatory sandbox remains at the design stage under a UNDP framework guide, and the Enterprise Uzbekistan special legal regime covering AI and regulatory testing takes effect only on 21 January 2027.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Digital Technologies, which drafts legislation and issued the Ethical Rules, with Uzkomnazorat as the supervisory inspectorate and the Coordination Commission for the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy providing inter-agency coordination. The unitary structure leaves no sub-national regulatory role, and independent judicial or ombudsman scrutiny of AI decisions has not materialised.
Actor Involvement: Participation runs through state-convened structures: the Artificial Intelligence Alliance of companies, banks and universities, ministerial consultations during the passage of Law No. ZRU-1115, and expert input from the AI and Digital Economy research centre. Internationally Uzbekistan works with UNESCO on the Recommendation on the Ethics of AI and its Readiness Assessment Methodology and with UNDP on sandbox design, and cooperates within the CIS, while independent domestic civil society has no standing role.
Enforcement Level: Penalties exist only for unlawful AI-based personal data processing, Uzkomnazorat supervises under its general informatisation remit, and no AI-specific enforcement decision or audit programme has been published since the rules took effect.
Specific Laws: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (PP-358, 2024), Law on Amendments and Supplements to Certain Laws in Connection with Artificial Intelligence Regulation No. ZRU-1115 (2026), Ethical Rules for the Creation, Implementation and Use of Artificial Intelligence-Based Solutions No. 3787 (2026), Presidential Decree No. PF-189 on Additional Measures for the Further Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies (2025), Presidential Resolution No. PP-320 on Additional Measures to Support Artificial Intelligence Projects (2025), Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 425 on Priority Projects in the Field of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in 2025-2026 (2025), Law on Informatisation (as amended), Law on Personal Data (as amended by Law No. ZRU-1125, 2026)

Regulation Status: Vanuatu regulates AI through general digital law rather than a dedicated AI instrument: the Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025 names "artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-related data services" as a permit category and gives the Department of Communications and Digital Transformation a statutory function to develop and enforce AI frameworks, while the Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 13 of 2024 grants a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. Coverage is confined to licensing and data protection, with no high-risk, transparency or conformity obligations. Implementing permit regulations, guidance and an operational enforcement body are absent.
Policy Lever: Levers are general digital-governance instruments plus regional principles: permits and penalties under the Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025, data protection rules on automated decisions, and the ethical-AI aspiration in the ICT Policy 2025. There is no AI funding scheme, sandbox, procurement rule, or resourced AI unit.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Department of Communications and Digital Transformation, with the Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulator covering telecoms and the Digital Safety Authority established on paper under Act No. 15 of 2024 but not yet operating. The statutory National Digital Transformation Steering Committee provides cross-government coordination, while provinces, courts and the Ombudsman play no part in shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Engagement is government-led, with industry input through ICT and digital legislation consultations and forum sessions, and universities and community groups appearing only as event participants. Vanuatu's most substantive AI activity is regional: it backed the Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles and pressed for enforceable protection of traditional knowledge used in AI systems at the 2026 Forum ICT Ministers Meeting.
Enforcement Level: Penalties attach to the AI permit category and to data protection breaches, but no AI enforcement action, audit or monitoring has occurred and no resourced authority exercises the powers.
Specific Laws: Digital Transformation Act No. 42 of 2025, Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 13 of 2024, Digital Safety Authority Act No. 15 of 2024, ICT Policy 2025, National Cyber Security Strategy 2030, Pacific Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technology Principles (2026, endorsed)

Regulation Status: Vatican City State regulates AI through one dedicated binding instrument, Decree No. DCCII of the Pontifical Commission (adopted 16 December 2024, in force 1 January 2025), which defines AI, sets principles of human dignity, transparency and data protection, prohibits discriminatory, manipulative and dignity-violating uses, assigns authorship of AI-generated content to the Governorate, and creates a five-member AI Commission. Coverage is institutional rather than horizontal: it binds the Governorate and Vatican City State bodies, not the whole Roman Curia or private actors. The promised follow-up laws and implementing regulations do not appear in the Governorate's published legislation, and the May 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas carries doctrinal rather than civil-law force.
Policy Lever: The lever mix is one binding decree plus an unusually dense body of ethical and doctrinal soft law: the Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020), Antiqua et Nova (2025) and the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026). There are no economic instruments, and institutional capacity rests on two thinly staffed commissions, one inside the Governorate and one spanning seven curial bodies.
Governance Type: Authority is concentrated in the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State and its Governorate, with an internal AI Commission chaired by the Secretary General drawing on the legal, telecommunications and security offices. Coordination across the Holy See runs through the Interdicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence (May 2026), while no subnational layer and no independent judicial or ombudsman review of AI exists.
Actor Involvement: Participation is internally clerical and externally diplomatic: the Pontifical Academies hold standing advisory roles, companies engage by signing the Rome Call for AI Ethics, and the Holy See speaks on AI at the United Nations, UNESCO and the G7. Domestic civil society has no channel into the Vatican's closed legislative process, and the Vatican does not sit in treaty-based technical standards bodies.
Enforcement Level: Prohibitions exist on paper under Decree No. DCCII, but no penalties are specified, the Governorate's AI Commission has published no decisions or monitoring reports, and oversight is limited to internal vetting of AI experimentation.
Specific Laws: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence – Decree No. DCCII of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State (2024, in force 2025), Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020), Antiqua et Nova – Doctrinal Note on Artificial Intelligence (2025), Magnifica Humanitas – Encyclical Letter of Pope Leo XIV on Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence (2026), Interdicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence – Rescript of Cardinal Michael Czerny (2026)
