Regulation Status: Venezuela's AI framework rests on a bill and a ministerial ethics code rather than enacted law: the Proyecto de Ley de Inteligencia Artificial cleared first discussion on 19 November 2024, creating a risk classification and a national AI agency, but has not advanced to second discussion. The Ministry of Science and Technology published the Código de Ética para el Desarrollo y Aplicación Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial on 19 February 2026, setting nine guiding principles without legal force. Binding obligations on AI systems do not exist in any sector.
Policy Lever: Policy runs through executive soft instruments: the 2026 Código de Ética, the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial built on talent formation, sovereign compute infrastructure and an ALBA regional AI agency, and a MINCYT directorate without legal powers. No funded scheme, sandbox or procurement rule for AI has been published.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the national executive, with MINCYT as sole rector and the National Assembly's Comisión Permanente de Educación, Salud, Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación handling the pending bill. Sub-national authorities and independent review bodies play no part.
Actor Involvement: Participation is government-led and outward-facing: ministers present the Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial at UNESCO, WSIS and ALBA fora, while domestic input from private industry, civil society and universities remains limited to announced consultation and training activity. No standing advisory body gives non-state actors a formal seat.
Enforcement Level: Nothing is enforced because no AI obligation is legally binding, and no authority holds an AI supervisory mandate.
Specific Laws: Proyecto de Ley de Inteligencia Artificial (2024, approved in first discussion 19 November 2024, pending second discussion), Código de Ética para el Desarrollo y Aplicación Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial (2026), Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (2025), Special Law Against Cybercrimes (2001)

Regulation Status: Vietnam governs AI through a dedicated horizontal statute, Law No. 134/2025/QH15, in force since 1 March 2026, with a three-tier risk classification, prohibited practices, transparency and deepfake labelling duties, and registration of medium- and high-risk systems through the national one-stop AI portal. Implementing detail arrived with Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP (effective 1 May 2026) and the Prime Minister's high-risk list in Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg (effective 15 August 2026), covering 46 system types across six sectors. Full application is still phased: general compliance deadlines fall on 1 March 2027 and 1 September 2027 for healthcare, education and finance, and the administrative-sanctions decree has not been issued.
Policy Lever: Vietnam combines binding instruments (Law 134/2025/QH15, Decree 142/2026/ND-CP, Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg) with soft-law guidance, notably the National AI Ethics Framework in Circular No. 05/2026/TT-BKHCN and Decision No. 1290/QD-BKHCN on responsible AI research. The Ministry of Science and Technology is the lead institution, operating the one-stop AI portal, self-declaration registration and a controlled sandbox, with fine schedules and exercised compliance powers still outstanding.
Governance Type: AI governance is concentrated in the Ministry of Science and Technology, which classifies, registers and supervises AI systems, with sectoral ministries in health, education, finance and transport applying the Decision 33 high-risk list in their fields and a Prime Minister-chaired National Committee on Artificial Intelligence providing top-level coordination. There is no subnational AI rule-making and no independent regulator or tribunal shaping AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Policy-making is state-led, with formal public consultation on the draft AI Law and implementing decree drawing domestic and foreign industry submissions and expert input from research institutes, while independent civil society has no structured role. Internationally Vietnam is active through ASEAN, hosting the Hanoi Digital Declaration and ASEAN AI safety cooperation, UNESCO ethics implementation, and bilateral AI cooperation with China, Japan and South Korea.
Enforcement Level: The AI Law provides suspension, recall and liability tools with the detailed administrative fine schedule still pending, and no AI-specific enforcement decision has been taken while transition deadlines run into 2027.
Specific Laws: Law on Artificial Intelligence No. 134/2025/QH15 (2025), Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP (2026), Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg on the list of high-risk AI systems (2026), Circular No. 05/2026/TT-BKHCN on the National AI Ethics Framework (2026), Decision No. 1290/QD-BKHCN on responsible AI research and development guidelines (2024), Law on Digital Technology Industry (2025), Decree No. 353/2025/ND-CP on digital technology sandbox (2025), National AI Strategy Decision No. 127/QD-TTg (2021)

Regulation Status: Yemen has no dedicated AI law, national AI strategy or AI regulator, and neither the internationally recognised government in Aden nor the de facto authority in Sana'a has published an AI framework. Digital policy activity is limited to the National Cybersecurity Strategy approved in January 2023, the March 2025 Strategic Orientation towards Digital Transformation Project of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, and a still-unenacted draft law on combating information technology crimes, none of which addresses AI systems. Armed conflict and parallel institutions leave AI unregulated.
Policy Lever: Yemen deploys no AI policy levers: no binding rules, no published guidance, no funding, procurement or sandbox programs, and no body with an AI mandate. Isolated civil-service training on AI tools and donor-supported digital projects are the only AI-adjacent public activity.
Governance Type: AI governance structures are absent, with the ministry that would normally lead digital policy split between the Aden government and the Sana'a authority. Neither subnational bodies nor courts or independent review mechanisms play any part in AI oversight.
Actor Involvement: No structured domestic engagement by industry, civil society or academia in AI policy exists. International involvement is limited to attendance at the 2024 Seoul summit on responsible military AI, UNESCO membership, and UN-convened workshops such as the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen session on AI and the Women, Peace and Security agenda at the Paris AI Action Summit.
Enforcement Level: AI enforcement does not exist: no penalties, authority, actions or monitoring of AI systems are in place anywhere in the country.

Regulation Status: Zambia's AI framework rests on the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched by the Ministry of Technology and Science in November 2024, which sets pillars on policy and regulation, skills, infrastructure, research and sectoral adoption and calls for a National AI Policy, a National AI Council and technical working groups. No AI-specific binding instrument exists or is before Parliament; AI-related conduct falls under the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 and the Cyber Security Act No. 3 of 2025 and Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, which replaced the Cyber Security and Cyber Crimes Act of 2021 and contain no provisions written for AI systems.
Policy Lever: Policy action is limited to a non-binding national strategy and its planned advisory structures, coordinated by the Ministry of Technology and Science with the Smart Zambia Institute. No AI-specific binding instrument, published guidance, procurement rule or regulatory sandbox is in operation.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralized in the Ministry of Technology and Science, supported by the Smart Zambia Institute and ZICTA, with the National AI Council and technical working groups envisaged by the strategy as the coordination mechanism. Provinces and districts play no role, and no court or independent review body has shaped AI rules.
Actor Involvement: Government-convened consultations have brought industry, academia, civil society, youth and development partners into strategy design and into the UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology 2.0 exercise held in June 2026, but none of these actors holds a standing formal role. Internationally, Zambia works through UNESCO, the African Union Continental AI Strategy and the Smart Africa Alliance rather than binding AI treaties.
Enforcement Level: No AI-specific obligations, sanctions or enforcement decisions exist, and oversight is confined to general cyber security and data protection regulators plus one-off readiness assessment work.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2026 (launched November 2024), Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021, Cyber Security Act No. 3 of 2025, Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, National ICT Policy (2023)

Regulation Status: Zimbabwe governs AI through the non-binding National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026–2030, approved by Cabinet in October 2025 and launched by President Mnangagwa at Parliament on 13 March 2026. The strategy's Pillar 4 promises a National AI Act with a risk-based framework and national AI technical standards, but no AI bill has been drafted or tabled. Binding obligations touching AI come only from the Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] (2021) and its 2024 licensing regulations, which address personal data generally.
Policy Lever: Policy action rests on a single soft-law instrument, the National AI Strategy 2026–2030, supplemented by data-protection law, with flagship economic initiatives — the Innovation Crucible sandbox, Project Pangolin and the Mugove/Umqele/Isabelo fund — announced but not yet funded or operating. Institutional capacity is limited to ministry-led coordination structures without legal AI powers.
Governance Type: AI governance is centralised in the Ministry of Information Communication Technology, Postal and Courier Services, with POTRAZ serving as data protection authority and host of the strategy's Steering Committee. A formal architecture — National Digital Regulatory Committee chaired by the President, National AI Council, AI Strategy Implementation Office, Technical Working Groups — is designed on paper, while subnational and independent-review roles are absent.
Actor Involvement: Industry, civil society, academia, diaspora representatives and development partners were consulted in 2025 workshops in Kadoma, Harare, Bulawayo and Masvingo that fed the strategy, but participation has been episodic rather than institutionalised. International engagement runs through UNESCO readiness assessment support, United Nations partnership, and African Union and SADC processes rather than binding instruments.
Enforcement Level: Enforcement touching AI exists only through POTRAZ's data protection mandate, whose mandatory controller inspections started on 1 September 2026, with no AI-specific penalties, decisions or audits.
Specific Laws: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026–2030 (2026), Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] (2021), Cyber and Data Protection (Licensing of Data Controllers and Appointment of Data Protection Officers) Regulations (2024), Postal and Telecommunications Act [Chapter 12:05]
